The group is the 9 in the box. The ones left over are the remainder.
The full box has 9 marbles in it. The ones left over are the remainder.

practice.question: You have 12 marbles and a box that holds 9. How many are left over?
practice.why: 9 go in the box. 12 − 9 = 3 are left over.
wrong: 9 is how many go in the box. Count the ones left over.
12 is all the marbles. Take away the 9 in the box.
You added 12 and 9. Take away: 12 − 9.

practice.question: You have 9 marbles and a box that holds 9. What is the remainder?
practice.why: All 9 marbles go in the box. Nothing is left over, so the remainder is 0.
wrong: The 9 marbles are in the box. None are left over.
The box is full and no marble is left over.
You added 9 and 9. Take away: 9 − 9.

practice.question: You have 7 sweets and a plate that holds 5. You fill the plate. What is the remainder?
practice.why: 5 sweets go on the plate. 7 − 5 = 2 are left over.
wrong: 5 is how many go on the plate. Count the ones left over.
You added 7 and 5. Take away: 7 − 5.
7 is all the sweets. Take away the 5 on the plate.

rounds.question: You have 10 eggs. A tray holds 6. You fill the tray. 4 eggs are left over. What is the 4 called?
rounds.why: The eggs left over are called the remainder.
wrong: The tray holds the eggs. The left over eggs are the remainder.
The full tray has 6 eggs. The 4 left over are the remainder.
The group is the 6 in the tray. The 4 left over are the remainder.

rounds.question: You have 14 pencils and a box that holds 10. You fill the box. How many are left over?
rounds.why: 10 pencils go in the box. 14 − 10 = 4 are left over.
wrong: 10 is how many go in the box. Count the ones left over.
14 is all the pencils. Take away the 10 in the box.
You added 14 and 10. Take away: 14 − 10.

rounds.question: You have 6 bananas and a bag that holds 6. You fill the bag. What is the remainder?
rounds.why: All 6 bananas go in the bag. Nothing is left over, so the remainder is 0.
wrong: 6 is how many go in the bag. None are left over.
No banana is left over. 6 − 6 = 0.
You added 6 and 6. Take away: 6 − 6 = 0.

rounds.question: You have 8 books and a shelf that holds 5. You fill the shelf. What is the remainder?
rounds.why: 5 books go on the shelf. 8 − 5 = 3 are left over.
wrong: 5 is how many go on the shelf. Count the ones left over.
8 is all the books. Take away the 5 on the shelf.
You added 8 and 5. Take away: 8 − 5.

rounds.question: What is the remainder?
rounds.why: The things that do not fit and are left over are called the remainder.
wrong: The things in the box fit. The remainder is what is left over.
The box holds things. The remainder is what is left over.
Some things go in the box. Only the left over ones are the remainder.

rounds.question: You have 11 crayons and a box that holds 8. You fill the box. How many are left over?
rounds.why: 8 crayons go in the box. 11 − 8 = 3 are left over.
wrong: 8 is how many go in the box. Count the ones left over.
11 is all the crayons. Take away the 8 in the box.
You added 11 and 8. Take away: 11 − 8.

rounds.question: A box holds 5 toys. Which number of toys leaves a remainder of 0?
rounds.why: 5 toys fill the box and nothing is left over. So the remainder is 0.
wrong: With 6 toys, 1 is left over.
With 7 toys, 2 are left over.
With 8 toys, 3 are left over.

rounds.question: Dad has 15 mangoes and a basket that holds 10. He fills the basket. What is the remainder?
rounds.why: 10 mangoes go in the basket. 15 − 10 = 5 are left over.
wrong: 10 is how many go in the basket. Count the ones left over.
15 is all the mangoes. Take away the 10 in the basket.
You added 15 and 10. Take away: 15 − 10.

entries.concept: what partial fractions are and why we want them
entries.evidence: The first lesson opens with '(px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) means…' without saying what splitting a fraction is or what it is for.

screens.title: Adding fractions, run backwards
text: You know how to add 1/2 + 1/3: over the common denominator 6 it is 5/6. Now go backwards: 5/6 can be split into the simpler pieces 1/2 and 1/3.
The same works with x. Adding 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x + 1) over the common denominator (x − 1)(x + 1) gives 2x/((x − 1)(x + 1)).
Partial fractions is the backward journey: start with one fraction whose denominator factorises, and split it into simple fractions, one for each factor. The unknown tops are called A and B.
We do this because the simple pieces are much easier to work with later, for example when integrating.

check.question: Which single fraction do the pieces 1/2 and 1/3 add up to?

screens.ask: Split 2x/((x − 1)(x + 1)) into A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 1).

why: This clears all the fractions. On the right, each bottom cancels with one of the two brackets.

steps.do: Choose x = 1 to make the B term vanish.
why: The equation is true for every x, so we may pick handy values. x = 1 makes (x − 1) zero, so B disappears.

steps.do: Choose x = −1 to make the A term vanish.
why: x = −1 makes (x + 1) zero, so only B is left.
Check by adding them back: the top becomes (x + 1) + (x − 1) = 2x.

practice.question: Splitting one fraction into simple fractions, one for each factor of its denominator, is called
practice.why: Partial fractions is adding fractions run backwards: one fraction is split into simple pieces.
wrong: That is used when adding fractions, the forward journey.
Integrating is what the pieces are useful for later, not the splitting itself.
Factorising the denominator is only the first step. The splitting is partial fractions.

practice.question: 7/10 is split into two simple pieces with denominators 2 and 5. What are they?
wrong: The tops add to 7, but 15/10 + 8/10 = 23/10. Use a common denominator.
7 and 10 are the top and bottom of the answer, not the denominators of the pieces.

practice.question: Which is the right way to set up partial fractions for 5/((x − 2)(x + 3))?
practice.why: One simple fraction for each factor, added, with unknown tops A and B.
wrong: The pieces are added, not multiplied.
This is still one fraction. Each factor gets its own fraction.
The factors keep their signs: x − 2 and x + 3.

practice.question: 4/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 1), so 4 = A(x + 1) + B(x − 1). Put x = 1. What is A?
practice.why: At x = 1 the B term is 0: 4 = A × 2, so A = 2.
wrong: At x = 1, x + 1 is 2, so 4 = 2A. Divide by 2.
That is B, found by putting x = −1. With x = 1 you get A = 2.
You divided the wrong way. 4 = 2A gives A = 4 ÷ 2.

rounds.question: In A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 1), what are A and B?
options: The unknown tops of the simple fractions
The values of x to put in
rounds.why: A and B are the unknown tops of the simple fractions. Finding them is the job.
wrong: The factors are x − 1 and x + 1, on the bottom.
The common denominator is (x − 1)(x + 1).
The values put in for x are numbers such as 1 and −1. A and B are the tops.

rounds.question: 8/15 is split into two simple pieces with denominators 3 and 5. What are they?
wrong: The denominators must be 3 and 5, the factors of 15.
You halved the top 8 and put 4 on each piece. That adds to 32/15.

rounds.question: Which is the right way to set up partial fractions for 3x/((x + 1)(x − 4))?
rounds.why: There is one simple fraction for each factor, added, with unknown tops: A/(x + 1) + B/(x − 4).
wrong: The signs in the factors changed. Keep x + 1 and x − 4.
The simple fractions are added, not multiplied.
The top 3x is not copied onto each piece. The tops are unknowns A and B.

rounds.question: 9/((x − 2)(x + 1)) = A/(x − 2) + B/(x + 1), so 9 = A(x + 1) + B(x − 2). Put x = 2. What is A?
rounds.why: At x = 2 the B term is 0, leaving 9 = A × 3. So A = 3.
wrong: 9 = 3A, so divide by 3.
−3 is B, found by putting x = −1. Putting x = 2 gives A.
You divided 3 by 9. From 9 = 3A, A = 9 ÷ 3.

rounds.question: Why do we split a fraction into partial fractions?
options: The simple pieces are easier to work with later
rounds.why: The simple pieces are much easier to work with later, for example when integrating.
wrong: The denominators get simpler, not bigger.
x stays in the simple pieces.
Finding a common denominator is adding. Partial fractions go the other way.

rounds.question: 2/(x − 1) + 1/(x + 1) is added over the common denominator (x − 1)(x + 1). What is the top?
wrong: You just added the tops 2 and 1. Each top is multiplied by the other denominator first.
A sign slipped: 2 − 1 = 1, so the number is +1.
You multiplied both tops by (x + 1). The second is multiplied by (x − 1).

rounds.question: 7 = A(x + 3) + B(x − 4). Which value of x makes the B term disappear?
rounds.why: At x = 4 the bracket (x − 4) is 0, so the B term is 0.
wrong: At x = −4, x − 4 = −8, not 0. Watch the sign.
x = −3 makes the A term disappear, not the B term.
At x = 0 neither bracket is 0.

rounds.question: 5/((x − 3)(x + 2)) = A/(x − 3) + B/(x + 2), so 5 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 3). Put x = −2. What is B?
rounds.why: At x = −2 the A term is 0, leaving 5 = B × (−5). So B = −1.
wrong: The bracket is −2 − 3 = −5, so B is negative.
5 = −5B, so divide by −5.
−5 is the value of the bracket. B = 5 ÷ (−5) = −1.

entries.concept: the letter n for 'any place' in a pattern
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'the n-th number is n − 1 jumps after it' but no earlier lesson says what the letter n stands for.

screens.title: n means any place you like
text: Children stand in a line: 1st, 2nd, 3rd. Each one has a place number.
We write n for any place you choose. Place n means that place, whichever it is.

check.question: If n is 7, what is n − 1?

screens.ask: Pattern: {@m}, {m2}, {m3}, {m4}, … What number is in place {@p}?

why: Each place holds its place number times {m}.
n stands for any place, so one rule covers them all.
Check the rule on a place you can see before you trust it.
Place {p} holds {p} times {m}, which is {ans}.

after: n − 1 means one less than the place. If n is 5, then n − 1 is 4.

practice.question: If n is 6, which number is 'the n-th number'?
practice.why: The n-th number is the number in place n. With n = 6 that is the 6th number.
wrong: That is place n − 1. The n-th number is in place 6.
That is one place too far. The n-th number is in place 6.
n is 6 here, so it is the 6th place, not the 1st.

practice.question: If n is 9, what is n − 1?
practice.why: n − 1 is one less than n: 9 − 1 = 8.
wrong: You added 1. The sign − means take away: 9 − 1.
That is n itself. n − 1 is one less.
1 is the number taken away. Work out 9 − 1.

practice.question: In a pattern, the number in place n is n × 2. Which place has the number 10?
practice.why: 5 × 2 = 10, so the number 10 stands in place 5.
wrong: 10 is the number, not its place. Find n with n × 2 = 10.
You multiplied 10 by 2. Find the place n with n × 2 = 10.
You took 2 away from 10. The rule multiplies: n × 2 = 10.

practice.question: Children stand in a line. The child in place n gets n + 2 sweets. How many sweets does the 4th child get?
practice.why: Here n is 4, so n + 2 = 4 + 2 = 6.
wrong: You multiplied 4 by 2. The rule is n + 2.
The 2 is not written beside the 4. Add: 4 + 2.
You took away. The rule adds: 4 + 2.

rounds.question: What do we write when we mean any place in a pattern?
rounds.why: To talk about any place at all, we write the letter n instead of a number.
wrong: 0 is one fixed number. n can stand for any place.
The first number is only place 1. n can be any place.
The biggest number is only one place. n can be any place.

rounds.question: If n is 12, what is n − 1?
rounds.why: n − 1 means one less than n. One less than 12 is 11.
wrong: 13 is one more than 12. n − 1 is one less.
12 is n itself. Take 1 away.
1 is what you take away. The answer is 12 − 1.

rounds.question: In a pattern, the number in place n is n × 3. What is the 5th number?
rounds.why: For the 5th number, n is 5. So it is 5 × 3 = 15.
wrong: You added 5 + 3. The rule says n × 3.
You wrote 5 and 3 side by side. The rule says 5 × 3.
5 is the place. The number in that place is 5 × 3.

rounds.question: Pots stand in a row. The pot in place n has n + 3 flowers. How many flowers does the 6th pot have?
rounds.why: For the 6th pot, n is 6. So it has 6 + 3 = 9 flowers.
wrong: You did 6 × 3. The rule says n + 3.
You wrote 6 and 3 side by side. The rule says 6 + 3.
3 is only the part added. The 6th pot has 6 + 3.

rounds.question: What does 'the n-th number' mean?
rounds.why: 'The n-th number' means the number standing in place n of the pattern.
wrong: n is the place. The n-th number is what stands in that place.
It is the number in place n, not the one after.
Nothing is added. It is the one number in place n.

rounds.question: If n − 1 is 6, what is n?
rounds.why: n − 1 is one less than n. So n is one more than 6, which is 7.
wrong: You took 1 away again. n is one more than n − 1.
6 is n − 1. n is one more.
1 is what was taken away. n is 6 + 1.

rounds.question: In a pattern, the number in place n is n × 5. Which place has the number 20?
rounds.why: We need n × 5 = 20. Since 4 × 5 = 20, it is place 4.
wrong: 20 is the number, not the place. Find n so that n × 5 = 20.
You did 20 × 5. Find n so that n × 5 = 20.
You took 5 from 20. Find n so that n × 5 = 20.

rounds.question: Steps go up a hill. Step n is n × 10 cm above the ground. How high is step 7?
rounds.why: For step 7, n is 7. So it is 7 × 10 = 70 cm high.
wrong: You added 7 + 10. The rule says n × 10.
You wrote 7 and 10 side by side. The rule says 7 × 10.
You used n − 1, which is 6. Step 7 uses n = 7.

entries.concept: the factorial sign n!
entries.evidence: The permutations lesson writes ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)! several lessons before the factorial sign is explained.

screens.title: What the ! sign means
text: Three friends stand in a row for a photo. The first place can be filled in 3 ways, the next in 2 ways, and the last in 1 way: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 rows.
Products like this, counting down to 1, come up so often that they have a short sign. n! is read 'n factorial' and means n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1.
So 3! = 6, 4! = 24 and 5! = 120. Also 1! = 1, and by agreement 0! = 1.
A big factorial contains the smaller ones: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3!. That is why factorials cancel so neatly in fractions.

check.question: What is 3!?

why: ! means multiply all the whole numbers from that number down to 1.
5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, and the part after 5 is 4!. So reuse 24.
Write 5! as 5 × 4 × 3!. The 3! on top and bottom cancel.

practice.question: What does 4! mean?
practice.why: n! is the product counting down to 1, so 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
wrong: A factorial multiplies the numbers, it does not add them.
That is 4 squared. 4! counts down: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
All the numbers in between are multiplied too: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.

practice.question: 5! = 120. What is 6!?
wrong: You added 6. A bigger factorial multiplies: 6 × 120.
You added 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1. A factorial multiplies.

practice.question: What is 6!/4!?
practice.why: 6! = 6 × 5 × 4!, so the 4! cancels and 6 × 5 = 30 is left.
wrong: You cannot cancel the ! signs and do 6 ÷ 4. Write 6! as 6 × 5 × 4! first.
You subtracted 6 − 4. Cancel the 4! instead: 6 × 5 is left.
You added 6 and 5. The numbers left after cancelling are multiplied.

practice.question: In how many ways can 5 different books stand in a row on a shelf?
practice.why: The places can be filled in 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 ways: 5! = 120.
wrong: That is 5 × 5. The choices go down each time: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
You added 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1. The choices are multiplied.
5 is only the choices for the first place. Multiply by the choices for the others.

rounds.question: How is n! read?
rounds.why: n! is read 'n factorial'. It means n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1.
wrong: n squared is n × n. The sign ! means factorial.
n! counts down to 1: n × (n − 1) × … × 1. It is read 'n factorial'.
Nothing is added. n! is read 'n factorial'.

rounds.question: 6! = 720. What is 7!?
wrong: You added 7. A bigger factorial multiplies: 7 × 6!.
7 × 7 is 7 squared. 7! = 7 × 6!.
You multiplied by 6. 7! = 7 × 6!.

rounds.question: What is 0!?
rounds.why: By agreement, 0! = 1.
wrong: 0! is not 0. By agreement it is 1.
It does have a value: by agreement 0! = 1.
A factorial is never negative. By agreement 0! = 1.

rounds.question: In how many orders can 4 different pictures hang in a row on a wall?
rounds.why: The places can be filled in 4, 3, 2 and 1 ways: 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
wrong: You did 4 × 4. Each place has one fewer choice: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
You added 4 + 3 + 2 + 1. The choices are multiplied.
4 is only the choices for the first place. Multiply on: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.

rounds.question: Which statement is true?
wrong: The 5 multiplies 4!. It is not added.
5 × 5! is 600, not 120. Use the smaller factorial 4!.

rounds.question: What is 3! + 2!?
wrong: You added 3 and 2 first and took 5!. Work out each factorial, then add.
You multiplied 6 and 2. The sign between them is +.
You added 3 and 2 without the factorials. 3! = 6 and 2! = 2.

rounds.question: What is 8!/6!?
wrong: You cancelled the ! signs to get 8/6. Write 8! as 8 × 7 × 6! first.
You took 6 from 8. Write 8! as 8 × 7 × 6! and cancel.
You added 8 and 6. Write 8! as 8 × 7 × 6! and cancel.

rounds.question: In how many orders can 6 beads of different colours be put in a row on a string?
rounds.why: The places can be filled in 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 ways: 6! = 720.
wrong: You did 6 × 6. Each place has one fewer choice: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
You added 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1. The choices are multiplied.
6 is only the choices for the first place. Multiply on down to 1.

entries.concept: the name p(x), the value p(2), and quotient and remainder for polynomials
entries.evidence: The lesson on dividing a cubic writes 'p(x) = (x − r) × quotient + remainder' before any lesson says what p(x) means or what dividing one polynomial by another gives.

screens.title: p(x) is a name, p(2) is a value
text: p(x) = x² + {@b}x gives the expression x² + {b}x a short name. Read p(x) as 'p of x'. It does not mean p times x.

check.question: p(x) = 2x + 1. What is p(3)?

screens.ask: Find p({@a}), p(0) and p(1).

why: p({a}) means: put {a} in place of every x.
Every term has an x in it, so with x = 0 everything is 0.
1 × 1 is 1 and {b} × 1 is {b}. Add them.

after: p({a}) = {v} is called the value of p(x) at x = {a}.

screens.title: Dividing leaves a quotient and a remainder
text: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, because 5 × 3 is 15 and 2 is left. Polynomials divide the same way.

check.question: In 17 = 5 × 3 + 2, which number is the remainder?

screens.ask: Divide x² + {@s}x + {@c} by x + {@d}.

why: x × (x + {d}) = {if d = 1}x² + x{else}x² + {d}x{end}. Take that away. {q}x + {c} is left.
{q} × (x + {d}) = {q}x + {dq}. Take that away: {c} − {dq} = {r} is left.
Like 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2: an answer and something left over.

steps.do: Check: multiply back, add the remainder.
why: Divisor × quotient + remainder gives back what we divided.

screens.note: Pick numbers that leave a remainder of 0 or more.
after: Dividing by x + {d} gave a quotient, x + {q}, and a remainder, {r}.
x² + {s}x + {c} = (x + {d}) × (x + {q}) + {r}. You can always check a division this way.

practice.question: What does p(3) mean?
options: Put 3 in place of every x and work it out
practice.why: p(3) is the value of the expression p(x) when x is 3.
wrong: The bracket is not multiplication. Put 3 in place of x.
Nothing is added. Put 3 in place of x.
Nothing is divided. Put 3 in place of x.

practice.question: p(x) = 4x + 3. What is p(2)?
wrong: You added 4 + 2 + 3. 4x means 4 × x.
You wrote 4 and 2 side by side as 42. 4x means 4 × 2.
You added 2 + 3 first. Multiply 4 × 2, then add 3.

practice.question: p(x) = x² + 2x. What is p(3)?
wrong: You took x² as 3 × 2. x² means 3 × 3 = 9.
You added 2 instead of 2 × 3. Put 3 in place of every x.
You wrote 2x as 23. 2x means 2 × 3.

practice.question: 23 sweets are packed 4 to a box: 23 = 4 × 5 + 3. What is the remainder?
practice.why: 5 boxes use 20 sweets, and 3 are left over. The left-over number is the remainder.
wrong: 5 is the quotient, the number of full boxes.
4 is the number you divide by.
23 is the number being divided. The remainder is what is left over.

rounds.question: How is p(x) read?
rounds.why: p(x) is read 'p of x'. It is a short name for an expression that has x in it.
wrong: p(x) does not mean p times x. It is a name, read 'p of x'.
Nothing is added. It is a name, read 'p of x'.
x is not a power here. It is a name, read 'p of x'.

rounds.question: p(x) = 5x − 2. What is p(3)?
rounds.why: Put 3 in place of x: 5 × 3 − 2 = 15 − 2 = 13.
wrong: You wrote 5 and 3 side by side as 53. 5x means 5 × x.
You added 5 and 3. 5x means 5 × x.
You added 2 instead of taking it away.

rounds.question: p(x) = x² + 5. What is p(4)?
rounds.why: Put 4 in place of x: 4 × 4 + 5 = 16 + 5 = 21.
wrong: You did 4 × 2. x² means x × x.
You wrote 4 and 2 side by side as 42. x² means 4 × 4.
You added 4 and 5 first and then squared. Square 4 first, then add 5.

rounds.question: 30 bananas are packed 7 to a bag: 30 = 7 × 4 + 2. What is the quotient?
rounds.why: 7 goes into 30 four times. The number of times is the quotient: 4.
wrong: 2 is what is left over, the remainder.
7 is the number you divide by.
30 is the number being divided.

rounds.question: 19 divided by 6 is written 19 = 6 × 3 + 1. What is the 1 called?
rounds.why: The 1 is what is left over after dividing. It is the remainder.
wrong: The quotient is 3, the number of times 6 goes in.
A value comes from putting a number in place of x. The left over part is the remainder.
6 does not divide 19 exactly. The 1 left over is the remainder.

rounds.question: p(x) = 2x + 7. What is p(5)?
rounds.why: Put 5 in place of x: 2 × 5 + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17.
wrong: You wrote 2 and 5 side by side as 25. 2x means 2 × x.
You added 2 + 5 + 7. 2x means 2 × x.
You added 5 and 7 first. Multiply 2 × 5, then add 7.

rounds.question: x² + 5x + 9 is divided by x + 2. The quotient is x + 3, and (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 5x + 6. What is the remainder?
rounds.why: Multiplying back gives x² + 5x + 6. To reach x² + 5x + 9 you must add 3, so the remainder is 3.
wrong: 6 comes from multiplying back. The remainder is what must still be added: 9 − 6.
9 is the last number of the polynomial. The remainder is 9 − 6.
You added 9 and 6. The remainder is the gap between them.

rounds.question: The cost in rupees of x pens is p(x) = 3x. What is p(6)?
rounds.why: Put 6 in place of x: 3 × 6 = 18 rupees.
wrong: You added 3 and 6. 3x means 3 × x.
You wrote 3 and 6 side by side. 3x means 3 × 6.
You divided 6 by 3. 3x means 3 × x.

entries.concept: the number i, complex numbers a + bi, conjugates and the set ℂ
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'The quadratic formula works over ℂ … √(b² − 4ac) = i√(4ac − b²) … a conjugate pair' without introducing i, ℂ or conjugates.

screens.title: A new number: i
text: The square of any real number is 0 or positive: 3 × 3 = 9 and (−3) × (−3) = 9. So no real number has square −1, and x² = −1 has no real solution.
Mathematicians add one new number to fix this. It is called i, and its defining property is i² = −1.
With i, every negative number gets a square root. (3i)² = 9 × i² = −9, so √(−9) = 3i. In general, for a positive number k, √(−k) = i√k.

check.question: What is √(−16)?

screens.ask: Write √(−4), √(−25) and √(−31) using i.

why: No ordinary number squared is negative. So we name a new number i with i² = −1, that is, i = √(−1).
Split off the −1: the square root of a negative number is the root of its size, times i.
25 is a perfect square, so the answer is a whole number times i.
31 is not a perfect square, so the root stays as √31, with i written after it. The i is outside the root: it is not √(31i).

screens.title: Complex numbers and conjugate pairs
text: A number of the form a + bi, with a and b real, is called a complex number. a is its real part and b is its imaginary part. The set of all complex numbers is written ℂ.
Changing the sign of the i part gives the conjugate: the conjugate of a + bi is a − bi. Together they are a conjugate pair.
A conjugate pair has a real sum and a real product: the sum is 2a and the product is a² + b², because (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² − b² × i² = a² + b².
The ± in the quadratic formula produces exactly such a pair when the discriminant is negative.

check.question: What is the conjugate of 4 + 7i?

screens.ask: Solve x² + 2x + 5 = 0.

why: It is negative, so there are no real roots. With i we can still go on.
√16 = 4, and the minus sign becomes i.
Divide both parts by 2: −2 ÷ 2 = −1 and 4i ÷ 2 = 2i.
The two roots differ only in the sign of the i part. Such a pair is called conjugate.
Adding, the ±2i parts cancel. Multiplying (−1 + 2i)(−1 − 2i) gives 1 − 4i² = 1 + 4.

practice.question: What is i²?
practice.why: i is defined by the property i² = −1.
wrong: That is the square of a real number like 1 or −1. i is the new number with i² = −1.
Squaring i does not leave it unchanged. i² = −1.
The square of i is a real number: −1.

practice.question: What is √(−49)?
wrong: (−7)² = 49, not −49. The square root of a negative number needs i.
Take the square root of 49 as well: √49 = 7.

practice.question: What is the conjugate of 3 − 5i?
practice.why: Change the sign of the i part only: 3 − 5i becomes 3 + 5i.
wrong: You changed the sign of the real part. Only the i part changes.
You changed both signs. The real part stays as it is.
The parts are not swapped. Only the sign of the i part changes.

practice.question: What is the product (2 + 3i)(2 − 3i)?
practice.why: A conjugate pair has product a² + b² = 4 + 9 = 13.
wrong: That is a² − b². Since i² = −1, the product is a² + b².
That is the sum of the pair, 2a. The product is a² + b².
i² is −1, not i: −9 × i² = +9, so the product is 4 + 9.

rounds.question: In the complex number 4 + 7i, what is the 7 called?
rounds.why: In a + bi, the number b in front of i is the imaginary part. Here it is 7.
wrong: The real part is 4, the part without i.
The conjugate is the whole number 4 − 7i.
The discriminant is b² − 4ac of a quadratic.

rounds.question: What is √(−36)?
wrong: (−6)² = 36, not −36. The root needs i.
Take the square root of 36 as well: √36 = 6.
You halved 36. The square root of 36 is 6.

rounds.question: What is the conjugate of −2 + 4i?
rounds.why: Change only the sign of the i part. The conjugate of −2 + 4i is −2 − 4i.
wrong: Both signs were changed. Only the i part changes sign.
The real part changed sign. Only the i part changes sign.
The two parts were swapped. Keep −2 and change the sign of 4i.

rounds.question: What is the sum (5 + 2i) + (5 − 2i)?
rounds.why: The i parts cancel: 2i − 2i = 0. The sum is 5 + 5 = 10, which is 2a.
wrong: 2i and −2i cancel. They do not add to 4i.
25 is 5 × 5. The question asks for the sum.
29 is the product, 25 + 4. The question asks for the sum.

rounds.question: Why does x² = −1 have no real solution?
options: The square of any real number is 0 or positive
x² is always bigger than x
rounds.why: A real number times itself is 0 or positive, so it can never equal −1.
wrong: −1 being whole or not does not matter. No real square is negative.
That is not always true, and it is not the reason. No real square is negative.
Real numbers can be negative. It is their squares that cannot.

rounds.question: What is (5i)²?
wrong: i² is −1, not 1. So the answer is negative.
i × i is i², which is −1. No i is left.
The 5 is squared too: 5 × 5 = 25.

rounds.question: What is √(−7)?
rounds.why: For a positive number k, √(−k) = i√k. So √(−7) = i√7.
wrong: (−√7)² = 7, not −7. The root needs i.
(7i)² = −49, not −7. Keep the square root: i√7.
(√7)² = 7, not −7. The root needs i.

rounds.question: x² + 4x + 13 = 0 has b² − 4ac = 16 − 52 = −36. What are its solutions?
wrong: You did not divide by 2a = 2.
Both parts are divided by 2: 6i ÷ 2 = 3i.
The formula starts with −b, which is −4. So the real part is −2.

entries.concept: a quadratic equation, its a, b, c, and the quadratic formula behind b² − 4ac
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'For ax² + bx + c = 0, work out the discriminant b² − 4ac', but no lesson states the quadratic formula that this comes from (the quadratics skill teaches only factorising, yet asks formula questions).

screens.title: A quadratic equation and its a, b and c
text: Multiply out (x − {@p})(x − {@q}). You get x² − {s}x + {c}.
An equation whose highest power is x² is a quadratic equation.

check.question: In 3x² + 4x − 7 = 0, what is c?

screens.ask: For x² − {s}x + {c} = 0, name a, b and c. Then test whether {p}, {q} and {t} are roots.

steps.do: Read off a, b and c.
why: The form is ax² + bx + c = 0. a goes with x², b goes with x, and c stands alone.
x² alone means 1x². The minus sign belongs to b: b is −{s}, not {s}.
A root makes the equation true. Put it in place of x and see if you get 0.
It gives 0 too, so {q} is also a root. A quadratic can have two roots.
{v} is not 0, so {t} does not make the equation true. It is not a root.

screens.note: Make the second number bigger than the first.
after: Every quadratic can be written ax² + bx + c = 0, the standard form. Each number keeps its sign. A missing term has number 0.
A root (or solution) is a value of x that makes the equation true.

screens.title: The formula, and why b² − 4ac decides
text: There is one formula that solves every quadratic equation: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ (2a). The sign ± means do it twice, once with + and once with −.
The number under the square root, b² − 4ac, is called the discriminant.

If it is positive, the + and the − give two different answers. If it is 0, adding or taking away 0 changes nothing, so there is one answer. If it is negative, it has no real square root, so there is no real answer.
So you can count the solutions from b² − 4ac alone, before solving.

check.question: If b² − 4ac = 0, how many different solutions are there?

screens.ask: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 with the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.

why: Take each with its sign. b is −5.
(−5)² is −5 × −5 = 25: a minus times a minus is a plus.
This number under the root is called the discriminant. It decides how many answers there are.
If the discriminant were negative there would be no real square root, and so no real solution. If it were 0 there would be just one.
−b is −(−5) = 5. The ± sign means do it twice: once adding the root, once subtracting it.
2a is 2 × 1 = 2. The two answers, 3 and 2, are the roots found by testing on the screen before.

practice.question: What is the number b² − 4ac called?
practice.why: The number under the square root in the quadratic formula, b² − 4ac, is the discriminant.
wrong: A root is a value of x that solves the equation.
The standard form is the equation written as ax² + bx + c = 0.
The formula is the whole expression for x. b² − 4ac is only the part under the root.

practice.question: In 2x² − 3x + 5 = 0, what is b?
practice.why: b is the number in front of x, and it keeps its sign: −3.
wrong: b keeps its sign. The term is −3x.
That is a, the number in front of x².
That is c, the number on its own.

practice.question: In x² − 9 = 0, what is b?
practice.why: There is no x term, so the number in front of x is 0.
wrong: −9 is the number on its own, so it is c.
That is a, the number in front of x².
9 has no x with it, so it is c (with its sign, −9). The x term is missing.

practice.question: How many real solutions does x² + 4x + 5 = 0 have?
practice.why: b² − 4ac = 16 − 20 = −4. It is negative, so there is no real square root and no real solution.
wrong: You added 16 and 20. The discriminant subtracts: 16 − 20.
You did 20 − 16. The order is b² − 4ac = 16 − 20 = −4.
The value is right, but a negative discriminant gives no real solution. One solution needs 0.

rounds.question: The form ax² + bx + c = 0 is called
rounds.why: Every quadratic equation can be arranged as ax² + bx + c = 0. This is the standard form.
wrong: The discriminant is the number b² − 4ac.
The quadratic formula gives x. This is the form of the equation.
A root is a value of x that makes the equation true.

rounds.question: In 3x² + 7x − 4 = 0, what is c?
rounds.why: c is the number on its own, and it keeps its sign. Here c = −4.
wrong: c keeps its sign. The number on its own is −4.
7 is b, the number in front of x.
3 is a, the number in front of x².

rounds.question: In x² − 4x + 1 = 0, what is a?
rounds.why: x² means 1x². So the number in front of x² is 1.
wrong: a is 0 only if there is no x² term. x² means 1x².
2 is the power, not the number in front.
−4 is b, the number in front of x.

rounds.question: How many real solutions does x² − 6x + 9 = 0 have?
rounds.why: b² − 4ac = 36 − 36 = 0. Adding or taking away √0 changes nothing, so there is one answer.
wrong: You added 36 and 36. It is 36 − 4 × 1 × 9 = 0.
A discriminant of 0 gives one answer. 'None' needs a negative one.
A discriminant of 0 gives one answer. 'Two' needs a positive one.

rounds.question: A value of x that makes a quadratic equation true is called
rounds.why: A solution of the equation is also called a root.
wrong: The discriminant is b² − 4ac. It only counts the roots.
The standard form is the way the equation is arranged.
c is the number on its own in the equation.

rounds.question: Is x = 4 a root of x² − 5x + 4 = 0?
rounds.why: Put x = 4: 16 − 20 + 4 = 0. The equation is true, so 4 is a root.
wrong: The middle term is −5x, so 20 is taken away.

rounds.question: What is b² − 4ac for x² + 3x − 4 = 0?
wrong: c is −4, so −4ac is +16, not −16.
You forgot the 4 in 4ac: it is 9 + 16, not 9 + 4.
5 is the square root of the discriminant. The discriminant is 25.

rounds.question: How many real solutions does 2x² + 3x + 1 = 0 have?
rounds.why: b² − 4ac = 9 − 4 × 2 × 1 = 1. It is positive, so there are two solutions.
wrong: A positive discriminant gives two answers. One answer needs 0.
b² is 3 × 3 = 9, not 3 × 2. So it is 9 − 8 = 1.
4ac is taken away: 9 − 8, not 9 + 8.

entries.concept: what a relation is, in everyday terms
entries.evidence: The first lesson defines a relation only as 'any subset of A × B', with nothing to say what a relation is for.

screens.title: A relation is a list of who goes with whom
text: 'Is the sister of', 'lives in', 'is less than': each of these links some things to other things. Maths calls such a link a relation.
To record one link we write an ordered pair (a, b), meaning 'a is related to b'. The order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different pairs.
A relation from A to B is then just the set of all the pairs that are linked, with the first entry from A and the second from B.
A × B is the set of every possible pair. A relation picks out some of them, which is why it is called a subset of A × B.

check.question: In the example, is (3, 2) in R?
check.answer: No, because 3 is not less than 2.

screens.ask: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3}. The link is 'a is less than b'. List the relation R.

why: Take each member of A in turn and ask which members of B it is linked to. A pair is written (from A, from B).
2 is not less than itself, so (2, 2) is not in the relation.
3 is not less than anything in B. A member of A is allowed to have no partner.
A × B has every possible pair: 3 × 2 = 6 of them. A relation keeps only the pairs where the link is true: here 3 of the 6.

practice.question: We write (a, b) to mean 'a is related to b'. What is (a, b) called?
practice.why: One link is recorded as an ordered pair (a, b), where the order matters.
wrong: A subset is a set picked out of a bigger set. (a, b) is one ordered pair.
A × B is the set of every possible pair. (a, b) is just one pair.
There is no = sign. (a, b) is an ordered pair.

practice.question: A = {1, 2} and B = {1, 2, 3}. The link is 'a is equal to b'. What is R?
practice.why: 1 in A equals 1 in B, and 2 in A equals 2 in B. Those are the only links.
wrong: 3 is not in A, so (3, 3) cannot be a pair. The first entry comes from A.
A relation is a set of ordered pairs, not of single numbers.
1 is not equal to 2. Each pair must obey the link.

practice.question: A = {2, 3} and B = {1, 4}. The link is 'a is greater than b'. What is R?
practice.why: 2 and 3 are both greater than 1, and neither is greater than 4.
wrong: The order is reversed. The first entry comes from A.
These are 'less than' links. 2 and 3 are not greater than 4.
3 is also greater than 1, so (3, 1) belongs too.

practice.question: A = {Asha, Ravi} and B = {Chennai, Madurai}. Asha lives in Madurai and Ravi lives in Chennai. What is the relation 'lives in' from A to B?
practice.why: Each pair has the person first (from A) and the city they live in second (from B).
wrong: The order matters. The first entry must come from A, the people.
These pairs do not obey the link. Asha lives in Madurai.
That is A × B. A relation picks only the pairs that are linked.

rounds.question: What is A × B?
options: The set of every possible pair
The elements in both A and B
The numbers of A times the numbers of B
rounds.why: A × B is the set of every possible pair, first entry from A and second from B.
wrong: The linked pairs form a relation, which is only part of A × B.
A × B is made of pairs, not of shared elements.
Nothing is multiplied. A × B is a set of ordered pairs.

rounds.question: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5}. The link is 'a + b = 6'. What is R?
rounds.why: 1 + 5 = 6 and 2 + 4 = 6. 3 would need 3, which is not in B. So R = {(1, 5), (2, 4)}.
wrong: The first entry must come from A and the second from B.
3 is not in B, so (3, 3) is not allowed.
A relation is a set of pairs, not the number 6.

rounds.question: A = {2, 3} and B = {4, 6, 9}. The link is 'b is double a'. What is R?
rounds.why: Double 2 is 4 and double 3 is 6. So R = {(2, 4), (3, 6)}.
wrong: The pairs are back to front. The entry from A is written first.
9 is three times 3, not double it.
These are three times, not double.

rounds.question: A = {Meena, John} and B = {cricket, chess}. Meena plays chess. John plays cricket and chess. What is the relation 'plays' from A to B?
rounds.why: List every link, child first: Meena with chess, John with cricket, John with chess.
wrong: The pairs are back to front. The entry from A comes first.
John plays chess too, so (John, chess) is missing.
Meena does not play cricket, so that pair is not in the relation.

rounds.question: Are (3, 7) and (7, 3) the same ordered pair?
options: Yes, they have the same numbers
rounds.why: In an ordered pair the order matters. (3, 7) says 3 is related to 7, not 7 to 3.
wrong: Same numbers is not enough. The order matters.
The sum does not matter. The order does.
Whichever sets are used, the two pairs are different.

rounds.question: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {1, 2}. The link is 'a is one more than b'. What is R?
rounds.why: 2 is one more than 1, and 3 is one more than 2. So R = {(2, 1), (3, 2)}.
wrong: The pairs are back to front. a comes first, and a is the bigger one.
3 is two more than 1, so (3, 1) does not belong.
These pairs are for 'a is equal to b'.

rounds.question: A has 4 elements and B has 2 elements. How many pairs are in A × B?
rounds.why: Each of the 4 elements of A pairs with each of the 2 elements of B: 4 × 2 = 8 pairs.
wrong: You added 4 and 2. Every element of A meets every element of B: 4 × 2.
Each element of A makes 2 pairs, not 1.
You did 4 × 4. B has only 2 elements.

rounds.question: A = {Kavi, Tara, Sam} and B = {red, blue}. Kavi likes blue. Tara likes red. Sam likes neither. What is the relation 'likes' from A to B?
rounds.why: Only the real links are listed: Kavi with blue and Tara with red. Sam has no pair.
wrong: Sam likes neither colour, so he is in no pair.
The pairs are back to front. The entry from A comes first.
The colours are swapped. Kavi likes blue and Tara likes red.

entries.concept: what a set is: elements, { }, ∈, the universal set U and n(A)
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts with 'A ∪ B collects every element in A or in B' and uses U, ∈ and n(A), but no lesson says what a set or an element is.

screens.title: A set is a clear collection
text: Think of your class cricket team. For any child you can say for sure: in the team, or not.
A clear collection like that is called a set. The things in it are called its elements.

check.question: A = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Is 5 ∈ A true?
check.answer: Yes, 5 is one of the elements of A.

screens.ask: V is the set of vowels. Write V, and say whether e and b are in it.

why: Curly brackets hold the elements of a set, each written once.
∈ means is an element of. e is in the list.
∉ means is not an element of. b is not in the list.
Count them. n(V) is the number of elements of V.

after: We write a set inside curly brackets, with commas: A = {2, 4, 6}. Each element once; the order does not matter.
4 ∈ A says 4 belongs to A. 5 ∉ A says 5 does not.

screens.title: The whole box U, and counting with n(A)
text: First say what we are choosing from, for example the numbers 1 to 10. This whole box is called the universal set, U.

check.question: B = {3, 6, 9}. What is n(B)?

screens.ask: U = {1, 2, …, 10}. A is the set of even numbers in U. Find A and n(A).

why: U is the whole box we choose from. Only numbers in U can go into A.
Even numbers are the ones in the 2 times table.
n(A) is how many elements A has.

after: Every set in the question is made from elements of U.
In a Venn diagram U is the rectangle and each set is a circle inside it.
n(A) is a count, not a set.

practice.question: What are the things in a set called?
practice.why: The things that belong to a set are its elements.
wrong: The curly brackets only hold the list. The things inside are elements.
Commas only separate the things. The things are elements.
A circle is how a set is drawn in a Venn diagram. The things in it are elements.

practice.question: A = {2, 5, 8}. What is n(A)?
practice.why: n(A) is the number of elements. A has three: 2, 5 and 8.
wrong: You added the elements. n(A) counts them.
That is the largest element. n(A) counts how many there are.
That is the set A itself. n(A) is a count, not a set.

practice.question: A team's scores in four games were 3, 3, 5 and 7. Which is the set of its scores?
practice.why: A set uses curly brackets and each element is written once.
wrong: Each element of a set is written only once.
A set is written with curly brackets { }.
The list must be put inside curly brackets { }.

practice.question: U is the set of the seven days of the week. A is the set of days whose names start with S. What is n(A)?
practice.why: A = {Saturday, Sunday}, so n(A) = 2.
wrong: That is n(U), all the days. Count only the days in A.
Two days start with S: Saturday and Sunday.
That counts the days not in A. Count the ones that start with S.

rounds.question: What does the sign ∈ mean?
rounds.why: ∈ means 'is an element of'. 4 ∈ A says that 4 belongs to A.
wrong: Equal is the sign =. ∈ says a thing belongs to a set.
The number of elements is written n(A).
∈ does not compare sizes. It says a thing belongs to a set.

rounds.question: B = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11}. What is n(B)?
rounds.why: n(B) is the number of elements. B has 6 elements.
wrong: You added the elements. n(B) counts them.
11 is the biggest element. n(B) counts how many there are.
Count again: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 is six elements.

rounds.question: Which set is the same as {1, 2, 3}?
rounds.why: The order does not matter in a set. {3, 1, 2} has the same elements 1, 2 and 3.
wrong: The element 3 is missing.
It has an extra element, 4.
12 is one element, not 1 and 2.

rounds.question: U is the set of the twelve months of the year. A is the set of months whose names start with J. What is n(A)?
rounds.why: January, June and July start with J. So n(A) = 3.
wrong: 12 is n(U). Count only the months that start with J.
There are three: January, June and July.
There are three: January, June and July.

rounds.question: What is the universal set U?
options: A set with nothing in it
The biggest set: everything we are talking about
The number of elements in a set
A circle inside a Venn diagram
rounds.why: U is the biggest set. Every other set in the question is made from its elements.
wrong: U holds every element we are talking about.
The number of elements is n(A). U is a set.
In a Venn diagram U is the rectangle. The circles are the other sets.

rounds.question: C = {10, 20, 30, 40}. Which statement is true?
rounds.why: 20 is in the list, so 20 belongs to C.
wrong: 25 is not in the list.
4 is n(C), the count. It is not an element.
100 is the sum of the elements. It is not an element.

rounds.question: Which of these is a set?
options: The tall children in your class
The children in your class taller than 140 cm
rounds.why: For every child it is clear whether they are taller than 140 cm or not. So this is a set.
wrong: 'Tall' is not clear: people may not agree who is tall.
'Nice' is not clear: people may not agree.
'Best' is not clear: people may not agree.

rounds.question: U is the set of letters in the word MANGO. A is the set of vowels in U. What is n(A)?
rounds.why: The vowels in MANGO are A and O. So A = {A, O} and n(A) = 2.
wrong: 5 is n(U). Count only the vowels.
3 is the number of letters that are not vowels: M, N, G.
There are two vowels: A and O.

entries.concept: reading a set written as a rule: {x ∈ U : …}
entries.evidence: The first worked example writes A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4} before any lesson explains how to read this notation.

screens.title: A set written as a rule
text: A long list is tiring to write. A rule is quicker, like 'everyone in class 6 who wears glasses'.
screens.ask: U = {1, 2, …, 12}. A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4}. List A.

lines: x from U, a multiple of 4
why: The colon is read "such that". A holds every x in U that obeys the rule.
No other number from 1 to 12 is in the 4 times table.

after: {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4} is read 'all x in U such that x is a multiple of 4'.
x stands for each element in turn. The colon : means such that. After it comes the test.
To list the set, go through U one element at a time and keep the ones that pass.

practice.question: In {x ∈ U : x is even}, what does the colon : mean?
practice.why: The colon is read 'such that'. The test comes after it.
wrong: Here the colon is not division. It is read 'such that'.
That is the sign ∈. The colon means 'such that'.
That is the sign =. The colon means 'such that'.

practice.question: U = {1, 2, 3, …, 10}. List {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 5}.
practice.why: Go through U: only 5 and 10 are multiples of 5.
wrong: 10 is in U and is also a multiple of 5.
15 is not in U. Only elements of U can be kept.
1 and 5 are factors of 5. The test asks for multiples.

practice.question: U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. List {x ∈ U : x is greater than 5}.
practice.why: Go through U and keep the numbers greater than 5: 6, 7 and 8.
wrong: 5 is not greater than 5, so it fails the test.
These are less than 5. The test is 'greater than 5'.
9 is not in U. Only elements of U can be kept.

practice.question: U = {a, b, c, d, e}. List {x ∈ U : x is a vowel}.
practice.why: Go through U: a and e are vowels, and b, c, d are not.
wrong: i, o and u are not in U. Only elements of U can be kept.
These fail the test. Keep the ones that pass.
e is in U and is a vowel too.

rounds.question: In {x ∈ U : x is odd}, what is x?
options: A stand-in name for each element in turn
rounds.why: x is just a stand-in name for each element of U in turn, as it is tested.
wrong: The universal set is U. x stands for one element at a time.
x stands for an element, not for a count.
x is not one fixed number. It stands for each element in turn.

rounds.question: U = {1, 2, 3, …, 12}. List {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 3}.
rounds.why: Go through U and keep the multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9 and 12.
wrong: 12 is in U and is a multiple of 3 too.
Keep every element that passes, not just the first.
15 is not in U. U stops at 12.

rounds.question: U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}. List {x ∈ U : x is less than 4}.
rounds.why: The elements of U that are less than 4 are 1, 2 and 3.
wrong: 4 is not less than 4.
These are greater than 4. The test is 'less than 4'.
0 is not in U. Only elements of U can be kept.

rounds.question: U = {Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday}. List {x ∈ U : x starts with T}.
rounds.why: Go through U: only Tuesday starts with T.
wrong: Thursday is not in U. Only elements of U can be kept.
These are the days that fail the test.
The elements are days, not letters.

rounds.question: How is {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 3} read?
options: x is U times a multiple of 3
All multiples of 3, in U or not
All x in U such that x is a multiple of 3
U divided by a multiple of 3
rounds.why: ∈ is read 'in' and the colon is read 'such that': all x in U such that x is a multiple of 3.
wrong: Nothing is multiplied. ∈ means 'in' and : means 'such that'.
x ∈ U says x must come from U.
The colon is not a division sign. It means 'such that'.

rounds.question: U = {1, 2, 3, …, 10}. List {x ∈ U : x is odd}.
rounds.why: Go through U and keep the odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.
wrong: These are the even numbers. The test is 'x is odd'.
11 is not in U. U stops at 10.
9 is odd and is in U, so it belongs too.

rounds.question: U = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}. List {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 3}.
rounds.why: Go through U: only 6 is a multiple of 3.
wrong: 3 and 9 are not in U. Only elements of U can be kept.
12 is not in U. U stops at 10.
These are the elements that fail the test.

rounds.question: U = {cat, cow, crow, hen}. List {x ∈ U : x is a bird}.
rounds.why: Go through U: the crow and the hen are birds.
wrong: A hen is a bird too.
These are the ones that fail the test.
A duck is a bird, but it is not in U.

entries.concept: the shorthand Σα, Σαβ for sums over the roots
entries.evidence: The worked example writes 'Σα = −1, Σαβ = 5' and 'Σαβ/αβγ' but the sign Σ is never explained.

screens.title: Σ means 'add up all of this kind'
text: α, β and γ (alpha, beta, gamma) are names for the three roots of a cubic, like x, y and z.
Σ (sigma) means: add up every term of this kind. Σα = α + β + γ, every root added.
Σαβ adds every product of two different roots, each pair once: αβ + βγ + γα.
αβγ, with no Σ, is the product of all three roots.

check.question: The roots are 1, 1 and 2. What is Σα?

screens.ask: The roots are {@r}, {@s} and {@t}. Find Σα, Σαβ and αβγ.

why: α, β, γ are names for the three roots. Σα means add every one of them.

steps.do: Σαβ: add every product of two.
why: Take each different pair once, multiply, and add. Three roots make three pairs.
One product of all the roots together.
The numbers {S1}, {S2} and {P} appear in the cubic, with signs − + −. That is the pattern Vieta's relations describe.

practice.question: A cubic has roots α, β and γ. What does Σα mean?
practice.why: Σ means 'the sum of all terms like this one', so Σα adds every root.
wrong: That is the product of the roots, written with no Σ.
That is Σαβ, the sum of products of two roots.
Nothing is squared. Σα is the sum of the roots themselves.

practice.question: The roots are 2, 3 and 4. What is Σα?
wrong: That is the product αβγ. Σα adds the roots.
That is Σαβ = 6 + 12 + 8. Σα adds the roots.
That is how many roots there are. Σα is their sum.

practice.question: The roots are 1, 2 and 4. What is Σαβ?
wrong: That is Σα, the sum of the roots. Σαβ adds the products of pairs.
That is αβγ, the product of all three. Σαβ adds the products of pairs.
You counted each pair twice. Each pair is taken once.

practice.question: The roots are 2, 2 and 3. What is Σαβ?
practice.why: The three pairs give 2 × 2 + 2 × 3 + 3 × 2 = 4 + 6 + 6 = 16.
wrong: You left out one pair. Three roots make three pairs, even when two roots are equal.
That is the product αβγ = 2 × 2 × 3.
That is Σα = 2 + 2 + 3. Σαβ adds the products of pairs.

rounds.question: A cubic has roots α, β and γ. What does Σαβ mean?
rounds.why: Σαβ is the sum of every product of two different roots, each pair once.
wrong: That is Σα, the sum of the roots.
That is the product of all three roots, with no Σ.
Each product uses two different roots, not a root with itself.

rounds.question: The roots are 1, 4 and 6. What is Σα?
rounds.why: Σα adds every root: 1 + 4 + 6 = 11.
wrong: 24 is the product αβγ. Σα is a sum.
34 is Σαβ, the sum of the pair products.
3 is the number of roots. Σα adds them.

rounds.question: The roots are 2, 3 and 5. What is Σαβ?
wrong: 30 is αβγ, all three multiplied.
10 is Σα, the roots added.
Each pair was counted twice. Each pair is used once.

rounds.question: The roots are −1, 2 and 3. What is Σαβ?
wrong: The minus sign of −1 was dropped. Two of the products are negative.
4 is Σα, the roots added.
−6 is αβγ, all three multiplied.

rounds.question: What does αβγ, with no Σ, mean?
options: The sum of the three roots
The product of all three roots
The sum of the products of pairs
rounds.why: Letters written side by side are multiplied. αβγ is the product of all three roots.
wrong: The sum of the roots is Σα.
The sum of the pair products is Σαβ.
All three letters are there, so all three roots are multiplied.

rounds.question: The roots are 2, 5 and 10. What is αβγ?
wrong: 17 is Σα, the roots added.
80 is Σαβ, the sum of the pair products.
3 is the number of roots. αβγ multiplies them.

rounds.question: The roots are 1, 2 and 5. What is Σαβ?
wrong: You squared each root and added. Σαβ uses two different roots in each product.
Each pair was counted twice. Each pair is used once.
10 is αβγ, all three multiplied.

rounds.question: A cubic has roots 0, 3 and 4. What is Σαβ?
wrong: 7 is Σα, the roots added.
0 is αβγ. In Σαβ the pair 3 × 4 does not contain 0.
You added Σα and Σαβ. Only the pair products are wanted.

entries.concept: what a derivative is (the slope of a curve at a point), and the notation f′(x), dy/dx, d/dx
entries.evidence: The lesson says 'Differentiable at c means the left and right derivatives at c are equal' and works out '2(1) + a = −3', but this is the first skill to use derivatives and no earlier lesson says what a derivative is or how it is written.

screens.title: How steep is a curve right here?
text: A car's speedometer shows your speed at this very moment, not your average speed for the whole trip. Calculus asks the same question about a graph: how steep is it at this one point?
For a straight line this is easy. Its slope is rise ÷ run, and it is the same everywhere. A curve is different: its steepness changes from point to point.

To find the steepness at a point P, take a second point Q on the curve near P. The straight line through P and Q is called a chord. Work out its slope. Now slide Q closer and closer to P. The chord slopes settle on one number. That number is the slope of the curve at P.
The straight line through P with exactly this slope just touches the curve at P. It is called the tangent at P.

check.question: A straight line rises 6 units for every 2 units across. What is its slope?

screens.ask: On y = x², how steep is the curve at P(3, 9)?

why: A chord is a straight line from P to another point Q on the curve. Its slope is rise ÷ run.
3.1² = 9.61. The closer Q is to P, the more the chord looks like the curve at P.
3.01² = 9.0601, so the rise is 0.0601 for a run of 0.01.

steps.do: See where the slopes are heading.
why: The slopes settle towards 6. That value is the slope of the curve at x = 3, called the derivative there.

screens.title: The derivative, and how we write it
text: The slope of the curve y = f(x) at a point is called the derivative of f at that point. It tells how fast f is changing there: how many units y moves for each unit of x, at that instant.

The slope is different at different x, so the derivative is itself a function. We write it f′(x), read 'f dash of x'. The same thing is also written dy/dx, read 'dee y by dee x'. Think of it as a tiny change in y divided by the tiny change in x that caused it.
Finding the derivative is called differentiating. The symbol d/dx written in front of an expression means 'differentiate this with respect to x'.

A function is differentiable at a point when it has one clear slope there, the same coming from the left as from the right. At a sharp corner the two sides give different slopes, so it is not differentiable there.

check.question: For f(x) = x² the derivative is f′(x) = 2x. What is f′(5)?

screens.ask: Find the derivative of f(x) = x² from a chord.

steps.do: Take a chord from x to x + h.
why: h is a small step to the right. The rise is how much f goes up over that step.
(x + h)² is (x + h)(x + h) = x² + 2xh + h². The x² parts cancel.
Every term on top has an h, so each can be divided by h.
As the step gets tiny, + h fades away. The result 2x is the slope at any x. At x = 3 it is 6, as found by the chords.

screens.title: Two slopes to remember
text: A straight line y = mx + c has slope m everywhere. The c only lifts the line, so it adds 0 to the slope.
The curve y = x² has slope 2x.
Slopes add. So x² + ax + b has slope 2x + a. These two facts are all this skill needs.

check.question: What is the derivative of 7x + 2?

screens.ask: Find the slope of y = −{@m}x + {@n}, and of y = x² + {@b}x + {@c} at x = {@x0}.

why: A straight line has the same slope everywhere: the number with x. The + {n} only moves the line up, so its slope is 0.
Each piece is done on its own and the results are added.
The derivative is a rule for the slope. Put in the x you want.

practice.question: The straight line through P that just touches the curve there, with the curve's own slope, is called
practice.why: The line through P with exactly the slope of the curve at P is the tangent at P.
wrong: A chord joins two points P and Q on the curve.
The x-axis is a fixed line of the graph, not the line touching the curve at P.
The derivative is the slope, a number. The line is the tangent.

practice.question: For f(x) = x² the derivative is f′(x) = 2x. What is f′(4)?
wrong: That is f(4) = 4². Use the derivative 2x.
You added 2 and 4. 2x means 2 × 4.
The x cannot be dropped. Put x = 4 into 2x.

practice.question: What is the derivative of 5x + 9?
practice.why: The line y = mx + c has slope m everywhere. Here m = 5, and the constant 9 gives 0.
wrong: The constant 9 does not change the steepness, so it gives 0, not 9.
9 only moves the line up. The slope is the number in front of x.
The slope of a straight line is the number m alone, with no x.

practice.question: What is the slope of the curve y = x² + 3x + 7 at x = 2?
practice.why: The derivative is 2x + 3. At x = 2 it is 2 × 2 + 3 = 7.
wrong: That is the value of y at x = 2. The slope comes from the derivative 2x + 3.
You kept the constant 7. A constant gives 0 in the derivative.
That is only 2x. The 3x term adds 3 to the slope.

rounds.question: The straight line through two points P and Q of a curve is called
rounds.why: The straight line through two points P and Q on the curve is called a chord.
wrong: A tangent just touches the curve at one point P.
The derivative is a slope, a number. The line through P and Q is a chord.
The axes are the number lines of the graph.

rounds.question: For f(x) = x² the derivative is f′(x) = 2x. What is f′(7)?
wrong: 49 is f(7), the height of the curve. The slope is 2 × 7.
You added 2 and 7. 2x means 2 × x.
2 is only the number in front. Multiply it by 7.

rounds.question: What is the derivative of x² + 6x + 2?
rounds.why: x² gives 2x, 6x gives 6 and the constant 2 gives 0. Slopes add: 2x + 6.
wrong: The constant 2 gives 0. It does not add to the slope.
The line part 6x has slope 6, not 6x.
x² has derivative 2x, not x.

rounds.question: A hill path follows the curve y = x² + 4x + 1. How steep is it at x = 3?
rounds.why: The derivative is 2x + 4. At x = 3 the slope is 2 × 3 + 4 = 10.
wrong: 22 is the height y at x = 3. The steepness is the derivative.
You left out the 4 that comes from 4x.
The constant 1 gives 0. It does not add to the slope.

rounds.question: What does d/dx written in front of an expression mean?
options: Differentiate this with respect to x
rounds.why: d/dx in front of an expression means 'differentiate this with respect to x'.
wrong: It is not a division by x. It is an instruction to differentiate.
Nothing is multiplied. It is an instruction to differentiate.
d is not a number here. d/dx is one symbol meaning 'differentiate'.

rounds.question: As Q slides towards P, the chord slopes are 5.1, 5.01, 5.001, … What is the slope of the curve at P?
rounds.why: The chord slopes settle on 5. That number is the slope of the curve at P.
wrong: 5.1 is one chord slope. The slopes keep moving, towards 5.
The gap between P and Q shrinks to 0, but the slopes head to 5.
The slopes are getting closer to 5, not to 6.

rounds.question: What is the derivative of x² + 10?
rounds.why: x² gives 2x. The constant 10 only moves the curve up, so it gives 0.
wrong: The constant 10 gives 0. It does not change the steepness.
That drops the 10 but does not differentiate x².
You added 2 and 10. x² gives 2x and 10 gives 0.

rounds.question: A car has gone y = x² + 5x metres after x seconds. Its speed is the derivative. What is its speed at x = 2?
rounds.why: The derivative is 2x + 5. At x = 2 it is 2 × 2 + 5 = 9.
wrong: 14 is the distance y at x = 2. The speed is the derivative.
You added 2 + 5. The first part is 2x = 4.
You left out the 5 that comes from 5x.

entries.concept: what a differential equation is and what solving one means
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts 'When dy/dx is a function of x times a function of y, separate the variables' without saying what a differential equation is, that its unknown is a function, or what the starting value is for.

screens.title: An equation about how fast something changes
text: A hot cup of tea cools fast at first, then slowly. We know how fast it changes, and we want the temperature itself.
An equation with a derivative in it, like dy/dx = 2x, is a differential equation. Its unknown is a whole function y.
Integrating brings in a constant C, so many functions fit. Together they are the general solution.
One known point fixes C. It is the starting value, or initial condition. The one function you then get is the particular solution.

check.question: Does y = x² + 1 satisfy dy/dx = 2x?
check.answer: Yes, the derivative of x² + 1 is 2x

screens.ask: Solve dy/dx = 2x, given y = {@y0} when x = {@x0}.

why: Which function has slope 2x? x² does. Any number added on has slope 0, so we add C for "some number".

steps.do: Use the given point to find C.
why: Put x = {x0} and y = {y0} into y = x² + C.
Differentiate the answer: you get back 2x. At x = {x0} it gives {sq} + {C} = {y0}.

screens.note: Pick a bigger y, so that C stays above 0.

practice.question: An equation that contains a derivative, such as dy/dx = 3y, is called
practice.why: An equation with a derivative in it is a differential equation. Its unknown is a function.
wrong: A quadratic has x² as its highest power and no derivative.
That is the family of answers, not the equation itself.
That is the extra fact, such as y = 5 when x = 0, that fixes C.

practice.question: Which function satisfies dy/dx = 2x?
practice.why: The derivative of x² − 4 is 2x, because the constant gives 0.
wrong: The derivative of 2x is 2. You need a function whose derivative is 2x.
Its derivative is 2x + 1, not 2x.
Its derivative is 2. You need a function whose derivative is 2x.

practice.question: dy/dx = 2x gives y = x² + C. You are told y = 3 when x = 1. What is C?
practice.why: Put the values in: 3 = 1² + C, so C = 2.
wrong: That would be right if x were 0. Here x = 1, so 3 = 1 + C.
You added 3 and 1. Solve 3 = 1 + C by subtracting.
You subtracted the wrong way. 3 = 1 + C gives C = 3 − 1.

practice.question: Water in a tank rises so that dy/dx = 3, which gives y = 3x + C. When x = 0, y = 10. What is y when x = 2?
wrong: You left out C. The starting value gives C = 10.
You did not multiply by x. 3x at x = 2 is 6.
You multiplied 3 by 10. C is added: y = 3x + 10.

rounds.question: What is the unknown in a differential equation?
rounds.why: The unknown of a differential equation is not a number. It is a whole function y.
wrong: An ordinary equation has a number as its unknown. Here it is a function.
The equation gives a rule for the slope everywhere. The unknown is the function.
C appears while solving, but the thing we look for is the function y.

rounds.question: Which function satisfies dy/dx = 3?
rounds.why: The derivative of 3x + 7 is 3, so it fits.
wrong: y = 3 is a constant, so its derivative is 0.
The derivative of x³ is 3x², not 3.
The derivative of 3x² is 6x, not 3.

rounds.question: dy/dx = 2x gives y = x² + C. You are told y = 10 when x = 2. What is C?
rounds.why: Put in x = 2 and y = 10: 10 = 4 + C. So C = 6.
wrong: 10 is y. Take away x² = 4 to get C.
You took away 2. It is x² = 4 that is taken away.
You added 4. From 10 = 4 + C, C = 10 − 4.

rounds.question: A plant grows so that dy/dx = 2, which gives y = 2x + C. When x = 0 its height y is 5 cm. What is y when x = 4?
rounds.why: x = 0 gives 5 = 0 + C, so C = 5. Then y = 2 × 4 + 5 = 13.
wrong: You left out C = 5, the starting height.
You added 4 and 5. The plant grows 2 × 4 = 8.
You added 2 and 5 first. Multiply 2 × 4, then add 5.

rounds.question: An extra fact that fixes C, such as 'y = 5 when x = 0', is called
rounds.why: The extra fact that fixes C is called the starting value or initial condition.
wrong: The general solution is all the functions, with C still free.
The derivative is dy/dx. The extra fact is the initial condition.
The differential equation is the rule with dy/dx in it.

rounds.question: Does y = x² + 9 satisfy dy/dx = 2x?
rounds.why: The derivative of x² is 2x, and the constant 9 gives 0. So dy/dx = 2x.
wrong: A constant has slope 0, so the 9 disappears.
Any constant C works. That is why there are many solutions.
The derivative of x² is 2x.

rounds.question: dy/dx = 3 gives y = 3x + C. You are told y = 4 when x = 2. What is the particular solution?
rounds.why: Put in x = 2 and y = 4: 4 = 6 + C, so C = −2. The solution is y = 3x − 2.
wrong: 4 is y, not C. Solve 4 = 6 + C.
C = 4 − 6 = −2. Watch the sign.
That is the general solution. The extra fact fixes C.

rounds.question: Water drains from a tank so that dy/dx = −2, which gives y = −2x + C. When x = 0, y = 20. What is y when x = 5?
rounds.why: x = 0 gives C = 20. Then y = −2 × 5 + 20 = 10.
wrong: The slope is −2, so the level falls. Take 10 away.
You left out C = 20, the starting level.
20 is the level at x = 0. After 5 it has fallen by 10.

entries.concept: curves not written as y = f(x): implicit equations and parameters
entries.evidence: The lesson opens with 'defines y implicitly as a function of x' and later 'a curve given in parametric form' without saying what implicit or parametric means.

screens.title: When y is not on its own
text: Most curves so far were written as y = something in x, such as y = x². That is called explicit: y stands alone on one side.
A circle of radius 5 round the origin is x² + y² = 25. Here x and y are mixed together. The equation still ties y to x: choose an x and it tells you which y fit. We say it gives y implicitly.

We can find the slope dy/dx without solving for y first. Differentiate every term with respect to x. Remember that y is a hidden function of x. So, by the chain rule, a term like y² gives 2y × dy/dx, not just 2y. Then solve for dy/dx.

check.question: Is the point (3, 4) on the curve x² + y² = 25?

screens.ask: On the circle x² + y² = 25, find dy/dx at (3, 4).

steps.do: Differentiate each term with respect to x.
why: y depends on x, so when we differentiate y² we get 2y, times dy/dx (the chain rule). The number 25 does not change.
Every term was differentiated, so the two sides are still equal.
Move 2x across (it changes sign), then divide by 2y.
At (3, 4) the circle is going down to the right, so a negative slope makes sense.

screens.title: A third letter that drives both
text: Watch an ant on a page. At time t seconds it is at x = 2t and y = t². Both follow the clock.
The extra letter t is called a parameter. Giving a curve this way is the parametric form. Each t gives one point (x, y).
For the slope, compare how fast y and x change with t: dy/dx = dy/dt ÷ dx/dt.

check.question: x = 2t and y = t². Where is the point when t = 1?

screens.ask: The ant is at x = 2t, y = t². Find the slope of its path at t = {@t}.

steps.do: How fast x changes with t.
why: Differentiate x = 2t with respect to t.

steps.do: How fast y changes with t.
why: Differentiate y = t² with respect to t.
For each small tick of t, y moves by dy/dt and x by dx/dt. Rise ÷ run is their ratio.
x = 2 × {t} = {x} and y = {t}² = {y}. The slope there is t = {t}.

practice.question: A curve is given by x = 3t and y = t². What is t called?
practice.why: The extra letter that drives both x and y is the parameter.
wrong: The slope is dy/dx. t is the parameter.
An implicit equation mixes x and y in one equation. t is a parameter.
t changes, and each value of t gives a different point.

practice.question: x = 3t and y = t². Where is the point when t = 2?
wrong: The coordinates are swapped. x = 3t comes first.
y is t², not t. 2² = 4.
You added 3 and 2. 3t means 3 × 2.

practice.question: In implicit differentiation, what does the term y² give when you differentiate with respect to x?
practice.why: y is a hidden function of x, so the chain rule gives 2y × dy/dx.
wrong: y depends on x, so the chain rule adds the factor dy/dx.
The term is y², so the result has 2y, times dy/dx.
The power still comes down: y² gives 2y, then times dy/dx.

practice.question: For the circle x² + y² = 100, dy/dx = −x ÷ y. What is the slope at the point (8, 6)?
wrong: The minus sign is part of the formula: −x ÷ y.
You did y ÷ x. The formula is −x ÷ y = −8 ÷ 6.
You did y ÷ x and dropped the minus sign. Use −x ÷ y.

rounds.question: In x² + y² = 25, x and y are mixed together. How does this equation give y?
rounds.why: y is not alone on one side, but the equation still ties y to x. It gives y implicitly.
wrong: Explicit means y stands alone, as in y = x².
A parameter is a third letter such as t. There is none here.
y changes as x changes, so it is not a constant.

rounds.question: A curve is given by x = t + 1 and y = 2t. Where is the point when t = 3?
rounds.why: x = 3 + 1 = 4 and y = 2 × 3 = 6. The point is (4, 6).
wrong: The coordinates are swapped. x comes first.
x is t + 1 = 4, not t.

rounds.question: Differentiate x² + y² = 49 with respect to x. What do you get?
rounds.why: x² gives 2x, y² gives 2y × dy/dx by the chain rule, and the constant 49 gives 0.
wrong: y is a hidden function of x, so y² gives 2y × dy/dx.
The constant 49 has derivative 0.
y² gives 2y × dy/dx. The power must come down.

rounds.question: A boat is at x = 3t and y = t² at time t. What is the slope of its path at t = 6?
rounds.why: dy/dt = 2t = 12 and dx/dt = 3. So dy/dx = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
wrong: The division is upside down. It is dy/dt ÷ dx/dt.
You multiplied the two rates. Divide dy/dt by dx/dt.
12 is dy/dt alone. Divide it by dx/dt = 3.

rounds.question: y = x² + 1 has y alone on one side. What is this form called?
rounds.why: When y stands alone on one side, the curve is written explicitly.
wrong: Implicit is when x and y are mixed, as in x² + y² = 25.
Parametric form uses a third letter such as t.
A parameter is the extra letter t. Here there is none.

rounds.question: A curve is given by x = t² and y = t + 3. Where is the point when t = 2?
rounds.why: x = 2² = 4 and y = 2 + 3 = 5. The point is (4, 5).
wrong: The coordinates are swapped. x comes first.
x is t² = 4, not t.

rounds.question: A curve has x = 4t and y = t². What is dy/dx at t = 6?
rounds.why: dy/dt = 2t = 12 and dx/dt = 4. So dy/dx = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
wrong: The division is upside down. It is dy/dt ÷ dx/dt.
You multiplied the two rates. Divide dy/dt by dx/dt.
12 is dy/dt alone. Divide it by dx/dt = 4.

rounds.question: The rim of a wheel is the circle x² + y² = 169, where dy/dx = −x ÷ y. What is the slope at the point (12, 5)?
wrong: The minus sign is missing. The formula is −x ÷ y.
x and y are the wrong way round. It is −x ÷ y.
It is −x ÷ y: x on top, and a minus sign.

entries.concept: what an integral is: the sign ∫, dx, antiderivative, + C, limits, area
entries.evidence: The first screen says 'We want ∫ from x = 0 to x = 1 of 2x(x² + 1)² dx' and this skill comes before the other integration skills, so nothing has yet said what ∫, dx, an antiderivative or the limits mean.

screens.title: Running differentiation backwards
text: Differentiate x² and you get 2x. Now go backwards: which function has derivative 2x? x² does. Going backwards is called integrating.
We write ∫ 2x dx = x² + C. ∫ means integrate. The dx says the variable is x. The function in between is the integrand.
Why + C? x² + 1 and x² − 7 also have derivative 2x, since a constant has slope 0. With no numbers on ∫, this is an indefinite integral.

check.question: The derivative of x² is 2x. What is ∫ 2x dx?

screens.ask: Find ∫ {@k}x² dx.

why: Bring the power 3 down: {a} × 3 = {k}. Integrating asks which function has this derivative.
Any constant has derivative 0, so adding 7 or taking away 2 also works. C stands for that unknown constant.
Differentiating your answer must give back what was inside the integral.

screens.note: Use a multiple of 3, like 6 or 12, so the answer has whole numbers.

screens.title: An integral between two numbers
text: Sometimes ∫ carries two numbers, as in ∫ from 0 to 3 of 2x dx. They are the lower and upper limits. This is a definite integral, and its answer is a number.
Find an antiderivative F. Work out F(upper limit) − F(lower limit). The C cancels, so leave it out.
When the graph is above the x-axis, the answer is the area under it between the limits. ∫ is a stretched S, for sum: very thin strips, height f(x) and width dx, added up.

check.question: An antiderivative of 2x is x². What is ∫ from 0 to 2 of 2x dx?

screens.ask: Work out the integral of 2x from 0 to {@n}.

why: x² has derivative 2x. For a definite integral the + C is not needed: it cancels.
Put the top number in, then the bottom number, and subtract.
Under y = 2x from 0 to {n} is a triangle. At x = {n} the height is 2 × {n} = {h}.

practice.question: In ∫ 2x dx, what is the function 2x called?
practice.why: The function between the ∫ sign and dx is the integrand.
wrong: The antiderivative is the answer, x². 2x is the integrand.
Limits are numbers written on the ∫ sign. 2x is the integrand.
The constant is C in the answer. 2x is the integrand.

practice.question: The derivative of x⁴ is 4x³. What is ∫ 4x³ dx?
practice.why: Integrating runs differentiation backwards, so it gives x⁴, and an indefinite integral needs + C.
wrong: An indefinite integral needs + C, since any constant has slope 0.
You differentiated again. Integrating goes backwards to x⁴.
That is the integrand unchanged. Its antiderivative is x⁴.

practice.question: An antiderivative of 2x is x². What is ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx?
practice.why: F(upper) − F(lower) = 3² − 1² = 9 − 1 = 8.
wrong: You left out the lower limit. Subtract 1² = 1.
You added the two values. It is upper minus lower: 9 − 1.
You put the limits into 2x. Put them into the antiderivative x².

practice.question: What is the area under the graph y = 2x between x = 0 and x = 4? (An antiderivative of 2x is x².)
practice.why: The area is the definite integral: 4² − 0² = 16.
wrong: That is the height 2 × 4 at the end, not the area.
That is 4 × 8, a full rectangle. The integral gives 4² − 0² = 16.
In a definite integral the C cancels, so the answer is just a number.

rounds.question: In ∫ 2x dx, what does the dx at the end say?
rounds.why: The dx at the end says that the variable is x.
wrong: dx is not a multiplier of the answer. It names the variable.
The answer is x² + C. dx only names the variable.
The constant is the + C. dx names the variable.

rounds.question: Which of these is an antiderivative of 2x?
rounds.why: The derivative of x² + 3 is 2x, so x² + 3 is an antiderivative of 2x.
wrong: 2 is the derivative of 2x. An antiderivative goes backwards.
The derivative of 2x² is 4x, not 2x.
The derivative of x is 1, not 2x.

rounds.question: An antiderivative of 2x is x². What is ∫ from 2 to 5 of 2x dx?
rounds.why: F(upper) − F(lower) = 5² − 2² = 25 − 4 = 21.
wrong: You left out the lower limit. Take away 2² = 4.
You added 25 and 4. It is upper minus lower.
You put the limits into 2x. Put them into the antiderivative x².

rounds.question: What is the area under the graph y = 3x² between x = 0 and x = 2? (An antiderivative of 3x² is x³.)
rounds.why: The area is the definite integral: 2³ − 0³ = 8.
wrong: 12 is the height of the graph at x = 2. Use the antiderivative x³.
You did 2 × 3. Use x³: 2³ = 8.
C cancels in a definite integral. The answer is a number.

rounds.question: An integral written with no numbers on the ∫ sign is called
rounds.why: With no limits on the ∫ sign it is an indefinite integral, and its answer has + C.
wrong: A definite integral carries two limits and gives a number.
The limits are the two numbers on the sign. Here there are none.
The integrand is the function between ∫ and dx.

rounds.question: In '∫ from 0 to 5 of 2x dx', which number is the upper limit?
rounds.why: The integral runs from 0 to 5. The upper limit is 5.
wrong: 0 is the lower limit.
2 is part of the integrand 2x.
25 is the value of the integral, not a limit.

rounds.question: The derivative of x³ is 3x². What is ∫ from 1 to 2 of 3x² dx?
rounds.why: F(upper) − F(lower) = 2³ − 1³ = 8 − 1 = 7.
wrong: You left out the lower limit. Take away 1³ = 1.
C cancels in the subtraction. A definite integral is a number.
You added 8 and 1. It is upper minus lower.

rounds.question: A car's speed after x seconds is 2x metres per second. The distance it goes is the area under the graph y = 2x. How far does it go from x = 0 to x = 5? (An antiderivative of 2x is x².)
rounds.why: The area is 5² − 0² = 25, so it goes 25 metres.
wrong: 10 is the speed at x = 5. The distance is the area: 5² − 0².
You did speed × time, 10 × 5. The speed is not steady, so use x².
5 is only the upper limit. Put it into x².

entries.concept: what a limit is and the notation lim (x → a)
entries.evidence: The first lesson screen ('0 ⁄ 0 does not mean the limit is 0') already uses 'the limit' and 'lim (x → 3)' before anything says what a limit is or how to read the arrow.

screens.title: Getting closer and closer
text: Walk towards a wall. With each step you cover half of the distance that is left. You never have to touch the wall, but everyone can say where you are heading: the wall.
A limit is the same idea for a function. We ask: as x gets closer and closer to some number a, what number does f(x) head towards? That number is called the limit of f(x) as x approaches a.
We write it lim (x → a) f(x). The arrow → is read 'approaches' or 'tends to'. It means x comes as near to a as we like, from the left and from the right, without having to be equal to a.
A limit is about where f(x) is heading, not about what happens exactly at x = a. So a limit can exist even at a place where the function itself has no value.

check.question: As x gets closer and closer to 4, what number does x + 1 get closer to?

v.says: A straight-line graph that rises to the right, with an open circle (a hole) on it above x = 1 at height 2.

figures.caption: f(x) = (x² − 1) ÷ (x − 1). There is a hole at x = 1: the function has no value there. But as x gets close to 1 from either side, the graph heads to 2. The limit is 2.

screens.ask: Find the limit of (x² − 1) ÷ (x − 1) as x → 1.

why: 0 ÷ 0 has no value. So we look at what happens near x = 1 instead.
From above the values are just over 2.
The limit is the value the function heads for, even though it is not defined at x = 1 itself.

practice.question: In lim (x → a), how is the arrow → read?
practice.why: The arrow is read 'approaches' or 'tends to': x comes as near to a as we like.
wrong: x does not have to be equal to a. It only comes closer and closer.
x comes close to a from both the left and the right.
