The arrow tells where x is heading: it 'approaches' a.

practice.question: As x gets closer and closer to 3, what number does 2x get closer to?
practice.why: When x is near 3, 2x is near 2 × 3 = 6.
wrong: You added 2 and 3. 2x means 2 × x.
3 is where x is heading. 2x heads to 2 × 3.
The 2 and 3 are not written side by side. 2x means 2 × 3.

practice.question: f(x) = (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2). At x = 1.9 it is 3.9, at x = 1.99 it is 3.99 and at x = 2.01 it is 4.01. What is lim (x → 2) f(x)?
options: There is no limit, because f(2) is 0 ÷ 0
practice.why: The values head towards 4 from both sides, so the limit is 4.
wrong: A limit is about where f(x) is heading, not about the value at x = 2 itself.
0 ÷ 0 is not 0. Look at where the nearby values are heading.
2 is where x is heading. The values of f(x) head to 4.

practice.question: A ball bounces to half its height each time: 8, 4, 2, 1, 1/2, … and so on for ever. What number are the heights heading towards?
practice.why: Halving again and again brings the heights closer and closer to 0.
wrong: That is only the last height written. The list goes on: 1/4, 1/8, …
The heights keep halving below 1.
8 is where the heights start. A limit is where they are heading.

rounds.question: The number that f(x) heads towards as x approaches a is called
rounds.why: The number f(x) heads towards as x gets close to a is the limit of f(x) as x approaches a.
wrong: f(a) is what happens exactly at a. The limit is where f(x) is heading.
The arrow is only the sign for 'approaches'.
The input is x. The limit is about the outputs f(x).

rounds.question: As x gets closer and closer to 5, what number does x + 4 get closer to?
rounds.why: As x heads to 5, x + 4 heads to 5 + 4 = 9.
wrong: 5 is where x is heading. x + 4 heads to 9.
You multiplied 5 by 4. The rule adds 4.
You took 4 from 5. The rule adds 4.

rounds.question: A function has no value at x = 5. Near 5 its values are 7.9, 7.99 on the left and 8.01, 8.1 on the right. What can you say?
options: There is no limit, as f(5) has no value
rounds.why: The values head towards 8 from both sides. A limit is about where f(x) is heading, not about x = 5 itself.
wrong: A limit can exist where the function has no value.
5 is where x is heading. The values of f(x) head to 8.
7.9 is one value on the way. The values keep moving, towards 8.

rounds.question: You eat half a pizza, then half of what is left, and so on for ever. The part eaten is 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, 15/16, … What number is it heading towards?
rounds.why: Each time the part left is halved, so the part eaten gets closer and closer to 1 whole pizza.
wrong: 15/16 is only the fourth step. The numbers keep growing towards 1.
There is only one pizza, so the part eaten cannot pass 1.
The part left heads to 0. The part eaten heads to 1.

rounds.question: What does lim (x → 2) f(x) ask?
options: What f(x) heads towards as x gets close to 2
rounds.why: The arrow means 'approaches'. The limit is the number f(x) heads towards as x comes near 2.
wrong: A limit is about where f(x) is heading, not the value exactly at 2.
x approaches 2. It is not f(x) that is set equal to 2.
Nothing is multiplied. The arrow means x approaches 2.

rounds.question: As x gets closer and closer to 4, what number does x² get closer to?
rounds.why: As x heads to 4, x² heads to 4 × 4 = 16.
wrong: You did 4 × 2. x² means x × x.
You added 4 + 2. x² means x × x.
4 is where x is heading. x² heads to 16.

rounds.question: As x approaches a, the values of f(x) head to 2 from the left but to 5 from the right. What is lim (x → a) f(x)?
rounds.why: For a limit, f(x) must head to the same number from the left and from the right. Here it does not.
wrong: That is only the left side. Both sides must agree.
That is only the right side. Both sides must agree.
The two sides are not averaged. They must head to the same number.

rounds.question: Hot milk cools in a room at 30°. Its temperature goes 60°, 45°, 37.5°, 33.75°, … with the gap above 30° halving each time. What is it heading towards?
rounds.why: The gap above 30° goes 30, 15, 7.5, 3.75, … towards 0. So the temperature heads to 30°.
wrong: It is the gap above 30° that heads to 0, not the temperature.
33.75° is only the fourth reading. It keeps falling towards 30°.
60° is where it started.

entries.concept: the number e and the natural logarithm (log to base e, also written ln)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Limits from the standard limits of sin x/x, (eˣ − 1)/x and log(1 + x)/x' uses e and log, and no lesson anywhere says what the number e is or that log here means the logarithm to base e.

screens.title: A special number called e
text: Put ₹1 in a bank that pays 100% interest a year. If the interest is added once, you end the year with ₹2. If it is added in two halves, 50% and then 50% again, you get 1.5 × 1.5 = ₹2.25. Added every month, you get about ₹2.61. Added every day, about ₹2.71.

Adding the interest more and more often helps, but less and less. The amount does not grow for ever. It settles on one number, about 2.718. This number is called e. Like π, its decimals never end, so it gets a letter of its own.
The function e^x means e raised to the power x. It is the growth function of calculus. e^0 = 1, e^1 is about 2.718 and e^2 is about 7.39.

check.question: Which whole number is e nearest to: 2, 3 or 10?

screens.ask: Invest 1 rupee at 100% a year. Compound it more and more often.

why: 100% interest doubles the money.
Each half year adds 50%, so multiply by 1.5 twice. Interest now earns interest.
Each quarter adds 25%, so multiply by 1.25 four times.
The total keeps growing, but by less each time, and settles towards 2.718… That number is called e.

screens.title: The natural logarithm
text: You met logarithms as the question 'which power?'. The log of 100 to base 10 is 2, because 10² = 100.
The natural logarithm asks the same question with base e: which power of e gives this number? It is written ln x. In calculus, and in these lessons, plain log x means this same base e logarithm.
So ln and e^x undo each other. If you raise e to a power and then take ln, you get the power back: ln(e^x) = x.

check.question: What is ln(e³)?

screens.ask: Find ln 1, ln e, ln(e²) and ln 7.39.

why: ln is the logarithm with base e: it asks "e to what power gives this number?" Any number to the power 0 is 1.
e to the power 1 is e itself.
ln undoes e to a power: the power is the answer.

practice.question: The number e is about
practice.why: The bank amounts settle on about 2.718, and that number is e.
wrong: That is π. e is about 2.718.
That is the amount when interest is added only twice. e is where the amounts settle.
That is the amount when interest is added once. e is where the amounts settle, about 2.718.

practice.question: What is ln(e⁵)?
practice.why: ln and e^x undo each other, so ln of e to the power 5 gives the power back: 5.
wrong: ln undoes the e, leaving only the power 5.
Nothing is multiplied by e. ln gives the power back.
ln 1 = 0, but here the power of e is 5.

practice.question: In calculus, plain log x with no base written means log to which base?
practice.why: In calculus, and in these lessons, plain log x means the natural logarithm, base e.
wrong: That was the meaning in earlier work. In calculus plain log means base e.
x is the number whose log is taken, not the base.
The base of the natural logarithm is e, about 2.718.

practice.question: ln x = 2. What is x?
practice.why: ln x = 2 means e to the power 2 gives x, so x = e².
wrong: The 2 is a power of e, not a multiplier.
That uses base 10. ln has base e.
2 is the power. x is e raised to that power.

rounds.question: What question does ln x ask?
options: What is x divided by e?
Which power of e gives x?
rounds.why: The natural logarithm asks: which power of e gives this number?
wrong: Base 10 is the ordinary log. ln uses base e.
A logarithm is a power, not a product.
A logarithm is a power, not the result of dividing.

rounds.question: What is ln(e⁹)?
rounds.why: ln and e^x undo each other: ln(e^x) = x. So ln(e⁹) = 9.
wrong: ln undoes the power of e and gives back the 9.
The answer is the power alone, with no e left.
ln e is 1. Here the power of e is 9.

rounds.question: ₹1 earns 100% interest a year, added more and more often. What happens to the amount at the end of the year?
rounds.why: Adding interest more often helps less and less. The amount settles on e, about 2.718.
wrong: It does not grow for ever. It settles on one number, e.
₹2 is for interest added once. More often gives more, up to about 2.718.
3.142 is π. This number is e, about 2.718.

rounds.question: ln x = 1. What is x?
rounds.why: ln x = 1 means e raised to the power 1 gives x. So x = e, about 2.718.
wrong: ln 1 is 0. For ln x = 1, x must be e.
10 would be right for base 10. ln uses base e.
ln 0 has no value. e to the power 1 is e.

rounds.question: What does e^x mean?
options: e raised to the power x
x raised to the power e
rounds.why: e^x means e raised to the power x. For example e^2 is about 7.39.
wrong: x is a power, not a multiplier.
Nothing is added. x is the power of e.
e is the base and x is the power, not the other way round.

rounds.question: What is ln 1?
rounds.why: e^0 = 1, so the power of e that gives 1 is 0. ln 1 = 0.
wrong: ln e is 1. For 1 the power needed is 0.
e is the base. The log is the power, which is 0.
It has a value: e^0 = 1, so ln 1 = 0.

rounds.question: e is about 2.718. About what is e^2?
rounds.why: e^2 means e × e, which is about 2.718 × 2.718 = 7.39.
wrong: That is 2 × e. e^2 means e × e.
That is e + 2. e^2 means e × e.
That is e ÷ 2. e^2 means e × e.

rounds.question: A calculator shows that ln 20 is about 3. What does that tell you?
rounds.why: ln 20 is the power of e that gives 20. So e raised to about 3 is 20.
wrong: The base is e and the result is 20, not the other way round.
ln uses base e, not base 10.
A logarithm is a power. 3 × e is only about 8.

entries.concept: a function of two variables f(x, y) and its partial derivatives f_x, f_y (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'The total differential and the linear approximation of f(x, y)' uses f(x, y), f_x and f_y before the partial-derivatives skill, and no lesson says what a function of two variables is.

screens.title: A function with two inputs
text: A rectangle's area depends on two things, its length x and its width y: area = xy.
A rule like this is a function of two variables, written f(x, y). Put in a pair of numbers, get one number out.
Its graph is a surface, like a hillside over a map: above each point (x, y) the height is f(x, y).

check.question: f(x, y) = xy. What is f(3, 4)?

why: Put the first number in for x and the second for y.
{if v1 = v2}Swapping the inputs gave the same answer here. That is luck: usually it changes.{else}Swapping the inputs changed the answer: {v1} against {v2}.{end}
The order matters: x always first, y second.

screens.title: Changing one input at a time
text: On a hillside, how steep it feels depends on which way you walk. Walk due east, so only x changes, and you feel one slope. Walk due north, so only y changes, and you feel another.

The slope when only x changes is called the partial derivative of f with respect to x. It is written ∂f/∂x, with a curly d, or f_x for short. To find it, treat y as a fixed number and differentiate in x as usual. The partial derivative with respect to y, written ∂f/∂y or f_y, treats x as the fixed number.
For a small step dx in x and dy in y together, the two effects add: f changes by about f_x × dx + f_y × dy.

check.question: f(x, y) = 5x + 2y. What is f_x?

screens.ask: f(x, y) = x²y. Find f_x and f_y at (3, 2), and estimate f(3.1, 2).

steps.do: f_x: treat y as a fixed number.
why: Differentiate with respect to x only. y behaves like a constant multiplier.

steps.do: f_y: treat x as a fixed number.
why: Now x² is the constant multiplier and y is the variable: the derivative of y is 1.

steps.do: Estimate a small step in x.
why: New value ≈ old value + slope × step. The estimate is very close because the step is small.

practice.question: What is ∂f/∂x called?
options: The partial derivative of f with respect to y
The value of f at x
The partial derivative of f with respect to x
practice.why: ∂f/∂x, also written f_x, is the slope when only x changes.
wrong: That is ∂f/∂y. The letter at the bottom tells which input changes.
A value is written f(x, y). ∂f/∂x is a slope.
The curly d signs are not numbers to divide. It means a slope in the x direction.

practice.question: f(x, y) = x² + 4y. What is f(3, 2)?
wrong: You swapped the inputs. In f(3, 2), x = 3 and y = 2.
You took x² as 2 × 3. x² means 3 × 3 = 9.
You added 4 and 2. 4y means 4 × 2.

practice.question: f(x, y) = xy². What is f_x?
practice.why: Treat y as a fixed number. The derivative of x times a number is that number: y².
wrong: That is f_y. For f_x, treat y as fixed and differentiate in x.
You differentiated y as well. For f_x, y² stays as a fixed number.
That adds f_x and f_y. f_x alone is y².

practice.question: At a point, f = 20, f_x = 3 and f_y = 5. You take a small step dx = 0.1 and dy = 0.2. About what is the new value of f?
practice.why: The change is about f_x × dx + f_y × dy = 0.3 + 1 = 1.3, so f is about 21.3.
wrong: That is only the change. Add it to the starting value 20.
You left out the y step. Add f_y × dy = 1 as well.
You added the slopes themselves. Multiply each by its small step first.

rounds.question: What does the graph of a function of two variables f(x, y) look like?
rounds.why: Above each point (x, y) of the map the height is f(x, y). Together these heights make a surface.
wrong: A curve is the graph of a function of one variable.
With two inputs the graph spreads over a whole map, as a surface.
Each pair (x, y) gives one point, but all of them together make a surface.

rounds.question: f(x, y) = 2x + y². What is f(1, 3)?
wrong: You swapped x and y. In f(1, 3), x = 1 and y = 3.
You did 3 × 2 for y². y² means 3 × 3.
You added 2 + 3. y² means 3 × 3 = 9.

rounds.question: f(x, y) = x² + 5y. What is f_y?
rounds.why: Treat x as a fixed number, so x² gives 0. 5y gives 5. So f_y = 5.
wrong: x is fixed for f_y, so x² gives 0, not 2x.
5y must be differentiated: it gives 5.
2x is f_x. For f_y, differentiate in y.

rounds.question: At a point, f = 50, f_x = 4 and f_y = −2. You take a small step dx = 0.5 and dy = 0.5. About what is the new value of f?
rounds.why: The change is about 4 × 0.5 + (−2) × 0.5 = 2 − 1 = 1. So f is about 50 + 1 = 51.
wrong: f_y is negative, so its part is −1, not +1.
1 is only the change. Add it to the old value 50.
The step in y matters too: it changes f by −1.

rounds.question: To find f_y, which letter do you treat as a fixed number?
rounds.why: f_y is the slope when only y changes. So x is treated as a fixed number.
wrong: y is the one that changes. x is held fixed.
f is the function being differentiated.
If both were fixed nothing would change. Only x is held fixed.

rounds.question: The area of a rectangle with length x and width y is f(x, y) = xy. What is f(6, 4)?
wrong: You added 6 and 4. xy means x × y.
That is the distance round the rectangle. The area is 6 × 4.
You wrote 6 and 4 side by side. xy means 6 × 4.

rounds.question: f(x, y) = 3xy. What is f_x?
rounds.why: Treat y as a fixed number. Then 3xy is (3y) × x, and its derivative in x is 3y.
wrong: 3x is f_y. For f_x, y is the fixed number.
y stays as a fixed number in the answer: 3y.
Only x changes for f_x. The answer is 3y alone.

rounds.question: On a hillside the height is f = 100 m and the slope to the east is f_x = 0.2. You walk 5 m due east, so dx = 5 and dy = 0. About how high are you now?
rounds.why: The change is about f_x × dx = 0.2 × 5 = 1. So the height is about 100 + 1 = 101 m.
wrong: You added the slope itself. Multiply it by the step: 0.2 × 5.
You added the step itself. Multiply it by the slope: 0.2 × 5.
1 m is only the change. Add it to the 100 m.

show.figure: a surface drawn over an x-y grid

entries.concept: second and higher derivatives and the notation f″, f⁽ⁿ⁾, d²y/dx²
entries.evidence: The Maclaurin lesson writes f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) and f″(a) although the skill on second-order derivatives comes later, and nothing before it says what these symbols mean.

screens.title: Differentiating again and again
text: Speed is how fast position changes. Acceleration is how fast speed changes: a derivative of a derivative.
Differentiate f to get f′. Differentiate f′ to get the second derivative f″ ('f double dash'), also written d²y/dx². It tells how fast the slope itself changes.
For the nth derivative we write f⁽ⁿ⁾(x). And f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) means: differentiate n times, then put x = 0.

check.question: f(x) = x². What is f″(x)?

screens.ask: f(x) = {@a}x³. Find its derivatives one after another.

why: Bring the power down: {a} × 3 = {b}. Then lower the power by one.
Differentiate {b}x²: {b} × 2 = {c}, and the power drops to 1.
The derivative of {c}x is {c}, like the slope of a straight line.
{c} is a constant: it does not change, so its derivative is 0. Every later one is 0 too.

practice.question: How is f″ read?
practice.why: f″ has two dashes and is read 'f double dash': the second derivative.
wrong: The dashes are not a power. They count how many times f is differentiated.
That is f′, with one dash. f″ has two.
Nothing is multiplied by 2. Two dashes mean differentiate twice.

practice.question: f(x) = 5x + 1. What is f″(x)?
practice.why: f′(x) = 5, and differentiating the constant 5 gives 0.
wrong: That is f′(x). Differentiate once more.
The constant 1 gives 0 when differentiated. f′ = 5 and f″ = 0.
Differentiating 5x + 1 gives 5, and differentiating again gives 0.

practice.question: f(x) = x³, so f′(x) = 3x² and f″(x) = 6x. What is f″(3)?
wrong: That is f′(3) = 3 × 9. Use the second derivative 6x.
Put x = 3 into 6x. 6 alone is the third derivative.
That is 3². Use f″(x) = 6x.

practice.question: A car's position at time t is f(t) = t². Its speed is f′(t). What is its acceleration f″(t)?
practice.why: f′(t) = 2t, and differentiating 2t gives 2.
wrong: That is the speed f′(t). Differentiate once more for acceleration.
That is the position. Differentiate twice for acceleration.
That is the third derivative. Acceleration is the second: 2.

rounds.question: What does f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) mean?
rounds.why: The number in small brackets counts derivatives. f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) means f differentiated n times.
wrong: The small brackets show it is not a power.
Nothing is multiplied. n counts how many times to differentiate.
The input is still x. n counts how many times to differentiate.

rounds.question: f′(x) = 2x + 9. What is f″(x)?
rounds.why: f″ is the derivative of f′. The derivative of 2x + 9 is 2.
wrong: 2x must be differentiated: it gives 2.
The constant 9 gives 0. The slope of 2x + 9 is 2.
You added 2 and 9. The constant gives 0.

rounds.question: f(x) = x² + 3x. What is f′(0)?
rounds.why: Differentiate first: f′(x) = 2x + 3. Then put x = 0: f′(0) = 3.
wrong: You put x = 0 first and then differentiated a number. Differentiate first.
That is f′(1). At x = 0, 2x is 0.

rounds.question: A train's speed at time t is f′(t) = 6t. What is its acceleration f″(t)?
rounds.why: Acceleration is the derivative of speed. The derivative of 6t is 6.
wrong: 6t is the speed. Differentiate it once more.
0 would be the derivative of a steady speed. 6t gives 6.
3t² is the position, going the other way. Differentiate 6t.

rounds.question: d²y/dx² is another way to write
rounds.why: d²y/dx² is the second derivative, the same thing as f″.
wrong: The small 2s are not squares. They mean 'differentiate twice'.
The first derivative is dy/dx.
It is the derivative of dy/dx, not double it.

rounds.question: f(x) = x² + 7x. What is f″(x)?
rounds.why: f′(x) = 2x + 7. Differentiate again: f″(x) = 2.
wrong: That is f′(x). Differentiate once more.
You added 2 and 7. The constant 7 gives 0.
0 is the third derivative. The second derivative is 2.

rounds.question: f(x) = x³ has third derivative f⁽³⁾(x) = 6. What is f⁽³⁾(0)?
rounds.why: f⁽³⁾(x) is 6 for every x. So at x = 0 it is still 6.
wrong: There is no x in 6 for the 0 to replace. It stays 6.
3 is the number of times you differentiate, not the value.
Nothing is multiplied by 3. The value is 6.

rounds.question: A lift moves at a steady speed f′(t) = 3. What is its acceleration f″(t)?
rounds.why: Acceleration is the derivative of speed. The derivative of the constant 3 is 0.
wrong: 3 is the speed. A steady speed does not change, so its derivative is 0.
3t is the position, going the other way.
A constant has slope 0, not 1.

entries.concept: what a series for a function is (a function written as an endless polynomial) and where its coefficients come from
entries.evidence: The lesson begins 'A Maclaurin series writes f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) xⁿ/n!' with no word on what it means to write a function as a series or why anyone would.

screens.title: A function as an endless polynomial
text: How does a calculator find e^0.1 or sin 0.1? It cannot look them up. But it is very good at adding and multiplying, and that is all a polynomial needs.

So the idea is to write a hard function as a polynomial that goes on for ever: a + bx + cx² + dx³ + ... Such an endless sum is called a series. The numbers a, b, c, d, ... in front of the powers are its coefficients.

You already know one. The geometric series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... adds up to 1 ÷ (1 − x) when x is between −1 and 1. So the function 1 ÷ (1 − x) is equal to that series. When x is small, the first few terms already give a very good value.

check.question: In the series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ..., what is the coefficient of x²?

screens.ask: Approximate 1 ÷ (1 − x) at x = 0.1 with 1 + x + x² + …

why: First work out 1 − 0.1, which is 0.9.
Start with the first two terms of the series.
Each new term is ten times smaller, so each adds one more correct digit.

screens.title: Where the coefficients come from
text: A Maclaurin series is the series of a function in powers of x. Its coefficients come from the derivatives of the function at 0: the coefficient of x to the power n is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) ÷ n!. Here n! means n × (n − 1) × ... × 2 × 1, so 3! = 6. The sign Σ in the formula only means 'add up all such terms'.

Why does this work? Put x = 0 in the series: only the constant term is left, so it must be f(0). Differentiate once and put x = 0: only the coefficient of x is left, so it is f′(0). Differentiate twice and put x = 0: you get 2 × (coefficient of x²), so that coefficient is f″(0) ÷ 2. Each further step works the same way.
A Taylor series about x = a does the same thing in powers of (x − a), using the derivatives at a instead of at 0. It is the right tool when you care about x near a.

check.question: In the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of x²?

screens.ask: Build the series for eˣ and test it at x = 1.

why: eˣ is the function that is its own derivative.
The Maclaurin rule: the coefficient of xⁿ is the n-th derivative at 0, divided by n! (n factorial: 1 × 2 × … × n).
Four terms already come close to e = 2.718…

practice.question: In a series a + bx + cx² + dx³ + ..., what are the numbers a, b, c, d called?
practice.why: The numbers in front of the powers of x are the coefficients of the series.
wrong: The coefficients come from derivatives, but the numbers in front of the powers are called coefficients.
A factorial is n!. The numbers in front of the powers are coefficients.
The powers are the small numbers on x. The numbers in front are coefficients.

practice.question: Use the first three terms of 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... to estimate 1 ÷ (1 − x) at x = 0.2.
wrong: That uses only two terms. Add x² = 0.04 as well.
You took x² as 2 × 0.2. x² means 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04.
That is the exact value 1 ÷ 0.8. Three terms give 1.24.

practice.question: In the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of x³?
practice.why: The coefficient of x to the power n is 1 ÷ n!, and 3! = 6.
wrong: Divide by 3!, not by 3. 3! = 6.
Each derivative at 0 is 1, but it must still be divided by 3!.
3! goes underneath: the coefficient is 1 ÷ 6.

practice.question: A function has f(0) = 2, f′(0) = 3 and f″(0) = 8. What is the coefficient of x² in its Maclaurin series?
practice.why: The coefficient of x² is f″(0) ÷ 2! = 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
wrong: f″(0) must be divided by 2! = 2.
That is f′(0), the coefficient of x.
You multiplied by 2. Divide f″(0) by 2!.

rounds.question: An endless sum such as a + bx + cx² + dx³ + ... is called
rounds.why: A polynomial that goes on for ever is called a series.
wrong: The coefficients are the numbers a, b, c, d in front of the powers.
Derivatives give the coefficients. The endless sum is a series.
n! is a factorial. The endless sum is a series.

rounds.question: Use the first three terms of 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... to estimate 1 ÷ (1 − x) at x = 0.3.
wrong: That is only two terms. Add x² = 0.09.
You took 0.3² as 0.6. It is 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09.
You used 0.3 again for x². It is 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09.

rounds.question: In the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of x⁴?
rounds.why: The coefficient of x to the power n is 1 ÷ n!. For n = 4, 4! = 24, so it is 1/24.
wrong: Divide by 4!, not by 4. 4! = 24.
It is 1 ÷ 4!, not 4! itself.
Every derivative at 0 is 1, but it must be divided by 4!.

rounds.question: A function has f⁽³⁾(0) = 12. What is the coefficient of x³ in its Maclaurin series?
rounds.why: The coefficient is f⁽³⁾(0) ÷ 3! = 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
wrong: The derivative must be divided by 3! = 6.
Divide by 3! = 6, not by 3.
You multiplied by 3. Divide by 3! = 6.

rounds.question: A Taylor series about x = a is written in powers of
rounds.why: A Taylor series about x = a uses powers of (x − a) and the derivatives at a.
wrong: Powers of x give the Maclaurin series, which is about 0.
a is a fixed number. The powers are of (x − a).
The sign is minus: (x − a) is 0 when x = a.

rounds.question: e^x = 1 + x + x² ÷ 2 + ... Use these three terms to estimate e^0.2.
wrong: That is only two terms. Add x² ÷ 2 = 0.02.
You forgot to divide x² by 2: 0.04 ÷ 2 = 0.02.
You took 0.2² as 0.4. It is 0.04.

rounds.question: In the Maclaurin series of f, what does the constant term equal?
rounds.why: Put x = 0 in the series: every term with x vanishes and only the constant is left. So it is f(0).
wrong: f′(0) is the coefficient of x.
The terms with x become 0, but the constant stays and equals f(0).
The series is put at x = 0, not x = 1.

rounds.question: The series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... adds up to 1 ÷ (1 − x) only for some x. For which of these x does it work?
rounds.why: It works when x is between −1 and 1. Only 0.5 is.
wrong: 2 is not between −1 and 1. The terms 1, 2, 4, 8 keep growing.
−3 is not between −1 and 1. The terms keep growing in size.
At x = 1 the terms are 1 + 1 + 1 + ..., and 1 ÷ 0 has no value.

entries.concept: the coordinate plane: x-axis, y-axis, origin, and what the two coordinates mean
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A point (x, y) is x across from the origin, then y up' without saying what the axes, the origin or coordinates are.

screens.title: Two number lines make a map
text: 'Third column, second row' tells a friend where you sit. Two numbers find the place.

check.question: Start at the origin, go 2 to the right and then 5 up. What are the coordinates of the point you reach?

screens.ask: Find the point ({@x}, {@y}). Is it the same as ({y}, {x})?

why: The origin is where the two number lines cross. Both read 0 there.
The first number always says how far across, along the flat line.
The second number says how far up, along the upright line.
That lands somewhere else. The order matters.

screens.note: Use two different numbers, so that swapping them gives a new point.
after: The flat number line is the x-axis. The upright one is the y-axis. They cross at the origin.
Right and up are positive. Left and down are negative.
The two numbers are the coordinates: the x-coordinate first, then the y-coordinate.

practice.question: What is the point where the x-axis and the y-axis cross called?
practice.why: The two axes cross at the origin, where both number lines read 0.
wrong: The x-axis is the whole flat number line. The crossing point is the origin.
A coordinate is one of the two numbers of a point. The crossing point is the origin.
The y-axis is the whole upright number line. The crossing point is the origin.

practice.question: Start at the origin, go 5 to the right and then 1 up. What are the coordinates of the point?
practice.why: The first number is how far across (5) and the second is how far up (1).
wrong: The order is swapped. Across comes first, then up.
You went 1 up, so the second number is 1, not 0.
You added the two moves. Write them separately: across, then up.

practice.question: How do you reach the point (−3, 2) from the origin?
practice.why: The x-coordinate −3 means 3 to the left. The y-coordinate 2 means 2 up.
wrong: A negative x-coordinate means go left, not right.
The first number goes with across and it is 3. The second is 2 up.
The first number is across, not down. −3 means 3 to the left.

practice.question: In a hall, a seat at (across, up) tells how far across and how far up it is. Anu sits at (2, 6). Balu sits 3 seats to her right in the same row. Where does Balu sit?
practice.why: Moving right changes only the first number: 2 + 3 = 5. The row stays 6.
wrong: Moving right changes the first number, not the second.
Only the first number changes. The row stays 6.
That is 3 to the left. Right means add: 2 + 3.

rounds.question: What is the number line that lies flat called?
rounds.why: The number line lying flat is the x-axis.
wrong: The y-axis is the number line standing straight up.
The origin is the point where the two axes cross.
A coordinate is one of the two numbers of a point.

rounds.question: Start at the origin, go 2 to the right and then 7 up. What are the coordinates of the point?
rounds.why: Across comes first, then up: 2 across and 7 up is (2, 7).
wrong: The order is swapped. How far across comes first.
The two moves are not added. Each gets its own number.
The two moves are not added. Each gets its own number.

rounds.question: How do you reach the point (4, −5) from the origin?
rounds.why: The x-coordinate 4 is positive: 4 right. The y-coordinate −5 is negative: 5 down.
wrong: The signs are on the wrong numbers. 4 is positive (right) and −5 is negative (down).
The numbers are swapped. The first number, 4, is how far across.
−5 is negative, so go down, not up.

rounds.question: On a treasure map a tree is at (3, 1). The treasure is 4 steps straight up from the tree. Where is the treasure?
rounds.why: Going up changes only the second number: 1 + 4 = 5. The treasure is at (3, 5).
wrong: You changed the first number. That would be 4 steps to the right.
You added 4 to both numbers. Only the up-and-down number changes.
You went 4 down. Up means add 4 to the second number.

rounds.question: In the point (6, 2), what does the first number tell you?
rounds.why: The first number is the x-coordinate. It says how far across the point is.
wrong: How far up or down is the second number, the y-coordinate.
It is only the distance across, not the whole distance from the origin.
The numbers give a position, not a count.

rounds.question: What are the coordinates of the origin?
rounds.why: Both number lines read 0 at the origin. So it is (0, 0).
wrong: Both axes read 0 at the origin, not 1.
The y-axis also reads 0 at the origin.
The x-axis also reads 0 at the origin.

rounds.question: Where is the point (0, −4)?
options: On the x-axis, 4 to the left
On the x-axis, 4 to the right
On the y-axis, 4 above the origin
On the y-axis, 4 below the origin
rounds.why: The x-coordinate is 0, so the point is not moved across: it is on the y-axis. −4 means 4 down.
wrong: The first number is 0, so there is no move left or right.
The first number is 0, so there is no move left or right.
−4 is negative, so the point is below the origin.

rounds.question: A game piece at (5, 4) moves 2 squares to the left and 1 square down. Where is it now?
rounds.why: Left takes 2 from the first number: 5 − 2 = 3. Down takes 1 from the second: 4 − 1 = 3.
wrong: You added. Left and down both take away.
Down takes 1 from the second number: 4 − 1 = 3.
The moves went on the wrong numbers. Left changes the first number.

entries.concept: why an equation in x and y can be a circle: x² + y² = r² and (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts from 'x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0' and completes the square; that a circle is the set of points at distance r from the centre, and so has such an equation, is only said seven lessons later.

screens.title: A circle as an equation
text: Tie a goat to a post with a 5 metre rope. Pulled tight, it walks a circle: every point is 5 m from the post.
A point (x, y) is √(x² + y²) from the origin. So the circle of radius r about the origin is x² + y² = r².
With centre (h, k) it is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Multiply out for the general form. Completing the square takes you back.

check.question: What is the radius of the circle x² + y² = 49?

screens.ask: Write the circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 5, and test two points. Then move the centre to ({@h}, {@k}), radius {@r}.

why: Every point on the circle is 5 from the centre. By Pythagoras, x² + y² is the square of that distance.
Equal to 25 means exactly on the circle. Less means closer than 5: inside.
Measure across and up from the new centre: x − {h} and y − {k}.
(x − {h})² = x² − {h2}x + {hh} and (y − {k})² = y² − {k2}y + {kk}. Then move {rr} across: {hh} + {kk} − {rr} = {if c < 0}−{nc}{else}{c}{end}.

practice.question: A circle is all the points at one fixed distance from one point. What is the fixed distance called?
practice.why: The fixed distance from the centre to every point of the circle is the radius.
wrong: The centre is the fixed point. The fixed distance is the radius.
The origin is the point (0, 0). The fixed distance is the radius.
The equation describes the circle. The fixed distance is the radius.

practice.question: What is the equation of the circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 6?
practice.why: x² + y² = r², and r² = 6² = 36.
wrong: The right side is r², not r: 6² = 36.
You doubled 6. r² means 6 × 6.
That is a straight line. The distance formula squares x and y.

practice.question: What is the centre of the circle (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 16?
practice.why: Compare with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²: h = 3, and y + 2 = y − (−2), so k = −2.
wrong: The signs are reversed. x − 3 gives h = 3 and y + 2 gives k = −2.
y + 2 means y − (−2), so k = −2.
x − 3 gives h = 3, not −3.

practice.question: A goat is tied to a post at (0, 0) with a 10 metre rope. Which spot is closer than 10 metres to the post?
practice.why: 25 + 64 = 89, which is less than 100, so the spot is inside the circle x² + y² = 100.
wrong: 36 + 64 = 100, so this spot is exactly 10 metres away, on the circle.
81 + 25 = 106, more than 100. Both numbers being under 10 is not enough.
0 + 121 = 121, more than 100. It is 11 metres away.

rounds.question: The fixed point that every point of a circle is equally far from is called
rounds.why: A circle is all the points at one fixed distance from one point. That point is the centre.
wrong: The radius is the fixed distance, not the point.
The centre can be at the origin, but it need not be.
The diameter is the width of the circle, not a point.

rounds.question: Where is the point (5, 12) for the circle x² + y² = 169?
rounds.why: 25 + 144 = 169, which equals r². So the point is on the circle.
wrong: Inside would need x² + y² less than 169. Here it is exactly 169.
Outside would need x² + y² more than 169. Here it is exactly 169.
The centre is (0, 0).

rounds.question: What is the centre of the circle (x + 1)² + (y − 4)² = 25?
rounds.why: Compare with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². x + 1 is x − (−1), so h = −1, and k = 4.
wrong: Both signs are flipped the wrong way. x + 1 gives −1 and y − 4 gives 4.
x + 1 means x − (−1), so the first coordinate is −1.
y − 4 gives k = 4, not −4.

rounds.question: A sprinkler at (0, 0) waters every spot closer than 5 metres. Which spot stays dry?
rounds.why: For (4, 4): 16 + 16 = 32, which is more than 25. It is further than 5 metres away.
wrong: 9 + 9 = 18 is less than 25, so this spot is watered.
16 + 4 = 20 is less than 25, so this spot is watered.
1 + 16 = 17 is less than 25, so this spot is watered.

rounds.question: From which form can you read off the centre and the radius of a circle?
rounds.why: In (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² the centre is (h, k) and the radius is r.
wrong: A circle's equation has x² and y². This is a straight line.
The squares are added for a circle, not subtracted.
The brackets must be squared. They come from the distance formula.

rounds.question: What is the equation of the circle with centre (4, 1) and radius 2?
rounds.why: Put h = 4, k = 1 and r = 2 into (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². r² = 4.
wrong: The brackets are x − h and y − k, with minus signs.
The right side is r² = 4, not r.
h goes with x and k with y. The centre is (4, 1).

rounds.question: What is the radius of the circle (x − 2)² + (y − 5)² = 64?
rounds.why: The right side is r². r² = 64, so r = 8.
wrong: 64 is r². Take its square root.
You halved 64. The radius is the square root of 64.
16 is the diameter. The radius is 8.

rounds.question: A lighthouse at (0, 0) lights every boat closer than 13 km. Which boat does it light?
rounds.why: For (5, 11): 25 + 121 = 146, which is less than 13² = 169.
wrong: 144 + 36 = 180 is more than 169, so it is too far.
100 + 81 = 181 is more than 169, so it is too far.
0 + 196 = 196 is more than 169, so it is too far.

entries.concept: what an ellipse and a hyperbola are, and their parts (foci, centre, vertices, a, b, c, eccentricity)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Eccentricity of an ellipse or a hyperbola' uses e = c/a, foci, semi-axis and c² = a² ∓ b² straight away; no lesson says what an ellipse or a hyperbola is.

screens.title: The ellipse: an oval from two pins
text: Push two pins into a board. Lay a loose loop of string round them, pull it tight with a pencil, and move the pencil all the way round. You draw an oval called an ellipse. The string does not change length, so for every point on the curve, (distance to one pin) + (distance to the other pin) is the same.

Each pin is a focus (plural: foci). The point midway between the foci is the centre. The longest width, through the foci, is the major axis, and half of it is called a. The shortest width is the minor axis, and half of it is b. The ends of the major axis are the vertices. The distance from the centre to a focus is c.
With the centre at the origin and the foci on the x-axis, the equation is x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, and c² = a² − b². The fixed sum of the two distances is 2a.

check.question: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, how long is the major axis?

v.says: An ellipse with centre at the origin, reaching 5 left and right and 3 up and down. Its two foci are at 4 left and 4 right of the centre. A point P at the top is joined to both foci.

figures.caption: x²/25 + y²/9 = 1. The foci F₁ and F₂ are at (−4, 0) and (4, 0). For P at the top, PF₁ = 5 and PF₂ = 5: the two distances add up to 10, as they do for every point on the curve.

screens.ask: For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, find the foci and check the sum of distances.

why: a is how far the ellipse reaches left and right; b how far up and down.
The foci are the two "pins" on the long axis.
√(4² + 3²) = 5 each. Every point on the ellipse has the same sum, 2a.

screens.title: The hyperbola: two branches
text: Look at the edge of the light that a table lamp with a round shade throws on the wall. That curve is a hyperbola. It comes from keeping the difference of the two distances to the foci fixed, instead of their sum. The result is two separate branches that open away from each other.

There are still two foci, and a centre midway between them. The two points where the curve crosses the line through the foci are the vertices. The distance from the centre to a vertex is a, and the segment joining the vertices is the transverse axis, of length 2a. The distance from the centre to a focus is c. Now c is bigger than a.
With the centre at the origin and the foci on the x-axis, the equation is x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, and c² = a² + b². The fixed difference of the distances is 2a.
The eccentricity e = c ÷ a says how far a curve is from being a circle. For a circle it is 0, for an ellipse it is between 0 and 1, and for a hyperbola it is more than 1.

check.question: An ellipse has a = 5 and c = 4. What is its eccentricity?

screens.ask: For x²/9 − y²/16 = 1, find the foci, the difference of distances and e.

why: The minus sign makes it a hyperbola.
For a hyperbola c² is a² plus b² (for an ellipse it was minus).
For a hyperbola the difference of the distances to the foci is always 2a.
e > 1 for every hyperbola; e < 1 for every ellipse.

practice.question: An ellipse is drawn with a loop of string round two pins. What is each pin called?
practice.why: Each pin is a focus. The two together are the foci.
wrong: The vertices are the ends of the major axis, on the curve itself.
The centre is the point midway between the two pins.
An axis is a width of the ellipse, not a point.

practice.question: For the ellipse x²/100 + y²/36 = 1, what is c?
practice.why: For an ellipse c² = a² − b² = 100 − 36 = 64, so c = 8.
wrong: That is c². Take the square root.
You added. For an ellipse c² = a² − b².
That is a − b = 10 − 6. Use c² = a² − b².

practice.question: For the hyperbola x²/16 − y²/9 = 1, what is c?
practice.why: For a hyperbola c² = a² + b² = 16 + 9 = 25, so c = 5.
wrong: That uses the ellipse rule a² − b². For a hyperbola c² = a² + b².
That is c². Take the square root.
That is a + b = 4 + 3. Use c² = a² + b².

practice.question: A curve has a = 4 and c = 5. What kind of curve is it?
practice.why: e = c ÷ a = 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25, which is more than 1, so it is a hyperbola.
wrong: You did a ÷ c. The eccentricity is c ÷ a = 1.25.
e is right, but an ellipse has e between 0 and 1.

rounds.question: What are the ends of the major axis of an ellipse called?
rounds.why: The ends of the major axis, the longest width, are the vertices.
wrong: The foci are the two pins, inside the ellipse.
The centre is the point midway between the foci.
The minor axis is the shortest width.

rounds.question: For the ellipse x²/169 + y²/25 = 1, what is c?
rounds.why: For an ellipse c² = a² − b² = 169 − 25 = 144. So c = 12.
wrong: 144 is c². Take its square root.
You added a² and b². For an ellipse they are subtracted.
You did a − b = 13 − 5. Use c² = a² − b².

rounds.question: For the hyperbola x²/25 − y²/144 = 1, what is c?
rounds.why: For a hyperbola c² = a² + b² = 25 + 144 = 169. So c = 13.
wrong: You subtracted, as for an ellipse. For a hyperbola c² = a² + b².
169 is c². Take its square root.
You did a + b = 5 + 12. Use c² = a² + b².

rounds.question: A curve has a = 10 and c = 6. What kind of curve is it?
rounds.why: e = c ÷ a = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6. That is between 0 and 1, so it is an ellipse.
wrong: A hyperbola has e more than 1. 0.6 is between 0 and 1.
You did a ÷ c. Eccentricity is c ÷ a.
e is 0 only when c is 0. Here e = 6 ÷ 10.

rounds.question: What stays fixed for every point on a hyperbola?
options: The sum of its distances to the two foci
The difference of its distances to the two foci
The product of its distances to the two foci
rounds.why: A hyperbola keeps the difference of the two distances to the foci fixed.
wrong: A fixed sum gives an ellipse.
A fixed distance to one point gives a circle.
It is the difference that stays fixed, equal to 2a.

rounds.question: For the hyperbola x²/36 − y²/64 = 1, how long is the transverse axis?
rounds.why: a² = 36, so a = 6. The transverse axis joins the vertices and has length 2a = 12.
wrong: 6 is a, from the centre to a vertex. The axis is 2a.
36 is a². The axis is 2a with a = 6.
16 is 2b. The transverse axis uses a.

rounds.question: For every point on the ellipse x²/49 + y²/16 = 1, what is the sum of its distances to the two foci?
rounds.why: a² = 49, so a = 7. The fixed sum is 2a = 14.
wrong: 7 is a. The sum is 2a.
49 is a². The sum is 2a with a = 7.
8 is 2b. The sum uses a, half the major axis.

rounds.question: A loop of string round two pins draws an ellipse with a = 5. Each pin is 3 from the centre, so c = 3. What is b?
rounds.why: c² = a² − b², so b² = 25 − 9 = 16 and b = 4.
wrong: 16 is b². Take its square root.
You added 25 and 9. For an ellipse b² = a² − c².
You did a − c = 5 − 3. Use b² = a² − c².

entries.concept: the absolute value bars | |
entries.evidence: The area formula 'Area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + ...|' and the step '½ × |−10| = 5' use the bars, but absolute value is only taught in a class 11 skill.

screens.title: The bars mean distance from 0
text: |x| is how far x is from 0. A distance is never negative.

check.question: What is |−7|?

why: −{n} is {n} steps from zero. The bars ask how far, not which way.
A positive number is already its own distance from zero.
Zero is no distance from itself.
Do the bars first, then multiply. The area formula does this, so an area is never negative.

scene.prompt: Slide the point to −4. Watch its distance from 0.
scene.success: −4 is 4 from 0, so |−4| = 4. The same as |4|.

screens.note: Use an even number, so that half of it is whole.
after: The area formula gives a plus answer going round a shape one way and a minus answer the other way. The bars keep the size and drop the direction.

practice.question: What is the absolute value of a number?
options: The number with a minus sign put on
The number with its sign changed
practice.why: The absolute value is how far the number is from 0 on the number line.
wrong: The bars remove a minus sign. They never add one.
The bars do not square. They give the distance from 0.
A positive number stays as it is. Only a minus sign is removed.

practice.question: What is |−12|?
practice.why: −12 is 12 steps from 0, so |−12| = 12.
wrong: The bars remove the minus sign. A distance is not negative.
0 is where the distance is measured from. −12 is 12 steps away.
The bars do not turn the number over. They give the distance from 0.

practice.question: Which statement is true?
practice.why: −6 and 6 are both 6 steps from 0, so both bars give 6.
wrong: An absolute value is never negative. |−6| = 6.
−6 is less than 5, but its size 6 is more than 5.
The bars leave a positive number as it is. |6| = 6.

practice.question: A formula for the area of a triangle gives ½ × |−18|. What is the area?
wrong: The bars remove the minus sign first. An area cannot be negative.
You forgot the ½. Half of 18 is 9.
The bars remove the minus sign, and then you halve: ½ × 18.

rounds.question: How is the absolute value of −3 written?
rounds.why: Absolute value is written with two upright bars: |−3|.
wrong: Curly brackets are used for sets. Absolute value uses upright bars.
Round brackets only group. Absolute value uses upright bars.
A minus sign in front changes the sign. Absolute value uses upright bars.

rounds.question: What is |−25|?
rounds.why: −25 is 25 steps from 0. The bars remove the minus sign: |−25| = 25.
wrong: The bars remove the minus sign. A distance is never negative.
5 is the square root of 25. The bars only remove the sign.
Only |0| is 0. −25 is 25 steps from 0.

rounds.question: What is |−4| + |3|?
rounds.why: |−4| = 4 and |3| = 3. So the sum is 4 + 3 = 7.
wrong: You added −4 and 3. Take the bars first: 4 + 3.
You took 3 from 4. Both sizes are added: 4 + 3.
The bars leave 3 positive and make −4 into 4. Nothing becomes negative.

rounds.question: A diver is at −15 metres, which means 15 metres below the surface of the sea. How far is the diver from the surface?
rounds.why: A distance does not care about direction. |−15| = 15.
wrong: A distance is never negative. Take the absolute value.
The diver is not at the surface. The distance is 15 metres.
The distance is not doubled. |−15| = 15.

rounds.question: Why are the bars used in an area formula built from coordinates?
options: The formula can come out negative, but an area never is
To turn a positive answer negative
rounds.why: Depending on the order of the points, the formula can give a negative number. The bars make it positive, as an area must be.
wrong: The bars do not change the size, only the sign.
The bars never make a number negative.
Halving is done by the ½. The bars only remove a minus sign.

rounds.question: What is |7|?
rounds.why: The bars leave a positive number as it is. |7| = 7.
wrong: The bars never put a minus sign on.
Only |0| is 0. 7 is 7 steps from 0.
Nothing is doubled. 7 is 7 steps from 0.

rounds.question: Which is bigger, |−9| or |4|?
rounds.why: |−9| = 9 and |4| = 4. 9 is more than 4.
wrong: Compare the sizes after the bars: 9 and 4.
|−9| = 9 and |4| = 4. These are different.
The bars turn −9 into 9, not 0.

rounds.question: Going round the corners of a field one way, an area formula gives −40 square metres. The area is the absolute value of this. What is the area?
rounds.why: |−40| = 40. An area can never be negative.
wrong: An area is never negative. Take the absolute value.
The bars remove the sign. They do not make the number 0.
Nothing is halved here. |−40| = 40.

entries.concept: three coordinates (x, y, z) for a point in space, and the z-axis
entries.evidence: The first lesson finds the distance between P(4, −2, 0) and Q(1, −5, −3) 'across the floor (x and y) and then up (z)' without any lesson saying what a third coordinate or the z-axis is.

screens.title: A third number for height
text: A fly is somewhere in your room. Saying '2 metres from this wall and 3 metres from that wall' fixes only a spot on the floor. The fly may be above it. You need a third number: its height.

In space we use three axes that meet at the origin, each at right angles to the other two. Think of a corner of the room: the x-axis and the y-axis run along the floor, and the z-axis runs straight up.

A point is written (x, y, z). To reach it from the origin, go x along the x-axis, then y in the direction of the y-axis, then z straight up (or down if z is negative). Points on the floor have z = 0, so (2, 3, 0) is the floor point directly below (2, 3, 4).

check.question: How high above the floor (the plane z = 0) is the point (5, 1, 7)?

v.says: Three axes x, y and z meeting at the origin O. A path goes 2 along x, then 3 along y, then 4 up, to the point (2, 3, 4).

figures.caption: To reach (2, 3, 4): go 2 along x, then 3 along y, then 4 up.

screens.ask: How far is (2, 3, 4) from the origin?

why: The three numbers are three moves at right angles.
On the floor, Pythagoras gives the square of the diagonal.
The upward move is at right angles to the floor diagonal, so use Pythagoras again.
In general, distance = √(x² + y² + z²).

practice.question: In the point (x, y, z), which number gives the height above the floor?
practice.why: The z-axis runs straight up, so z is the height above the floor z = 0.
wrong: x is a distance along the floor, not up; height is z.
y is a distance along the floor, not up; height is z.
Adding x and y still stays on the floor; height is the third number z.

practice.question: Which floor point (z = 0) lies directly below (4, 1, 6)?
practice.why: Directly below keeps x and y the same and makes z = 0, giving (4, 1, 0).
wrong: You kept the height and dropped x and y; keep x and y and set z to 0.
You set y to 0 instead of z; the floor is z = 0.
You set x to 0 instead of z; the floor is z = 0.

practice.question: How far is the point (1, 2, 2) from the origin?
wrong: You added the coordinates; add their squares and then take the square root.
You stopped at 9; the distance is the square root of 9.
You left out z; after the floor step 1² + 2² = 5, add 2² as well.

practice.question: A point is at (2, 5, −3). Where is it compared with the floor z = 0?
practice.why: z = −3, and a negative z means go down, so the point is 3 below the floor.
wrong: You ignored the minus sign; a negative z means down.
You read x; the height comes from z, which is −3.
You read y; the height comes from z, which is −3.

rounds.question: How many numbers are needed to fix a point in space?
rounds.why: A point in space is written (x, y, z): two numbers for the floor spot and a third for the height.
wrong: One number fixes a place on a line only; space needs x, y and z.
Two numbers fix only a spot on the floor; the height z is still missing.
There are only three axes, so three numbers are enough.

rounds.question: To reach (5, 2, 7) from the origin, how far do you go straight up?
rounds.why: The third number is z, the distance straight up. Here z = 7.
wrong: 5 is x, the distance along the x-axis; the height is the third number.
2 is y, the distance in the y direction; the height is the third number.
You added all three numbers; only z, the third one, is the height.

rounds.question: How far is the point (2, 3, 6) from the origin?
wrong: You added the coordinates; square each one, add, then take the square root.
49 is the sum of the squares; you still have to take the square root.
You left out z; add 6² as well: 13 + 36 = 49.

rounds.question: A drone is at (3, 4, 10) and a bird is at (3, 4, 6), in metres, with the ground as z = 0. How far above the bird is the drone?
rounds.why: Both are above the same floor point (3, 4, 0). The heights are 10 and 6, and 10 − 6 = 4.
wrong: You added the two heights; the gap between them is 10 − 6.
10 m is the drone's height above the ground, not above the bird.
6 m is the bird's height above the ground; the gap is 10 − 6.

rounds.question: Every point on the floor has which coordinate equal to 0?
rounds.why: z is the height above the floor, so on the floor z = 0.
wrong: x measures along the floor; it is the height z that is 0.
y measures along the floor; it is the height z that is 0.
x and y can be anything on the floor; only the height z must be 0.

rounds.question: Which point is 3 straight above the floor point (6, 2, 0)?
rounds.why: Going straight up changes only z. So z goes from 0 to 3 and the point is (6, 2, 3).
wrong: You added 3 to x; that moves along the floor. Going up changes z.
You added 3 to y; that moves along the floor. Going up changes z.
You added 3 to every number; only z changes when you go straight up.

rounds.question: How far is the point (−2, 1, 2) from the origin?
wrong: You took (−2)² as −4; a square is never negative: (−2)² = 4.
9 is the sum of the squares; take its square root.
You added the sizes 2 + 1 + 2; square each one first, then take the root.

rounds.question: A corner of a room is the origin. A bulb is 1 m along x, 2 m along y and 3 m up. What are its coordinates?
rounds.why: The order is (x, y, z): 1 along x, 2 along y, 3 up.
wrong: You put the height first; the order is x, then y, then the height z last.
That is the floor point below the bulb; the bulb is 3 up, so z = 3.
You swapped x and y; x comes first and here x = 1.

entries.concept: the vector equation of a line r = a + λb (a point plus multiples of a direction), the parameter λ, direction ratios
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Parallel, intersecting or skew lines' gives lines as r⃗ = (…) + λ(…) and the first worked example says 'Direction ratios: B − A', before the form is explained four lessons later; direction ratios are never defined.

screens.title: A line is a start point plus steps
text: To describe a straight road, you can name one place on it and say which way it runs. A line in space is described the same way.

Let a be the position vector of one known point of the line, and let b be a vector that points along the line. Start at a and add any amount of b: r = a + λb. Here λ (the Greek letter lambda) is any number, positive, negative or a fraction. It is called a parameter. Each value of λ gives one point of the line, and every point of the line comes from some λ. A second line usually uses another letter, μ (mu).

The three components of b are called direction ratios of the line. Any multiple of b points along the same line, so (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6) are direction ratios of the same direction. Divide them by the length of b and you get the direction cosines.

check.question: On the line r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(2, 1, −1), which point has λ = 2?

screens.ask: Write the line through (1, 0, 2) with direction (2, 1, −1) and find three points on it.

why: Start at the point, then take λ steps of the direction. λ can be any number, so every point of the line is reached.
No steps: the start point.
One whole step forward along the direction.
A negative λ walks backwards along the same line.

practice.question: In r = a + λb, what is λ called?
practice.why: λ is the number that changes; each value gives one point of the line. It is called a parameter.
wrong: Direction ratios are the components of b, not λ.
The position vector of the known point is a, not λ.
Direction cosines come from dividing b by its length; λ is the parameter.

practice.question: On the line r = (2, 1, 0) + λ(1, 3, 2), which point has λ = 2?
wrong: You used λ = 1; multiply the direction by 2.
You forgot to add the start point (2, 1, 0).
You doubled the start point instead of the direction; λ multiplies b.

practice.question: A line has direction ratios (1, −2, 3). Which of these are also direction ratios of the same line?
practice.why: Any multiple of b points along the same line, and 3 × (1, −2, 3) = (3, −6, 9).
wrong: You added 1 to each number; only multiplying keeps the direction.
You dropped the minus sign, which changes the direction.
You reversed the order of the numbers, which gives another direction.

practice.question: On the line r = (3, 0, 1) + λ(1, 1, −2), which value of λ gives the point (1, −2, 5)?
wrong: λ = 2 gives (5, 2, −3); the sign is wrong, so step backwards.
λ = −1 gives (2, −1, 3); one more backward step is needed.
λ = 1 gives (4, 1, −1); the point lies in the backward direction.

rounds.question: In r = a + λb, what does the vector b give?
rounds.why: b is a vector that points along the line, so it gives the direction.
wrong: The known point of the line is a; b points along the line.
The parameter is the number λ; b is the direction vector.
The origin is where the axes meet; b is the direction of the line.

rounds.question: On the line r = (1, 2, 3) + λ(2, 0, 1), which point has λ = 3?
wrong: That is the point for λ = 1; here you add 3 times the direction.
You left out the start point; add 3b to a = (1, 2, 3).
You multiplied the start point by 3 too; only b is multiplied by λ.

rounds.question: A line has direction ratios (2, 4, −6). Which of these are also direction ratios of the same line?
rounds.why: (1, 2, −3) is half of (2, 4, −6). Any multiple of b points along the same line.
wrong: The sign of the last number changed, so this is not a multiple of (2, 4, −6).
You subtracted 2 from each number; you must multiply or divide all three by one number.
Swapping the first two numbers gives a different direction.

rounds.question: On the line r = (0, 2, 1) + λ(2, −1, 3), which value of λ gives the point (6, −1, 10)?
wrong: 6 is the x-coordinate; solve 2λ = 6 to get λ = 3.
λ = −3 gives (−6, 5, −8); the sign is wrong.

rounds.question: The three components of b in r = a + λb are called
rounds.why: The components of the direction vector b are the direction ratios of the line.
wrong: Direction cosines come only after dividing b by its length.
The parameter is the number λ, not the components of b.
A position vector gives a point, such as a; b gives the direction.

rounds.question: On the line r = (4, −1, 2) + λ(1, 2, −3), which point has λ = −1?
wrong: That is the point for λ = 1; for λ = −1 you subtract b.
That is only −b; you must add it to the start point (4, −1, 2).
That is the point for λ = 0; λ = −1 moves one step back along b.

rounds.question: Which line has the same direction as r = (1, 1, 1) + λ(1, 3, 2)?
rounds.why: The direction is the vector after the parameter. (2, 6, 4) = 2 × (1, 3, 2), so it is the same direction.
wrong: The same start point does not give the same direction; (2, 3, 1) is not a multiple of (1, 3, 2).
Here a and b are swapped; the direction is now (1, 1, 1).
The sign of the last number changed, so (1, 3, −2) is a different direction.

rounds.question: A drone's position after λ seconds is r = (0, 0, 10) + λ(3, 4, 0). Where is it after 2 seconds?
wrong: That is the position after 1 second; use λ = 2.
You left out the start point; the drone starts at height 10.
You doubled the start point too; only the direction is multiplied by λ.

entries.concept: what the equation of a plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is, and its normal (a, b, c)
entries.evidence: The first lesson measures a distance to 'the plane 2x + 2y − z + 1 = 0' 'along the normal (a, b, c)' before anything says that such an equation is a plane or why (a, b, c) is perpendicular to it.

screens.title: A flat surface and its normal
text: A table top is part of a plane: a flat surface that goes on for ever in every direction. A table leg stands at right angles to it. A direction at right angles to a plane is called its normal.

In space, one equation in x, y and z describes a surface, not a line. The simplest are flat: z = 0 is the floor, and z = 3 is a flat ceiling 3 units up. In general a plane has an equation ax + by + cz + d = 0. A point is on the plane exactly when its coordinates fit the equation.
The numbers in front of x, y and z make a normal vector of the plane: (a, b, c) is at right angles to it. That is why these three numbers appear in the formulas for distances and angles.

check.question: Is the point (1, 2, 0) on the plane x + y + z − 3 = 0?

v.says: A flat four-sided piece of a plane, with an arrow standing straight up from it, labelled normal.

figures.caption: A plane is a flat surface. Its normal is a direction at right angles to it, like a table leg to the table top.

screens.ask: Which points lie on the plane x + y + z − 3 = 0? Why is (1, 1, 1) its normal?

why: A point is on the plane when its numbers make the left side exactly 0.
(0, 3, 0) and (1, 1, 1) also give 0.
Any value other than 0 means the point is above or below the plane.
Subtract two points on the plane: the arrow between them lies flat in the plane.
A dot product of 0 means the two arrows are at right angles. (1, 1, 1), the numbers in front of x, y and z, is at right angles to the plane: its normal.

practice.question: A direction at right angles to a plane is called its
practice.why: Like a table leg standing at right angles to the table top, this direction is the normal.
wrong: The origin is a point where the axes meet, not a direction at right angles to a plane.
An axis is a reference line; the direction at right angles to a plane is its normal.
Slope measures steepness of a line; the word here is normal.

practice.question: What is a normal vector of the plane 2x − y + 5z + 7 = 0?
practice.why: The numbers in front of x, y and z are 2, −1 and 5, so the normal is (2, −1, 5).
wrong: You dropped the minus sign in front of y.
You used d = 7; the normal uses only the numbers in front of x, y and z.
You skipped the y number and used d; take a, b, c only.

practice.question: Which point is on the plane x + 2y + z − 6 = 0?
practice.why: 1 + 2 × 2 + 1 − 6 = 0, so (1, 2, 1) fits the equation.
wrong: You forgot to double y: 2 + 4 + 2 − 6 = 2, not 0.
You used d as a coordinate: 0 + 0 − 6 − 6 = −12, not 0.
1 + 4 + 3 − 6 = 2, not 0; put the point in and check that you get 0.

practice.question: A flat ceiling is 4 units above the floor z = 0. What is its equation?
practice.why: Every point of the ceiling has height 4, so its equation is z = 4.
wrong: x = 4 is an upright wall; height is given by z.
z = 0 is the floor itself, not the ceiling.
That plane is tilted: it contains the floor point (4, 0, 0). A flat ceiling needs only z = 4.

rounds.question: The normal of a plane is a direction that
options: is at right angles to the plane
rounds.why: A direction at right angles to a plane is called its normal, like a table leg under a table top.
wrong: A direction inside the plane is not the normal; the normal stands at right angles to it.
The normal depends on the plane; it is the direction at right angles to it.
A normal is a direction, not a line through a fixed point; it is at right angles to the plane.

rounds.question: What is a normal vector of the plane 3x + 4y − z − 2 = 0?
rounds.why: The normal is made of the numbers in front of x, y and z: 3, 4 and −1.
wrong: The number in front of z is −1, not 1; keep the sign.
−2 is the constant d; the third number is the one in front of z.
You left out the number in front of x and used the constant.

rounds.question: Which point is on the plane 2x + y − z − 4 = 0?
rounds.why: Put in (1, 3, 1): 2 + 3 − 1 − 4 = 0, so it fits the equation.
wrong: Those are the coefficients, not a point on it: 4 + 1 + 1 − 4 = 2, not 0.
0 + 0 − 4 − 4 = −8, not 0; the z term is subtracted.
2 + 1 − 1 − 4 = −2, not 0, so it is off the plane.

rounds.question: One wall of a room is the plane x = 0. The opposite wall is parallel to it and 5 units away on the positive side. What is its equation?
rounds.why: Every point of that wall is 5 units along x, so the wall is x = 5.
wrong: z = 5 is a flat ceiling 5 units up, not a wall.
x = 0 is the first wall itself.
y = 5 is a wall facing the other way; this wall is 5 units along x.

rounds.question: In the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0, which numbers make a normal vector?
rounds.why: The numbers in front of x, y and z, that is (a, b, c), are at right angles to the plane.
wrong: d is the constant; the third number must be c, in front of z.
You left out a, the number in front of x, and used the constant d.
(x, y, z) is a point; the normal uses the numbers in front of x, y and z.

rounds.question: What is a normal vector of the plane 4x + y + 2z − 9 = 0?
rounds.why: The numbers in front of x, y and z are 4, 1 and 2.
wrong: y alone means 1y, so its number is 1, not 0.
−9 is the constant; the third number is the 2 in front of z.
You left out the 4 in front of x and used the constant.

rounds.question: What is a normal vector of the plane 2x + 3z − 6 = 0?
rounds.why: There is no y term, so the number in front of y is 0. The normal is (2, 0, 3).
wrong: −6 is the constant; with no y term the middle number is 0.
The 3 belongs to z, the third place; the missing y gives 0 in the middle.
−6 is the constant, not the number in front of z; that number is 3.

rounds.question: A table top is the plane z = 2. Which direction is a normal of it, like a table leg?
rounds.why: z = 2 is 0x + 0y + 1z − 2 = 0, so the normal is (0, 0, 1): straight up.
wrong: (1, 0, 0) runs along the table top; the leg points up, along z.
(1, 1, 0) lies flat in the table top; the normal has only a z part.
(0, 1, 0) runs along the table top; the leg points up, along z.

entries.concept: what slope measures (rise ÷ run) and what the equation of a line y = mx + c means
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A straight line has the same slope everywhere' and uses m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and y = mx + c, but no lesson says what slope measures or why such an equation is a line.

screens.title: Slope: how steep?
text: A ramp that climbs 1 m for every 2 m forward is gentle. One that climbs 3 m for every 2 m is steep.

check.question: A line passes through (0, 0) and (2, 4). What is its slope?

screens.ask: A is ({@x1}, {@y1}) and B is ({@x2}, {@y2}). Find the slope of the line AB.

steps.do: Rise: how far up from A to B?
why: The second number of a point is its height. B is at {y2} and A at {y1}.
The first number says how far across. Subtract the same way both times: B minus A.
Slope is how much the line climbs for each 1 step right. Here it climbs {m} for every 1 across.

screens.note: Put B to the right of A and higher, with the climb a whole number of times the step across.
after: The slope's letter is m. Any two points on a straight line give the same slope.
Uphill is positive, downhill is negative, flat is 0. An upright line has no slope: its run is 0.
Where people slip: run ÷ rise, or subtracting one way on top and the other way below.

screens.title: An equation that draws a line
text: The rule y = {@m}x + {@c} gives a y for every x. Plot the points and they lie on one straight line.

check.question: What is the slope of the line y = 5x − 2?

screens.ask: For y = {m}x + {c}, find the slope, find where it crosses the y-axis, and test the point ({@t}, {y}).

steps.do: Find two points on the line.
why: Choose an x, use the rule, and get its y. So (0, {c}) and (1, {mc}) are on the line.
The slope is the number multiplying x. In y = mx + c that number is m.
On the y-axis x is 0. Only the number on its own is left: that is c.
A point is on the line when its numbers make the rule true. x = {t} gives {y}, the y of the point.

after: c is called the y-intercept: where the line crosses the y-axis.
The equation of a line is true for every point on it and no other. To write it you need the slope and one point.

practice.question: Which of these gives the slope of a line?
practice.why: Steepness is measured by rise ÷ run: change in y divided by change in x.
wrong: You turned the fraction upside down; rise goes on top.
Slope divides rise by run; it does not multiply them.
Slope divides rise by run; it does not subtract them.

practice.question: A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, 9). What is its slope?
practice.why: Rise = 9 − 3 = 6 and run = 4 − 1 = 3, so slope = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
wrong: You did run ÷ rise; slope is rise ÷ run.
3 is only the run; divide the rise 6 by it.
6 is only the rise; divide it by the run 3.

practice.question: Where does the line y = 3x − 4 cross the y-axis?
practice.why: Put x = 0: y = 3 × 0 − 4 = −4. So c = −4 is the y-intercept.
wrong: 3 is the slope m; the crossing point is c.
You dropped the minus sign; c is −4.
You put x = 1; the y-axis is where x = 0.

practice.question: A ramp rises 2 metres for every 8 metres forward. What is its slope?
practice.why: Slope = rise ÷ run = 2 ÷ 8 = 1/4.
wrong: You did run ÷ rise; rise goes on top.
You multiplied; slope is rise ÷ run.
You subtracted; slope is rise ÷ run.

rounds.question: In y = mx + c, what does m stand for?
rounds.why: In y = mx + c the number m is the slope of the line.
wrong: The y-intercept is c, where the line crosses the y-axis.
The run is the change in x; m is rise ÷ run.
The rise is only the change in y; m is rise ÷ run.

rounds.question: A line passes through (2, 1) and (5, 13). What is its slope?
rounds.why: Rise = 13 − 1 = 12 and run = 5 − 2 = 3, so the slope is 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
wrong: You divided run by rise; slope is rise ÷ run = 12 ÷ 3.
12 is only the rise; divide it by the run, 3.
You subtracted the run from the rise; slope is rise ÷ run.

rounds.question: What is the slope of the line y = 5 − 2x?
rounds.why: Write it as y = −2x + 5. The slope is the number multiplying x, which is −2.
wrong: 5 is where the line crosses the y-axis; the slope is the number with x.
You dropped the minus sign; the number with x is −2.
You worked out 5 − 2; the slope is the number multiplying x.

rounds.question: A road climbs 30 metres over 600 metres forward. What is its slope?
rounds.why: Slope = rise ÷ run = 30 ÷ 600 = 1/20.
wrong: You divided run by rise; slope is rise ÷ run.
You subtracted; slope is rise ÷ run, not run − rise.
You added rise and run; slope is rise ÷ run.

rounds.question: In y = mx + c, the number c is called
rounds.why: x = 0 gives y = c, so c is where the line crosses the y-axis: the y-intercept.
wrong: The slope is m, the number multiplying x.
The rise is the change in y between two points, not c.
The run is the change in x between two points, not c.

rounds.question: A line passes through (0, 5) and (4, 7). What is its slope?
rounds.why: Rise = 7 − 5 = 2 and run = 4 − 0 = 4, so the slope is 2 ÷ 4 = 1/2.
wrong: 2 is the rise, or you did run ÷ rise; slope is rise ÷ run = 2 ÷ 4.
You multiplied rise by run; slope is rise ÷ run.
You added rise and run; slope is rise ÷ run.

rounds.question: A line passes through (3, 1) and (3, 6). What is its slope?
rounds.why: The run is 3 − 3 = 0, and we cannot divide by 0. The line goes straight up and down, so it has no slope.
wrong: Slope 0 is a flat line; this line goes straight up, with run 0.
5 is the rise only; the run is 0, so rise ÷ run cannot be done.
You cannot divide by a run of 0, so there is no slope.

rounds.question: A slide goes downhill from left to right. It drops 3 metres while going 4 metres forward. What is its slope?
rounds.why: The rise is −3 (it goes down) and the run is 4, so the slope is −3/4.
wrong: Downhill from left to right means the slope is negative.
You divided run by rise; slope is rise ÷ run = −3 ÷ 4.
You divided run by rise and lost the minus sign; slope is −3 ÷ 4.

entries.concept: what a protractor is and how to place it
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'A protractor has two scales running in opposite directions' without saying what a protractor is, where its centre is, or how it is laid on an angle.

screens.title: Meet the protractor
text: A ruler measures length. A protractor measures angles.
It is a half circle. Round its curved edge are marks from 0 to 180. Each mark is 1 degree.

check.question: The first arm is on 0 and the other arm is on 90 of the same row. How big is the angle?

screens.ask: Read the angle with a protractor.

steps.do: Put the centre on the corner.
why: The small mark in the middle of the straight edge is the centre.

lines: Arm on 0 of the inner row
why: The straight edge through the centre is the zero line. Lay it along one arm.

steps.do: Read where the other arm crosses.
why: Use the same row that showed 0 on the first arm.
The outer row shows 120 there. It counts from the other side, so we do not use it.

after: There are two rows of numbers so you can start from the left or the right. Always use the row that is 0 on your first arm.

practice.question: Which tool measures angles?
practice.why: A protractor is the half circle marked from 0 to 180 that measures angles.
wrong: A ruler measures length, not angles.
A tape measures length, not angles.
Scissors make an angle when opened, but they do not measure it.

practice.question: Where do you put the centre of the protractor?
options: On the corner of the angle
On the end of one arm
In the middle of one arm
practice.why: The centre mark must sit exactly on the corner of the angle.
wrong: The end of an arm is not the corner; the centre goes where the two arms meet.
The centre goes where the two arms meet, not part of the way along an arm.
It must be exactly on the corner, or the reading will be wrong.

practice.question: The first arm is on 0 of the outer row. The other arm crosses a mark where the outer row says 50 and the inner row says 130. How big is the angle?
practice.why: Use the row that shows 0 on the first arm. That is the outer row, which says 50.
wrong: You read the inner row; use the row that shows 0 on the first arm.
You added the two rows; read only the row that starts at 0 on the first arm.
You subtracted the two rows; read only the outer row.

practice.question: How big is each small step on the curved edge of a protractor?
practice.why: The marks go from 0 to 180 and each small step is 1 degree.
wrong: The numbers are often printed every 10, but each small step is 1 degree.
Centimetres measure length; a protractor's steps are degrees.
180 is the whole curved edge, not one step.

rounds.question: What shape is a protractor?
rounds.why: A protractor is a flat half circle with marks from 0 to 180 on its curved edge.
wrong: A full circle would go to 360; a protractor is a half circle, 0 to 180.
A protractor has a curved edge, so it is not a square.
That is a ruler, which measures length; a protractor is a half circle.

rounds.question: The centre is on the corner of the angle. What must lie along one arm?
rounds.why: Turn the protractor until the zero line lies along one arm. Then you can read the other arm.
wrong: The curved edge is where you read the number; the zero line goes on the arm.
If 90 is on the arm you cannot count from 0; put the zero line on the arm.
A ruler measures length; the zero line of the protractor goes on the arm.

rounds.question: The first arm is on 0 of the inner row. The other arm crosses a mark where the inner row says 110 and the outer row says 70. How big is the angle?
rounds.why: Use the row that shows 0 on the first arm. That is the inner row, and it says 110.
wrong: 70 is on the outer row; the first arm is on 0 of the inner row.
You added the two rows; read only the row that starts at 0 on the first arm.
You subtracted the two rows; read only the inner row: 110.

rounds.question: Which numbers are at the two ends of the curved edge of a protractor?
rounds.why: The marks on a protractor go from 0 to 180, because it is a half circle.
wrong: 360 is a full circle; a protractor is a half circle and stops at 180.
90 is only half way along the curved edge; it goes on to 180.
The marks start at 0 and end at 180, not 100.

rounds.question: What is the small mark in the middle of the straight edge of a protractor called?
rounds.why: The small mark in the middle of the straight edge is the centre. It goes on the corner of the angle.
wrong: The zero line is the whole line along the straight edge, through the centre.
A degree is one small step on the curved edge.
An arm is a line of the angle, not a part of the protractor.

rounds.question: Where do you read the size of the angle?
options: Where the other arm crosses the curved edge
rounds.why: With one arm on the zero line, the number where the other arm crosses the curved edge is the angle.
wrong: The centre only sits on the corner; the number is read on the curved edge.
The first arm shows 0; the size is read where the other arm crosses.
180 is the end of the scale; read where the other arm crosses the curved edge.

rounds.question: Asha puts the zero line along one arm, but the centre is not on the corner of the angle. Is her reading right?
options: Yes, the zero line is enough
Yes, if she uses the outer row
No, she must use a ruler
No, the centre must be on the corner
rounds.why: Both things are needed: the centre exactly on the corner and the zero line along one arm.
wrong: The zero line alone is not enough; the centre must sit on the corner too.
Changing the row does not help; the centre must sit on the corner.
A ruler measures length; she must move the centre onto the corner.

rounds.question: A door is open a little. One arm of the angle is on 0 of the outer row. The other arm crosses a mark where the outer row says 30 and the inner row says 150. How wide is the door open?
rounds.why: The first arm is on 0 of the outer row, so read the outer row: 30°.
wrong: 150 is on the inner row, which does not show 0 on the first arm.
You added the two rows; read only the outer row.
You subtracted the two rows; read only the outer row: 30.

entries.concept: what an angle is, and what a degree (the sign °) means
entries.evidence: The first lesson opens with 'A right angle (90°) is a square corner' before any lesson has said what an angle is or what the sign ° measures.

screens.title: What is an angle?
text: Open a pair of scissors a little, then wide. Both blades start at one point. Watch the gap between them grow.

check.question: Which makes the bigger angle: scissors opened wide, or scissors opened a little?

screens.ask: Open a book slowly. Watch the two covers.

why: The covers lie on top of each other. Neither has turned.
One cover has turned a little away from the other.
The more the cover turns, the bigger the gap.
The covers now point opposite ways: half of a full turn.

after: The turn between two lines that start at one point is called an angle.
Long covers or short covers do not matter. Only the turn does.

screens.title: Measuring a turn in degrees
