text: Turn all the way round until you face the front again. That is one full turn.
A full turn is cut into 360 equal tiny turns. Each one is 1 degree, written 1°.

check.question: How many degrees is a right angle?

screens.ask: A full turn is 360°. How big is a half turn? A quarter turn?

why: Half of a full turn leaves you facing the other way.
Four quarter turns make one full turn.
The corner of a page is a quarter turn.

after: A half turn, 180°, makes a straight line.
A quarter turn, 90°, makes a square corner. It is called a right angle.

practice.question: Two straight lines start from one point. The opening between them is called
practice.why: The opening between two lines that start from one point is an angle.
wrong: A degree is the unit we measure with; the opening itself is an angle.
The lines make the opening; the opening is called an angle.
A full turn is one special size, 360°; any opening is called an angle.

practice.question: How many degrees is a half turn?
practice.why: A full turn is 360°, and 360° ÷ 2 = 180°.
wrong: 90° is a quarter turn; a half turn is 360° ÷ 2.
360° is a full turn; halve it.
You halved a quarter turn; halve the full turn, 360°.

practice.question: Long scissors and short scissors are opened the same amount. Which makes the bigger angle?
practice.why: The size of an angle does not depend on how long the lines are, only on the opening.
wrong: Longer blades do not make a bigger angle; only the opening counts.
Shorter blades do not make a bigger angle; only the opening counts.
We can tell: the same opening gives the same angle.

practice.question: You make three quarter turns. How many degrees is that?
practice.why: One quarter turn is 90°, and 90° × 3 = 270°.
wrong: 180° is two quarter turns; count three.
360° is four quarter turns, a full turn.
You added 3 to 90; take 90° three times.

rounds.question: What does an angle tell us?
options: How far one line has turned away from the other
rounds.why: An angle is the opening between two lines from one point. It tells how far one has turned from the other.
wrong: Length is measured in centimetres; an angle is about turn, not length.
Thick or thin lines make the same opening; an angle is about turn.
An angle always has two lines; it tells how far one has turned.

rounds.question: How many degrees is a quarter turn?
rounds.why: A full turn is 360°. A quarter turn is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.
wrong: You cut the turn into 8; a quarter turn is 360° ÷ 4.
180° is a half turn; a quarter turn is 360° ÷ 4.
360° is the full turn; a quarter of it is 90°.

rounds.question: Ravi draws an angle with lines 3 cm long. Then he makes both lines 6 cm long without turning them. What happens to the angle?
rounds.why: The size of an angle does not depend on how long the lines are. The opening has not changed.
wrong: Longer lines do not open the angle more; only turning changes it.
Longer lines do not close the angle; only turning changes it.
The lines were not turned, so the opening is the same as before.

rounds.question: The hand of a clock makes two half turns. How many degrees is that?
rounds.why: A half turn is 180°. Two half turns are 180° + 180° = 360°, a full turn.
wrong: 180° is one half turn; there are two of them.
You added 2 to 180; two half turns are 180° + 180°.
You doubled a full turn; two half turns make just one full turn, 360°.

rounds.question: How is 90° read?
rounds.why: The small raised circle is the sign for degrees, so 90° is 90 degrees.
wrong: Centimetres measure length; the sign ° means degrees.
The sign ° means degrees; 90° is only a quarter of one turn.
The small circle is not a zero; it is the sign for degrees.

rounds.question: How many degrees is a full turn?
rounds.why: People agreed to cut one full turn into 360 equal tiny turns, each 1 degree.
wrong: A full turn is cut into 360 tiny turns, not 100.
180° is a half turn; a full turn is twice that.
90° is a quarter turn; a full turn is four of them.

rounds.question: A book is laid flat, so its two covers make one straight line. How big is the angle between the covers?
rounds.why: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180°.
wrong: 90° is a square corner; a straight line is a half turn, 180°.
0° is a closed book; a flat book is opened a half turn.
360° is a full turn back to the start; flat is only a half turn.

rounds.question: A window opens a quarter turn. Then it opens one more quarter turn. How many degrees has it turned in all?
rounds.why: A quarter turn is 90°. Two of them are 90° + 90° = 180°.
wrong: 90° is only one quarter turn; there are two.
You halved 90; two quarter turns are 90° + 90°.
360° is four quarter turns; here there are only two.

entries.concept: cevian, and the ratio in which a point divides a side
entries.evidence: The lessons multiply 'the three ratios (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB)' and speak of 'the cevians' meeting, without saying what a cevian is or what BD/DC measures.

screens.title: Cevians and the parts of a side
text: Tie a string from one corner of a triangular frame to any point on the opposite side. A segment like this, from a corner to a point on the opposite side, is called a cevian (after the mathematician Ceva). Medians, altitudes and angle bisectors are all cevians.
The point D where a cevian from A lands on BC cuts BC into two parts, BD and DC. The ratio BD : DC compares them, and BD/DC is the same ratio written as a fraction.

In the same way, let the cevian from B land at E on CA, and the cevian from C land at F on AB. Go round the triangle one way: B to C, C to A, A to B. That gives three ratios: BD/DC, CE/EA and AF/FB. Ceva's theorem says three cevians pass through one point exactly when these three multiply to 1.

check.question: D is on BC with BD = 2 cm and DC = 6 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?

v.says: Triangle ABC. A segment from corner A to a point D on the side BC.

figures.caption: AD is a cevian: it goes from the corner A to a point D on the opposite side. D cuts BC into two parts, BD and DC.

screens.ask: In triangle ABC, D, E and F are the midpoints of BC, CA and AB. Show that the three medians meet at one point.

why: A midpoint cuts its side into two equal parts. Any length divided by an equal length is 1.

steps.do: The same on the other two sides.
why: E is the midpoint of CA and F is the midpoint of AB, so each of these ratios is 1 as well.
Ceva's theorem says: three cevians meet at one point exactly when these three ratios multiply to 1.
They do, so the three medians meet at a single point. It is called the centroid.

practice.question: A segment from a corner of a triangle to a point on the opposite side is called
practice.why: Any segment from a corner to a point on the opposite side is a cevian.
wrong: A ratio compares two lengths; the segment itself is a cevian.
A side joins two corners; a cevian goes from a corner to the opposite side.
A midpoint is a point, not a segment.

practice.question: D is on BC with BD = 4 cm and DC = 10 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?
practice.why: BD : DC = 4 : 10. Divide both by 2 to get 2 : 5.
wrong: You wrote DC first; the order is BD then DC.
You compared BD with the whole side BC; compare BD with DC.
You compared BD with the whole side BC (4 : 14); compare BD with DC.

practice.question: BC = 12 cm and D is on BC with BD = 3 cm. What is BD : DC?
wrong: You used the whole side BC; first find DC = 12 − 3 = 9.
You wrote DC first; the order is BD then DC.
You compared BC with BD; find DC = 9 and compare BD with it.

practice.question: Three cevians have BD/DC = 2 and CE/EA = 3. What must AF/FB be for them to pass through one point?
practice.why: The three ratios must multiply to 1: 2 × 3 × AF/FB = 1, so AF/FB = 1/6.
wrong: You multiplied 2 × 3; the product of all three must be 1, so the third is 1/6.
You added the ratios; they are multiplied, and the product must be 1.
Each ratio need not be 1; only their product must be 1.

rounds.question: A cevian joins a corner of a triangle to
options: a point on the opposite side
the midpoint of a side that starts at that corner
rounds.why: A cevian is a segment from a corner to a point on the opposite side.
wrong: Joining a corner to the next corner gives a side, not a cevian.
A cevian lands on the opposite side, not outside the triangle.
It must land on the opposite side, not on a side that starts at that corner.

rounds.question: D is on BC with BD = 9 cm and DC = 6 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?
rounds.why: BD : DC = 9 : 6. Divide both by 3 to get 3 : 2.
wrong: That is DC : BD; BD comes first, so it is 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.
You compared BD with the whole of BC; compare BD with DC.
That is BD : BC in simplest form; the ratio asked is BD : DC.

rounds.question: BC = 20 cm and D is on BC with DC = 5 cm. What is BD : DC?
wrong: That is BC : DC; first find BD = 20 − 5 = 15.
That is DC : BD; BD comes first: 15 : 5.
That is DC : BC; find BD = 15 and compare it with DC.

rounds.question: Three cevians have BD/DC = 4 and CE/EA = 1/2. What must AF/FB be for them to pass through one point?
rounds.why: The three ratios must multiply to 1. 4 × 1/2 = 2, so AF/FB = 1/2.
wrong: 2 is the product of the two given ratios; the third must bring the product to 1.
You added the ratios; Ceva's theorem multiplies them.
Each ratio need not be 1; only the product of all three must be 1.

rounds.question: D is on BC. The ratio BD : DC written as a fraction is
rounds.why: BD : DC compares BD with DC, and as a fraction it is BD/DC.
wrong: That is upside down; BD comes first, so it goes on top.
That compares BD with the whole side BC, not with DC.
A ratio is a division, not a product.

rounds.question: D is on BC with BD = 5 cm and DC = 20 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?
rounds.why: BD : DC = 5 : 20. Divide both by 5 to get 1 : 4.
wrong: That is DC : BD; BD comes first.
That is BD : BC (5 : 25); compare BD with DC.
You used 20 − 5 = 15 for DC; DC is 20 cm.

rounds.question: D is on BC with BD : DC = 2 : 3, and BC = 10 cm. How long is BD?
rounds.why: There are 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts in 10 cm, so each part is 2 cm. BD is 2 parts: 4 cm.
wrong: 2 is the ratio number, not the length; each part is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 cm and BD has 2 parts.
6 cm is DC, the 3 parts; BD is the 2 parts.
D is not the midpoint; the parts are in the ratio 2 : 3.

rounds.question: Three cevians have BD/DC = 2, CE/EA = 1/2 and AF/FB = 3. Do they pass through one point?
rounds.why: 2 × 1/2 × 3 = 3. The product must be 1, so they do not pass through one point.
wrong: You multiplied only two ratios; all three must multiply to 1.
A product of 3 fails the test; it must be exactly 1.
The test uses the product of the ratios, not the sum.

entries.concept: tangent, point of contact and secant
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts 'A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at a right angle' and asks for 'the length of the tangent from P'; what a tangent is appears only in the fourth lesson.

screens.title: A line that just touches
text: A bicycle wheel on a flat road touches the road at one point only. The spoke straight down to the road is upright.

check.question: At how many points does a tangent meet a circle?

v.says: A circle with centre O. A tangent from the outside point P touches the circle at one point, T; the radius OT meets the tangent at a right angle. A secant cuts the circle at two points.

figures.caption: The tangent touches the circle at one point, T (the point of contact). The radius OT meets it at 90°. The secant cuts the circle at two points.

screens.ask: A circle has centre O and radius OT = {@r} cm. P is outside with OP = {d} cm, and PT is a tangent. Find PT.

why: A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at a right angle. So OTP is a right triangle.
The longest side faces the right angle. The right angle is at T, so it is OP.
The squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side.
We want a shorter side, so we subtract: {d}² − {r}².
Which number times itself is {tt}? It is {t}.

screens.note: Use 3, 6, 9, 12 or 15, so that the lengths come out whole.
after: A line that touches a circle at exactly one point is a tangent. That point is the point of contact.
A line that cuts a circle at two points is a secant. From a point outside you can draw two tangents.
The length of the tangent from P is the distance PT.

practice.question: A line that cuts a circle at two points is called
practice.why: A line meeting the circle at two points is a secant.
wrong: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point.
A radius goes from the centre to the circle; it is not a line cutting through.
The point of contact is where a tangent touches, not a line.

practice.question: At what angle does the radius drawn to the point of contact meet the tangent?
practice.why: The radius to the point of contact always meets the tangent at a right angle, 90°.
wrong: 180° would make them one straight line; they meet at a right angle.
The angle is always a right angle, 90°, not half of it.
The angle does not vary; it is always 90°.

practice.question: O is the centre, the radius OT = 6 cm, and PT is a tangent with OP = 10 cm. How long is PT?
practice.why: The right angle is at T, so PT² = 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64 and PT = 8 cm.
wrong: You subtracted the lengths; subtract their squares and take the root.
You added the lengths; use PT² = OP² − OT².
You added the squares; OP is the longest side, so subtract 6² from 10².

practice.question: PT is a tangent of length 12 cm and the radius OT = 5 cm. How far is P from the centre O?
practice.why: The right angle is at T, so OP² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169 and OP = 13 cm.
wrong: You added the lengths; add their squares and take the root.
You subtracted the lengths; add the squares, since OP is the longest side.
You subtracted the squares; OP is the longest side, so add them.

rounds.question: A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point is called
rounds.why: A line that just touches a circle at one point is a tangent.
wrong: A secant cuts the circle at two points.
A radius joins the centre to the circle; it is not a touching line.
The point of contact is the point where the tangent touches, not the line.

rounds.question: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point outside it?
rounds.why: From a point outside the circle you can draw two tangents, one on each side.
wrong: There is one on each side of the circle, so two in all.
A point outside the circle always has tangents; there are two.
Only two lines from the point just touch the circle.

rounds.question: O is the centre, the radius OT = 5 cm, and PT is a tangent with OP = 13 cm. How long is PT?
rounds.why: The right angle is at T, so PT² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144 and PT = 12 cm.
wrong: You subtracted the lengths; subtract the squares: 169 − 25 = 144.
You added the lengths; use PT² = OP² − OT².
You added the squares; OP is the longest side, so subtract: 169 − 25.

rounds.question: A wheel with centre O and radius 6 cm stands on a flat road and touches it at T. An ant on the road at P is 8 cm from T. How far is the ant from O?
rounds.why: OT meets the road at a right angle, so OP² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 and OP = 10 cm.
wrong: You added the lengths; add the squares and take the root.
You subtracted the lengths; OP is the longest side: OP² = 36 + 64.
You subtracted the squares; OP is the longest side, so add them.

rounds.question: The point where a tangent touches the circle is called
rounds.why: The one point where a tangent meets the circle is the point of contact.
wrong: The centre is the middle of the circle, not a point on it.
A secant is a line that cuts the circle at two points.
The radius is a line from the centre to the circle, not a point.

rounds.question: A line meets a circle at two points. Is it a tangent?
options: Yes, it has two points of contact
rounds.why: A tangent meets the circle at exactly one point. A line that meets it at two points is a secant.
wrong: Touching means meeting at one point only; this line cuts through.
A tangent has only one point of contact; two points make a secant.
A radius starts at the centre; a line cutting the circle twice is a secant.

rounds.question: PT is a tangent to a circle with centre O, and T is the point of contact. Which side of triangle OTP is the longest?
options: OT and PT are both longest
rounds.why: The radius OT meets the tangent at 90°, so the right angle is at T. The side opposite it, OP, is the longest.
wrong: OT is a side next to the right angle; the longest side is opposite the right angle.
PT is a side next to the right angle; the longest side is opposite the right angle.
The longest side is the one opposite the right angle at T, which is OP.

rounds.question: A round pond has centre O and radius 8 m. A straight path from a gate P just touches the pond at T, and PT = 15 m. How far is the gate from O?
rounds.why: The right angle is at T, so OP² = 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289 and OP = 17 m.
wrong: You added the lengths; add the squares and take the root.
You subtracted the lengths; OP is the longest side: OP² = 64 + 225.
You subtracted the squares; OP is the longest side, so add them.

entries.concept: the angle an arc makes (subtends) at the centre and on the circle; segment; cyclic quadrilateral
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'An arc makes twice the angle at the centre that it makes at any point on the rest of the circle ... angles in the same segment ... cyclic quadrilateral' with none of these ideas set up (the parts of a circle come three lessons later).

screens.title: The angle an arc makes
text: From your seat in a round stadium, look at the two goalposts A and B. The opening between your two lines of sight is an angle.

check.question: The angle at the centre is 80°. What is the angle at a point on the circle, on the same arc?

screens.ask: Arc AB makes an angle of {@c}° at the centre O. What angle does it make at a point C on the rest of the circle?

steps.do: Halve the angle at the centre.
why: The angle an arc makes at the centre is twice the angle it makes on the circle. So on the circle it is half.

steps.do: Try another point D on the same side.
why: The rule gives half of {c}° wherever the point is. So angles in the same segment are equal.

steps.do: The special case of a diameter.
why: If AB passes through the centre, the angle at the centre is a straight line, 180°. Half of that is 90°: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

screens.note: Use an even number of degrees, so that half of it is whole.
after: Angle AOB is the angle the arc makes at the centre. Angle ACB is the angle it makes at a point on the circle.
Books say the arc subtends these angles. Subtends only means makes.

screens.title: Segments and cyclic quadrilaterals
text: Mark four points on one circle and join them in order. The shape is a cyclic quadrilateral.

check.question: Where do the four corners of a cyclic quadrilateral lie?

screens.ask: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle A = {@a}°. Find angle C.

why: Going round the shape the corners are A, B, C, D. The corner across from A, not next to it, is C.

steps.do: Use the rule: opposite angles add to 180°.
why: All four corners are on one circle. So each pair of opposite angles adds up to 180°.
If {a}° and C together make 180°, then C is what is left after taking {a}° away.

after: A chord cuts the inside of a circle into two segments. Angles in the same segment are equal.
Points that lie on one circle are called concyclic.

practice.question: A quadrilateral with all four corners on one circle is called
practice.why: Four corners on one circle make a cyclic quadrilateral.
wrong: A segment is a piece of the circle cut off by a chord.
A semicircle is half a circle, cut by a diameter.
A chord is a straight line joining two points of a circle.

practice.question: An arc makes an angle of 35° at a point on the circle. What angle does it make at the centre?
practice.why: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle: 2 × 35° = 70°.
wrong: You halved; the centre angle is the bigger one, twice 35°.
The two angles are not equal; the centre angle is double.
You took it from 180°; that rule is for opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.

practice.question: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle B = 85°. What is angle D?
practice.why: D is opposite B, and opposite angles add up to 180°: 180° − 85° = 95°.
wrong: Opposite angles are not equal; they add up to 180°.
You took it from 360°; opposite angles add up to 180°.
You took it from 90°; opposite angles add up to 180°.

practice.question: C and D are on a circle, on the same side of the chord AB. Angle ACB = 40°. What is angle ADB?
practice.why: Angles in the same segment stand on the same arc, so they are equal: 40°.
wrong: Doubling gives the angle at the centre, but D is on the circle.
Halving is not needed; both angles are on the circle, so they are equal.
180° − 40° is for opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral; these are in the same segment.

rounds.question: A chord cuts the inside of a circle into two pieces. Each piece is called
rounds.why: The two pieces a chord cuts the inside of a circle into are called segments.
wrong: An arc is a part of the circle's curved edge, not a piece of its inside.
A diameter is a chord through the centre, not a piece of the circle.
A cyclic quadrilateral is a four-cornered shape with its corners on the circle.

rounds.question: An arc makes an angle of 140° at the centre. What angle does it make at a point on the rest of the circle?
rounds.why: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle, so the angle is 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.
wrong: You doubled; the angle at the circle is half the angle at the centre.
The two angles are not equal; the one at the circle is half.
You took 140° from 180°; halve the angle at the centre.

rounds.question: PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle P = 110°. What is angle R?
rounds.why: R is opposite P, and opposite angles add up to 180°. So angle R = 180° − 110° = 70°.
wrong: Opposite angles are not equal here; they add up to 180°.
You took 110° from 360°; opposite angles add up to 180°.
You took away 90°; use 180° − 110°.

rounds.question: A round stadium has centre O. The goalposts A and B are on the circle, and angle AOB = 64°. From a seat C on the rest of the circle, what is angle ACB?
rounds.why: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle, so angle ACB = 64° ÷ 2 = 32°.
wrong: You doubled; the angle at the circle is half the angle at the centre.
The angle at the seat is half the angle at the centre, not equal to it.
You took 64° from 180°; that rule is for cyclic quadrilaterals.

rounds.question: Points that lie on one circle are called
rounds.why: Points that all lie on one circle are called concyclic.
wrong: Segments are the pieces a chord cuts the inside of a circle into.
A chord is a straight line joining two points of a circle.
Semicircles are the two equal pieces made by a diameter.

rounds.question: AB is a diameter of a circle and C is another point on the circle. What is angle ACB?
rounds.why: A diameter makes 180° at the centre, so the angle at the circle is 180° ÷ 2 = 90°.
wrong: 180° is the angle at the centre; the angle at the circle is half of it.
You halved twice; half of 180° is 90°.
The angle on a diameter is always 180° ÷ 2 = 90°.

rounds.question: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle A = 100°. Which angle must be 80°?
rounds.why: Opposite angles add up to 180°. The angle opposite A is C, so angle C = 180° − 100° = 80°.
wrong: B is next to A, not opposite; the rule is for opposite angles.
D is next to A, not opposite; the rule is for opposite angles.
Angle A is given as 100°.

rounds.question: Four chairs A, B, C and D stand in order round the edge of a round table. In quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 65°. What is angle C?
rounds.why: All four corners are on one circle, so opposite angles add up to 180°. Angle C = 180° − 65° = 115°.
wrong: Opposite angles are not equal here; they add up to 180°.
You took 65° from 90°; use 180° − 65°.
You took 65° from 360°; opposite angles add up to 180°.

entries.concept: compasses, centre, radius and arc in a construction
entries.evidence: The first worked construction says 'With centres A and B and radius r > 3 cm, draw arcs' although the skill that explains what compasses do comes after this one.

screens.title: What compasses draw
text: Open the compasses, press the point on the paper and swing the pencil round. You get a circle. Swing part of the way and you get a piece of it, an arc.

check.question: An arc is drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. How far from A is any point on the arc?

screens.ask: Draw arcs from A and from B with the same opening of {@r} cm. They cross at P. How far is P from A and from B?

lines: Every point is {r} cm from A
why: The opening does not change, so every point drawn is the same distance from A.

steps.do: Arc with centre B, same opening.
lines: Every point is {r} cm from B
why: The opening was not changed, so this arc is {r} cm from B.
P is on both arcs, so it is {r} cm from both points.

after: Where the point sits is the centre. The opening is the radius.
'Centre A, radius {r} cm' means: open to {r} cm on a ruler, put the point on A, and draw.

practice.question: A piece of a circle drawn with compasses is called
practice.why: Swinging the pencil only part of the way round gives a piece of a circle, called an arc.
wrong: The radius is the opening of the compasses, not the curve.
The centre is where the sharp point stands.
The gap is the opening between point and pencil; the curve is an arc.

practice.question: An arc is drawn with centre B and radius 7 cm. P is a point on the arc. How long is PB?
practice.why: Every point of the arc is the same distance from the centre, the radius 7 cm.
wrong: You doubled the radius; the distance from the centre is the radius itself.
You halved the radius; the distance from the centre is the radius itself.
We can tell: every point of the arc is 7 cm from B.

practice.question: An arc with centre A and radius 3 cm crosses an arc with centre B and radius 5 cm at P. Which is true?
practice.why: P is on both arcs, so it is 3 cm from A and 5 cm from B.
wrong: PA = PB only when both arcs use the same opening; here they are 3 cm and 5 cm.
You swapped them; the arc with centre A has radius 3 cm.
Adding the radii does not give AB; the arcs only tell us PA and PB.

practice.question: A goat is tied to a post with a 6 m rope. It walks round with the rope tight. What is the post?
practice.why: The goat stays 6 m from the post all the time, so the post is the centre.
wrong: The rope, 6 m, is the radius; the post is the centre.
Part of the goat's path is an arc; the post is the centre.
The goat's path is the circle; the post is its centre.

rounds.question: The gap between the point and the pencil of the compasses is
rounds.why: The gap you choose between the point and the pencil is the radius.
wrong: The centre is the place where the sharp point is pressed.
The arc is the curve the pencil draws.
The circle is what you draw by swinging the pencil all the way round.

rounds.question: Compasses are opened to 5 cm. An arc is drawn with centre A, and Q is a point on the arc. How long is AQ?
rounds.why: Every point of the arc is the same distance from the centre: the radius, 5 cm.
wrong: You doubled the radius; the distance from the centre is the radius itself.
You halved the radius; the distance from the centre is the radius itself.
We can tell: every point of the arc is 5 cm from A.

rounds.question: Compasses are opened to 6 cm. One arc is drawn with centre A and one with centre B, with the same opening. They cross at P. Which is true?
rounds.why: P is on both arcs, and both have radius 6 cm. So PA = 6 cm and PB = 6 cm.
wrong: The opening gives the distance from each centre to P, not from A to B.
Both arcs have the same radius, so PB is 6 cm too.
The opening is not shared out; each distance is the full 6 cm.

rounds.question: The seat of a swing hangs by a 2 m chain from a hook. As it swings, the seat draws a curve in the air. What is the curve?
rounds.why: The seat stays 2 m from the hook, so it moves along a piece of a circle: an arc.
wrong: The radius is the chain's length, 2 m, not the curve.
The centre is the hook, where the chain is fixed.
The seat stays the same distance from the hook, so its path is curved.

rounds.question: The place where you press the sharp point of the compasses is
rounds.why: The sharp point is pressed at the centre of the circle or arc.
wrong: The radius is the gap between the point and the pencil.
The arc is the curve drawn by the pencil.
The gap is the opening of the compasses, which is the radius.

rounds.question: P and Q are two points on one arc with centre O. OP = 6 cm. How long is OQ?
rounds.why: Every point of an arc is the same distance from its centre, so OQ = OP = 6 cm.
wrong: You doubled; both points are one radius, 6 cm, from O.
You halved; both points are one radius, 6 cm, from O.
We can tell: all points of the arc are the same distance from O.

rounds.question: An arc has centre A and radius 4 cm. A point R is 5 cm from A. Is R on the arc?
options: No, every point of the arc is 4 cm from A
Yes, 5 cm is close to 4 cm
Yes, any point near A is on the arc
No, it would have to be 8 cm from A
rounds.why: Every point of the arc is exactly 4 cm from A. R is 5 cm away, so it is not on the arc.
wrong: Close is not enough; the distance must be exactly the radius, 4 cm.
Only points exactly 4 cm from A are on the arc.
Points of the arc are one radius, 4 cm, from A, not double.

rounds.question: The minute hand of a clock is 10 cm long. As it goes round, how far is its tip from the middle of the clock?
rounds.why: The tip moves on a circle whose radius is the hand, so it is always 10 cm from the middle.
wrong: You doubled the hand; the tip is one hand length from the middle.
You halved the hand; the tip is one hand length from the middle.
The hand does not change length, so the distance stays 10 cm.

entries.concept: bisect, midpoint, perpendicular bisector and angle bisector
entries.evidence: The lesson defines the perpendicular bisector only as 'the set of all points the same distance from A and from B' and never says that to bisect is to cut into two equal parts.

screens.title: Cutting exactly in half
text: Fold a strip of paper so its two ends meet. The fold cuts it into two equal parts. Cutting into two equal parts is called bisecting.

check.question: An angle of 60° is bisected. How big is each part?

v.says: Segment AB with midpoint M. A dashed line through M crosses AB at a right angle: the perpendicular bisector.

figures.caption: M is the midpoint of AB, so AM = MB (same marks). The dashed line through M at 90° is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

screens.ask: AB = {@L} cm. Find its midpoint and perpendicular bisector. Then bisect an angle of {@g}°.

why: Half of {L} cm is {h} cm. M cuts AB into two equal parts.
Bisector: it cuts AB in half. Perpendicular: it meets AB at a right angle.
An angle bisector cuts the angle into two equal angles.

screens.note: Use even numbers, so the halves are whole.
after: The midpoint M cuts AB in half, so AM = MB.
The perpendicular bisector is the line through M at a right angle (90°) to AB.
The angle bisector is the line from the corner that cuts the angle into two equal angles.

practice.question: To bisect something means to cut it into
practice.why: Bisect means cut into two equal parts, like a fold that makes the ends meet.
wrong: The two parts must be equal.
Bisect means two parts, not three.
Bisect means two parts, not four.

practice.question: AB = 10 cm and M is its midpoint. How long is AM?
practice.why: The midpoint cuts AB into two equal parts: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
wrong: That is the whole segment; AM is half of it.
You doubled; the midpoint halves the segment.
You halved twice; halve only once.

practice.question: A line crosses AB at its midpoint, at an angle of 60°. Is it the perpendicular bisector of AB?
options: Yes, because it passes through the midpoint
Yes, any line that crosses AB is one
No, it must pass through A
No, it must cross AB at 90°
practice.why: A perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint and crosses at a right angle, 90°. This one crosses at 60°.
wrong: The midpoint is not enough; it must also cross at 90°.
It must pass through the midpoint and cross at 90°.
It passes through the midpoint M, not through A; what is missing here is the 90°.

practice.question: An angle bisector cuts an angle into two angles of 35° each. How big was the whole angle?
practice.why: The two equal parts make the whole: 35° + 35° = 70°.
wrong: 35° is one part; the whole angle is two parts.
You halved 35°; add the two parts instead.
You doubled twice; there are only two parts of 35°.

rounds.question: The point that cuts a line segment into two equal parts is its
rounds.why: The midpoint M of AB cuts it into two equal parts, so AM = MB.
wrong: An end point is A or B itself; the midpoint lies half way between them.
An angle bisector cuts an angle, not a line segment.
A right angle is 90°; the point half way along is the midpoint.

rounds.question: M is the midpoint of AB, and AM = 4 cm. How long is AB?
rounds.why: AM = MB = 4 cm, so AB = 4 + 4 = 8 cm.
wrong: 4 cm is only one half; AB is both halves together.
You halved AM; AB is twice AM.
You doubled twice; AB is 4 + 4.

rounds.question: AB = 10 cm. A line crosses AB at 90°, at a point 2 cm from A. Is it the perpendicular bisector of AB?
options: No, it must pass through the midpoint of AB
Yes, any line at 90° to AB is one
No, it must cross AB at 45°
rounds.why: A perpendicular bisector needs two things: 90° and the midpoint. The midpoint is 5 cm from A, not 2 cm.
wrong: 90° is only half of the rule; it must also pass through the midpoint.
It must also cut AB into two equal parts, at the midpoint.
The angle must be 90°; what is missing here is the midpoint.

rounds.question: A ribbon 24 cm long is folded so that its two ends meet. How far is the fold from each end?
rounds.why: The fold bisects the ribbon: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm from each end.
wrong: 24 cm is the whole ribbon; the fold cuts it into two equal parts.
You doubled; bisecting means cutting into two equal parts.
You halved twice; one fold gives two parts of 12 cm.

rounds.question: The line from the corner of an angle that cuts it into two equal angles is the
rounds.why: The angle bisector starts at the corner and cuts the angle into two equal angles.
wrong: A perpendicular bisector cuts a line segment in half at 90°.
A midpoint is a point on a line segment, not a line through an angle.
An arm is one of the two lines that make the angle.

rounds.question: An angle of 50° is bisected. How big is each of the two angles?
rounds.why: To bisect is to cut into two equal parts: 50° ÷ 2 = 25°.
wrong: Each part is half of the angle, not the whole angle.
You doubled; bisecting halves the angle.
You took away 2; bisect means divide by 2.

rounds.question: A line from the corner cuts an angle of 90° into angles of 30° and 60°. Is it the angle bisector?
options: Yes, it starts at the corner
No, it must cut the angle into three parts
No, the two angles must be equal
rounds.why: An angle bisector makes two equal angles. Here they would be 45° and 45°, not 30° and 60°.
wrong: Starting at the corner is not enough; the two angles must be equal.
Any line from the corner makes parts that add to 90°; a bisector makes them equal.
To bisect is to cut into two equal parts, not three.

rounds.question: A pizza slice has an angle of 60° at its tip. A cut from the tip bisects it. What is the angle of each new piece?
rounds.why: Bisecting cuts the angle into two equal parts: 60° ÷ 2 = 30°.
wrong: Each piece is half of the slice, not the whole 60°.
You doubled; bisecting halves the angle.
You cut it into three parts; bisect means two equal parts.

entries.concept: congruent triangles, the SSS rule and CPCT
entries.evidence: Step 4 of the worked bisector says 'triangle PAQ ≅ triangle PBQ (SSS)' and the next lesson ends 'by CPCT', but congruence is not taught until class 7.

screens.title: Shapes that fit exactly
text: Put one 10 rupee coin on another. They match exactly: same shape, same size. Shapes that fit exactly on each other are called congruent.

check.question: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. Which corner of PQR matches B?

v.says: Two triangles, ABC and PQR, of the same shape and size. AB and PQ carry one mark, BC and QR two marks, CA and RP three marks.

figures.caption: Triangle PQR fits exactly on triangle ABC. Sides with the same marks are equal: PQ = AB, QR = BC, RP = CA.

screens.ask: Triangle PQR is congruent to triangle ABC. AB = {@a} cm, BC = {@b} cm and CA = {@c} cm. Find the sides of PQR.

lines: P ↔ A, Q ↔ B, R ↔ C
why: The order of the letters tells which corner goes on which.
First and second letters in both names.

steps.do: QR matches BC, RP matches CA.
why: Matching sides of congruent shapes are equal.

screens.note: Those sides cannot make a triangle. Keep the longest side shorter than the other two added.
after: Congruent triangles match in all three sides and all three angles.
'Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR' means A lies on P, B on Q and C on R. In the lessons, an equals sign with a small wave on top means 'is congruent to'.

screens.title: SSS and CPCT
text: Take three sticks of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Join them into a triangle. However you join them, you get the same triangle.

check.question: Two triangles each have sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Are they congruent?

screens.ask: Show that the compass construction really cuts angle O in half.

why: One opening of the compasses gives two equal lengths.

steps.do: Arcs from P and Q meet at R.
why: Same opening again gives PR = QR. OR belongs to both triangles OPR and OQR.
SSS: if all three sides match, the triangles are congruent.
CPCT: corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal. So OR cuts the angle in half.

after: So if the three sides of one triangle equal the three sides of another, they are congruent. This rule is called SSS: side, side, side.
Then every matching part is equal, the angles too. This is called CPCT: corresponding (matching) parts of congruent triangles.
In the lessons a double arrow between two statements means 'so'.

practice.question: Two shapes that fit exactly on top of each other are called
practice.why: Same shape and same size, fitting exactly: the shapes are congruent.
wrong: Corresponding means matching parts; the shapes themselves are congruent.
SSS is a rule that proves triangles congruent, not the name for the shapes.
CPCT says matching parts are equal; the shapes are called congruent.

practice.question: Triangle DEF is congruent to triangle XYZ. Which side matches EF?
practice.why: E matches Y and F matches Z (2nd and 3rd letters), so EF matches YZ.
wrong: XY matches DE, the first two letters.
ZX matches FD, the last and first letters.
DE is a side of the same triangle; look for the matching side in XYZ.

practice.question: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle RPQ. Which corner matches C?
practice.why: The order of the letters tells the match: C is third, and the third letter of RPQ is Q.
wrong: R is first in RPQ, so it matches A; go by the order written, not the alphabet.
P is second in RPQ, so it matches B.
B is in the same triangle; the matching corner is in RPQ.

practice.question: Triangles ABC and PQR are congruent by SSS, with A on P, B on Q and C on R. Angle B = 50°. Which is true?
practice.why: B matches Q, and matching parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT), so angle Q = 50°.
wrong: P matches A, not B.
The angle is right, but SSS proves the triangles congruent; CPCT gives the equal angles.
R matches C, not B.

rounds.question: What does SSS stand for?
rounds.why: SSS is side, side, side: three sides of one triangle equal three sides of the other.
wrong: Each S stands for a side of the triangle.
Each S stands for a side; the rule compares three sides.
There is no square in the rule; all three letters mean side.

rounds.question: Triangle KLM is congruent to triangle PQR. Which side matches KM?
rounds.why: K lies on P and M lies on R (first and third letters), so KM matches PR.
wrong: PQ matches KL, the first two letters.
QR matches LM, the last two letters.
LM is a side of the same triangle; the matching side is in PQR.

rounds.question: Triangle PQR is congruent to triangle ZXY. Which corner matches Q?
rounds.why: The order of the letters tells the match. Q is the second letter, and the second letter of ZXY is X.
wrong: You matched in alphabet order; match by position: second letter with second letter.
Z is the first letter, so it matches P.
R is a corner of the same triangle; the match is in ZXY.

rounds.question: Two triangular flags each have sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Are they congruent?
options: No, we must measure the angles too
rounds.why: The three sides of one equal the three sides of the other, so they are congruent by SSS.
wrong: Three equal sides are enough; SSS needs no angles.
CPCT is used after the triangles are known to be congruent; the reason here is SSS.
Three sticks of fixed lengths make only one triangle, so the flags match.

rounds.question: In CPCT, what does 'corresponding' mean?
rounds.why: CPCT is corresponding parts of congruent triangles, and corresponding just means matching.
wrong: Congruent means fitting exactly; corresponding means matching.
The parts are matching ones, not opposite ones.
The matching parts turn out equal, but the word itself means matching.

rounds.question: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XYZ, and AB = 7 cm. Which side of triangle XYZ is 7 cm?
rounds.why: AB uses the first two letters, so it matches XY. Matching sides are equal, so XY = 7 cm.
wrong: YZ matches BC, the last two letters.
ZX matches CA, the third and first letters.
Only the side that matches AB must be 7 cm, and that is XY.

rounds.question: Two triangles have only two pairs of equal sides. Can we say they are congruent by SSS?

rounds.question: Two set squares fit exactly on each other: triangle ABC on triangle DEF, with A on D, B on E and C on F. Angle C = 30°. Which angle of triangle DEF is 30°?
rounds.why: C lies on F, so angle F matches angle C. By CPCT, angle F = 30°.
wrong: D matches A, not C.

entries.concept: point, line segment and line, and naming them with letters
entries.evidence: The first lesson counts 'line segments' and 'lines' through points A, B, C and writes AB and BA, without saying what a point, a line segment or a line is.

text: Press a sharp pencil on paper. The dot is a point. We name it with a capital letter: A.
Make a point B. Join A to B with a ruler. This straight path is a line segment, AB. It stops at A and at B.

check.question: How many end points does a line segment have?

figures.caption: A point. We name it A.

figures.caption: The line segment AB. It stops at A and at B.

screens.ask: Mark A, B and C, not in a row. Join every pair. How many line segments?

why: A point marks one place. It has no size.
A line segment is the straight path between two points. It stops at both ends.

practice.question: A dot that marks one place is called
practice.why: A dot marks one place. It is called a point.
wrong: A line is a straight path that goes on and on, not one dot.
A line segment is a straight path with two ends, not one dot.

practice.question: A string is pulled tight between two nails. It is like
practice.why: The string is straight and has two ends, the nails. So it is like a line segment.
wrong: A point is one place; the string is a straight path.
A line never stops, but the string stops at the nails.
An arrow only shows that a line goes on; the string has two ends.

rounds.question: A straight path that joins two points is called

wrong: A point is only one place; the path between two points is a line segment.
A dot marks one point; it is not a path.
An arrow only shows that a line goes on; the path is a line segment.

rounds.question: How many ends does a line segment have?
rounds.why: A line segment AB stops at A and at B, so it has two ends.
wrong: A line has no ends; a line segment stops at both ends.
It stops at both A and B, so there are two ends.
It has just the two ends A and B.

rounds.question: How many ends does a line have?
options: None. It goes on both ways
rounds.why: A line does not stop. It goes on and on both ways, so it has no ends.
wrong: A line segment has 2 ends; a line never stops.
A line goes on both ways, so it has no end on any side.

rounds.question: The tip of a sharp pin is like
rounds.why: The tip marks just one place, like a dot. That is a point.
wrong: A line is a long straight path that never stops; the tip is one place.
A line segment is a path with two ends; the tip is one place.

rounds.question: How do we name a point?
rounds.why: We name a point with a capital letter, such as A.
wrong: Points are named with capital letters like A and B, not numbers.
Arrows are put at the ends of a line, not used as names.

rounds.question: What do the small arrows at the ends of a line show?

wrong: A line segment stops; the arrows mean the line does not stop.
A point is one dot; the arrows show the line goes on.

rounds.question: Mark three points P, Q and R, not in a row. Join every pair. How many line segments do you get?

rounds.question: A straight road is drawn with a small arrow at each end. It is drawn as
rounds.why: Arrows at both ends show that it goes on and on both ways. That is a line.
wrong: A point is one place; this is a straight path that goes on.
A line segment stops at two ends; the arrows show this one does not stop.
A dot marks one place; this is a straight path that goes on.

entries.concept: right angle (square corner)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Parallel, perpendicular or neither' says perpendicular lines 'meet at a right angle', but right angles are first taught in class 4.

screens.title: The square corner
text: Feel the corner of your book. It is a square corner.
A door, a window and a floor tile have square corners too.
Put a page corner into a corner. If it fits exactly, it is a square corner.
A square corner is called a right angle. Two lines that meet at a right angle are perpendicular.

check.question: Is the corner of a square tile a right angle?

screens.ask: Are the top bar and the stem of the letter T perpendicular?

why: Look at the corner where the two lines touch.
A page corner is a square corner, so it fits only a right angle.
Two lines meeting at a square corner are called perpendicular.

practice.question: What is another name for a square corner?
practice.why: A square corner has a special name: a right angle.
wrong: The name is right angle; there is no left angle.
A straight line has no corner.
A square corner is made by two straight lines, so it is not round.

practice.question: Two straight lines meet and make a square corner. The lines are called

wrong: Equal is about length; the word for a square corner is perpendicular.
They are straight, but the name for making a square corner is perpendicular.

practice.question: You put a page corner into a corner. The two lines are wider apart than the page corner. Is it a right angle?
options: No, it is wider than a square corner
Yes, all corners are right angles
Yes, wide corners are right angles
No, the lines are closer together

wrong: In V the lines are closer together than a page corner.

In Z the lines at each corner are closer together than a page corner.

rounds.question: A right angle is
rounds.why: Right angle is the special name for a square corner, like the corner of a page.
wrong: A round corner has no straight lines meeting; a right angle is a square corner.
A straight line has no corner; a right angle is a square corner.

wrong: A ball is round and has no corner to test with.

rounds.question: You put a page corner into a corner. The two lines are closer together than the page corner. Is it a right angle?
options: Yes, all corners are right angles
No, it is smaller than a square corner
Yes, small corners are right angles
No, it is wider than a square corner
rounds.why: A right angle fits the page corner exactly. This corner is closer, so it is smaller than a square corner.
wrong: Only corners that fit the page corner exactly are right angles.

rounds.question: Which of these has square corners?

wrong: A coin is round and has no corners.
A ball is round all over and has no corners.

rounds.question: Two lines are perpendicular. What does this mean?
options: They meet and make a square corner

wrong: Perpendicular is about the corner the lines make, not how long they are.
Perpendicular lines are straight and meet in a square corner.
Perpendicular lines meet; they make a square corner.

rounds.question: A page corner fits exactly into a corner. Both edges of the page lie along the two lines. The corner is
rounds.why: If the page corner fits exactly, the corner is a square corner: a right angle.
wrong: The lines are straight and fit the page corner, so it is not round.
Two lines meet here and make a corner, so it is not one straight line.
It fits the page corner exactly, so it is a right angle.

rounds.question: A square corner points to the left. Is it still a right angle?
options: Yes, every square corner is a right angle
No, it is a left angle
No, it must point to the right
Yes, but only on a page
rounds.why: A right angle is any square corner. It does not matter which way it points.
wrong: There is no left angle; every square corner is a right angle.
The name does not mean pointing right; any square corner is a right angle.
Square corners are right angles anywhere, such as on doors and tiles.

rounds.question: Look at the plus sign +. Its two bars are
options: wider apart than a page corner
rounds.why: The two bars meet and make square corners, so they are perpendicular.
wrong: Both bars are straight, and they make square corners.
The bars cross in the middle, so they do meet.
A page corner fits exactly where the bars cross.

entries.concept: full turn, half turn and quarter turn
entries.evidence: The lesson on the four directions says 'a quarter turn right' and 'a half turn', but turns and quarters have not been taught by class 2.

screens.title: Full turn, half turn, quarter turn
text: Stand and face the door. Turn all the way round until you face it again. That is a full turn.
Face the door. Turn until your back is to it. That is a half turn.
Face the door. Turn until your shoulder points at it. That is a quarter turn.
2 half turns make a full turn. 4 quarter turns make a full turn.

check.question: How many quarter turns make one full turn?

screens.ask: Ravi faces North and makes two quarter turns to the right. Which way does he face?

why: Turning right goes the way your right hand points: North, East, South, West.
One more quarter turn right moves one more direction on.
Two quarters make a half. A half turn always faces you the opposite way.

practice.question: You turn all the way round and face the door again. What is this turn?
practice.why: Turning all the way round once is a full turn.
wrong: After a half turn your back is to the door.
After a quarter turn your shoulder points at the door.
You did turn, all the way round. That is a full turn.

practice.question: How many half turns make one full turn?
practice.why: Two half turns make one full turn.
wrong: 4 is for quarter turns. Two half turns make a full turn.
One half turn only gets you to face the opposite way.
Three is too many. Two half turns bring you back.

practice.why: After a half turn you face the opposite way, so her back is to the door.
wrong: Her face points at the door after a full turn, not a half turn.
A shoulder points at the door after a quarter turn, not a half turn.
A shoulder points at the door after a quarter turn, not a half turn.

practice.question: Sita makes 2 quarter turns. This is the same as

wrong: A full turn needs 4 quarter turns.

Two full turns need 8 quarter turns.

rounds.why: After a half turn you face the opposite way, so your back is to the door.
wrong: After a full turn you face the door again.
After a quarter turn your shoulder points at the door.
With no turn you still face the door.

rounds.question: How many quarter turns make one full turn?
rounds.why: Four quarter turns make one full turn.
wrong: 2 quarter turns make only a half turn.
1 quarter turn is only a part of a full turn; it takes 4.
3 quarter turns are not all the way round; it takes 4.

rounds.question: Anu faces the window. She makes a quarter turn. What points at the window now?
rounds.why: After a quarter turn your shoulder points at the thing you faced.
wrong: Her face points at the window only before the turn, or after a full turn.
Her back points at the window after a half turn.
Turning round does not move her head to point at the window.

rounds.question: A toy car faces the wall. It makes a quarter turn. Then it makes one more quarter turn the same way. What faces the wall now?
rounds.why: Two quarter turns make a half turn. After a half turn the back faces the wall.
wrong: The front faces the wall only after a full turn.
The side faces the wall after one quarter turn; the car made two.
Turning round does not make the top face the wall.

rounds.question: Which turn is half of a half turn?
rounds.why: A quarter turn is half of a half turn.
wrong: A full turn is two half turns, not half of one.
A half turn is not half of itself; half of it is a quarter turn.
Half of a half turn is still a turn: a quarter turn.

rounds.question: After a half turn, which way do you face?
rounds.why: A half turn makes you face the opposite way.
wrong: You face the same way only after a full turn.
You face to the right after a quarter turn right.
Turning round does not make you face up.

rounds.question: Ravi faces North. He makes a half turn. Which way does he face now?
rounds.why: A half turn makes him face the opposite way. The opposite of North is South.
wrong: East is where he faces after a quarter turn right.
He faces North again only after a full turn.
A half turn takes him to the opposite of North, which is South.

rounds.question: Tara makes a half turn. Then she makes one more half turn. She has made
rounds.why: Two half turns make one full turn.
wrong: A quarter turn is smaller than a half turn; two half turns make a full turn.
One half turn is only the first part; she made two.
She made two half turns, and they make one full turn.

entries.concept: names of polygons with 7 to 10 sides, and the base of a solid

screens.title: Naming shapes by their sides
text: Count the sides of each shape below. A shape's name tells how many sides it has.

check.question: How many sides does an octagon have?

nonagon: 9 sides
decagon: 10 sides

why: {if s = 5}"Penta" means five{end}{if s = 6}"Hexa" means six{end}{if s = 7}"Hepta" means seven{end}{if s = 8}"Octa" means eight{end}{if s = 9}"Nona" means nine{end}{if s = 10}"Deca" means ten{end}. The base has {s} sides and {s} corners.
All the sloping faces meet at one point at the top.
Count the corners of the base, then the point at the top.

after: triangle 3, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10.

practice.question: A hexagonal prism stands on a table. What shape is the face it stands on?
practice.why: A prism is named after its base, so a hexagonal prism stands on a hexagon.
wrong: A heptagon has 7 sides; hexagonal means a hexagon, 6 sides.

An octagon has 8 sides; hexagonal means a hexagon, 6 sides.

rounds.question: What is a polygon with 9 sides called?
rounds.why: The name tells the number of sides: a nonagon has 9 sides.
wrong: An octagon has 8 sides.
A decagon has 10 sides.
A heptagon has 7 sides.

rounds.question: How many corners does a heptagon have?
rounds.why: A heptagon has 7 sides, and a polygon has as many corners as sides.
wrong: 6 is for a hexagon; a heptagon has 7 sides and 7 corners.
8 is for an octagon; a heptagon has 7 sides and 7 corners.
5 is for a pentagon; a heptagon has 7 sides and 7 corners.

rounds.question: How many vertices does a nonagonal pyramid have in all?
rounds.why: The base is a nonagon with 9 corners. Add the point at the top: 9 + 1 = 10.
wrong: You forgot the point at the top; 9 + 1 = 10.
You doubled the base; a pyramid has only one more corner, at the top.
You added 2; a pyramid has just 1 point at the top.

rounds.question: A tent is a decagonal pyramid. What shape is its floor?
rounds.why: A pyramid is named after its base. A decagonal pyramid stands on a decagon.
wrong: A nonagon has 9 sides; decagonal means a base with 10 sides.
The sloping faces are triangles, but the floor is the base: a decagon.
An octagon has 8 sides; decagonal means a base with 10 sides.

rounds.question: What is another name for a corner of a polygon?
rounds.why: A corner is also called a vertex. For more than one we say vertices.
wrong: A side is a straight edge of the polygon, not a corner.
The base is the flat face a solid stands on.
A face is a flat surface of a solid, not a corner.

rounds.question: A polygon has 9 sides. How many vertices does it have?
rounds.why: A polygon has as many corners (vertices) as sides, so it has 9.
wrong: There is one vertex for each side, so 9, not 8.
There is one vertex for each side, so 9, not 10.
You doubled; there is one vertex for each side.

rounds.question: A hexagonal prism has a hexagon at the bottom and another at the top. How many vertices does it have in all?
rounds.why: Each hexagon has 6 corners. 6 at the bottom and 6 at the top make 12.
wrong: You counted only the bottom hexagon; the top has 6 more.
6 + 1 is the rule for a pyramid; a prism has a whole hexagon on top.
Each hexagon has 6 corners, so there are 6 + 6.

rounds.question: A pencil box is an octagonal prism standing on its end. How many sides does its base have?
rounds.why: A prism is named after its base. The base is an octagon, with 8 sides.
wrong: 6 sides make a hexagon; an octagon has 8.
7 sides make a heptagon; an octagon has 8.
10 sides make a decagon; an octagon has 8.

entries.concept: polyhedron, and what F, V and E stand for
entries.evidence: The lesson states 'For every polyhedron without holes, faces + vertices − edges = 2' without saying what a polyhedron is.

screens.title: What is a polyhedron?
text: Pick up a matchbox and a ball. The matchbox has only flat faces. The ball has no flat face at all.

check.question: Is a cricket ball a polyhedron?

figures.caption: A cube is a polyhedron: 6 flat faces, 12 edges and 8 corners. Three faces, three edges and one corner are hidden at the back.

screens.ask: Count the faces, vertices and edges of a cube and work out F + V − E.

why: A face is a flat side. A cube has top, bottom and four sides.
4 corners on top and 4 on the bottom. 4 edges on top, 4 on the bottom and 4 upright.
F + V − E = 2 for every polyhedron without holes. This is Euler's rule.

after: A solid whose faces are all flat is called a polyhedron. Cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids are polyhedra. Cylinders, cones and spheres are not: they curve.
A face is a flat side. An edge is where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner (more than one: vertices).
F is the number of faces, V the number of vertices and E the number of edges.

practice.question: In the formula, what does E stand for?
practice.why: E is the number of edges, the lines where two faces meet.
wrong: Faces are counted by F.
Vertices are counted by V.
The formula is about one solid; E counts its edges.

practice.question: Which of these is a polyhedron?
practice.why: A cuboid has only flat faces, so it is a polyhedron.
wrong: A cylinder has a curved surface, so it is not a polyhedron.
A cone has a curved surface, so it is not a polyhedron.
A sphere has no flat face at all.

practice.question: The line where two faces meet is called
practice.why: Two faces meet along a line, and that line is an edge.
wrong: A vertex is a corner point where edges meet.
A face is a flat surface, not a line.
A corner is a vertex, a point where edges meet.

practice.question: A solid has F = 5, V = 6 and E = 9. What is F + V − E?
wrong: You added all three; E is subtracted.
You worked out F + E − V; it is F + V − E.
You worked out V + E − F; it is F + V − E.

rounds.question: In the formula, what does V stand for?
rounds.why: V is the number of vertices, the corners where edges meet.
wrong: The number of faces is F.
The number of edges is E.
The formula counts parts of one solid; V is its vertices.

rounds.question: Which of these is NOT a polyhedron?
rounds.why: A cone has a curved surface, so its faces are not all flat polygons.
wrong: A cube has only flat square faces, so it is a polyhedron.
A pyramid has only flat faces, so it is a polyhedron.
A prism has only flat faces, so it is a polyhedron.

rounds.question: A corner where edges meet is called
rounds.why: A vertex is a corner where edges meet.
wrong: An edge is the line where two faces meet, not the corner.
A face is a flat surface of the solid.
A polygon is the flat shape of a face, not a corner.

rounds.question: A solid has F = 7, V = 10 and E = 15. What is F + V − E?
wrong: You added all three; E is subtracted.
You stopped at F + V; now take away E = 15.
You worked out F − V + E; the formula is F + V − E.

rounds.question: A solid whose faces are all flat polygons is called
rounds.why: A solid with only flat polygon faces is a polyhedron.
wrong: A sphere has no flat face at all.
A cylinder has a curved surface, so it is not one.
A vertex is a corner of a solid, not the solid.

rounds.question: Why is a cylinder not a polyhedron?
rounds.why: All the faces of a polyhedron must be flat polygons. A cylinder has a curved surface.
wrong: The reason is the curved surface; a polyhedron needs all faces flat.
Height does not matter; what matters is that all faces are flat polygons.
A flat top is fine; the trouble is the curved surface round the side.

rounds.question: How many faces does a cube have?
rounds.why: A cube has 6 flat square faces: F = 6.
wrong: 8 is the number of vertices (corners) of a cube.
12 is the number of edges of a cube.
Count the top and the bottom too: 4 + 2 = 6.

rounds.question: A square pyramid has F = 5 and V = 5, and F + V − E = 2. What is E?
wrong: 10 is F + V; take away 2 to get E.
You added 2; E is 10 − 2.
2 is the value of F + V − E, not the number of edges.

entries.concept: the square of a number and the square root (the signs ² and √)
entries.evidence: The first lesson writes 'c² = a² + b²' and '√5476 = 74' although squares and square roots are a class 8 skill and no lesson here says what ² or √ mean.

screens.title: Squaring a number
text: Lay tiles in 3 rows of 3. You need 3 × 3 = 9 tiles, and they make a square.

check.question: What is 6²?

screens.ask: Find {@a}², {@b}² and {@c}² + {@d}².

why: The small 2 means times itself. It is not {a} × 2.
{b} rows of {b} tiles make a square of {b2} tiles.
Square each one first, then add.

after: A number times itself is called its square. 3² is read '3 squared'.
A square of side 5 cm has area 5² = 25 cm². That is why it is called squaring.

screens.title: Going back: the square root
text: A square garden has an area of 25 m². How long is a side? Find the number that times itself makes 25. It is 5.

check.question: What is √36?

steps.do: Square the shorter sides and add.

√ asks: which number times itself makes {c2}? {c} × {c} = {c2}.
The longest side is always opposite the right angle.

screens.note: Use 3, 6, 9, 12 or 15. The other side follows from it.
after: Going back from a square is called taking the square root. Its sign is √. √25 = 5 because 5 × 5 = 25.
In a right-angled triangle, add the squares of the two shorter sides. The square root of that is the longest side.

practice.question: What does 8² mean?

wrong: The raised 2 does not mean times 2; it means 8 × 8.

wrong: You did 9 × 2; squaring means 9 × 9.
You did 9 + 2; squaring means 9 × 9.
You did 9 × 8; multiply 9 by itself.

wrong: You halved 81; find the number that multiplied by itself gives 81.

You divided by 10; find the number that multiplied by itself gives 81.

practice.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the longest side?
wrong: You added the sides; add their squares, then take the square root.
