screens.title: Square roots
text: Now go backwards. Which number times itself makes 9? It is 3.
We say 3 is the square root of 9, and write √9 = 3.

check.question: What is √16?

screens.ask: Find √36.

why: √36 asks: which number times itself makes 36?
6 times itself is exactly 36.
Finding a square root undoes squaring.

after: The sign √ asks: which number times itself gives this number?
Most numbers are not squares. 4 × 4 = 16 and 5 × 5 = 25, so √20 is between 4 and 5.

practice.question: How is 6² read?
practice.why: The small raised 2 is read as squared: 6² is 6 squared, which means 6 × 6.
wrong: The small 2 does not mean times 2; it means 6 × 6.
The square root uses the sign √; the small raised 2 means squared.
The small raised 2 is not a digit of the number; it means squared.

practice.question: What is 7²?
wrong: That is 7 × 2; 7² means 7 × 7.
That is 7 + 2; 7² means 7 × 7.
The small 2 is not a digit to write after 7; 7² means 7 × 7.

practice.question: What is √64?
practice.why: √ asks which number times itself gives 64. 8 × 8 = 64, so √64 = 8.
wrong: You halved 64; the square root is the number that times itself gives 64.
You doubled 64; the square root is the number that times itself gives 64.
7 × 7 = 49, which is too small; try 8.

practice.question: √30 lies between which two whole numbers?
practice.why: 5 × 5 = 25 and 6 × 6 = 36. 30 is between 25 and 36, so √30 is between 5 and 6.
wrong: 4 × 4 = 16 and 5 × 5 = 25; 30 is bigger than both.
6 × 6 = 36 is already more than 30.
You halved 30; look for numbers whose squares are near 30.

rounds.question: What does the sign √ ask?
options: What is half of this number?
Which number times itself gives this number?
What is this number times itself?
rounds.why: √ asks: which number times itself gives this number? For example √9 = 3 because 3 × 3 = 9.
wrong: A square root is not a half: √9 is 3, not 4 and a half.
√ does not double a number.
That is squaring; the square root goes backwards.

rounds.question: What is 8²?
rounds.why: 8² means 8 × 8 = 64.
wrong: You did 8 × 2; 8² means 8 × 8.
You added 8 and 2; 8² means 8 × 8.
You wrote 8 and 2 side by side; the small 2 means 8 × 8.

rounds.question: What is √100?
wrong: You halved 100; find the number that times itself gives 100.
You doubled 100; find the number that times itself gives 100.
You squared 100; the square root goes backwards.

rounds.question: A square floor has 9 rows of tiles with 9 tiles in each row. How many tiles are there?
rounds.why: 9 rows of 9 is 9² = 9 × 9 = 81 tiles.
wrong: You did 9 × 2; 9 rows of 9 is 9 × 9.
You wrote 9 and 9 side by side; multiply them.
You did 9 × 3; 9 rows of 9 is 9 × 9.

rounds.question: What is a number multiplied by itself called?
rounds.why: A number multiplied by itself is called its square. The square of 3 is 3 × 3 = 9.
wrong: The square root goes backwards: from 9 back to 3.
The double is the number times 2, not times itself.
Half is the number divided by 2.

rounds.question: What is √16?
wrong: You halved 16; find the number that times itself gives 16.
You doubled 16; find the number that times itself gives 16.
You took 2 away; find the number that times itself gives 16.

rounds.question: Which of these is a perfect square?
rounds.why: 6 × 6 = 36, so 36 is a whole number times itself.
wrong: 12 is 6 × 2, not a number times itself.
18 is 9 × 2, not a number times itself.
20 is 10 × 2, not a number times itself.

rounds.question: A gardener sets 49 plants in a square: the number of rows is the same as the number of plants in each row. How many rows are there?
rounds.why: We need the number that times itself gives 49. 7 × 7 = 49, so there are 7 rows.
wrong: 14 × 14 is far more than 49; try 7 × 7.
You doubled 49; find the number that times itself gives 49.
You took 2 away; find the number that times itself gives 49.

entries.concept: what interest, principal, rate and amount are
entries.evidence: 'Simple interest, amount, rate or time' starts 'simple interest is the same every year: R% of the principal' and uses SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, but nothing says what interest is or what the principal is.

screens.title: The price of borrowing money
text: Your uncle borrows money from a bank for one year. He must pay it all back, and a little extra. The extra is called interest.

check.question: 100 rupees is lent for 1 year at 10% per year. How much is the interest?

screens.ask: He borrows ₹{@P} at {@R}% a year. Find the interest, what he pays back after 1 year, and the interest for 2 years.

why: {R}% means {R} for every 100. {P} has {hh} {hh|hundred|hundreds}, so {hh} × {R} = {I}.
He pays back the money borrowed plus the interest.
In simple interest, the interest is the same every year.

screens.note: Use whole hundreds of rupees, like 300 or 1500.
after: The money borrowed is called the principal, P. The rate, R, is the interest each year as a per cent of P. The time, T, is the number of years.
Everything paid back at the end is called the amount: principal plus interest.
It works the other way too. Keep money in a bank and the bank pays you interest.

practice.question: What is the money borrowed at the start called?
practice.why: The money borrowed at the start is the principal, P.
wrong: Interest is the extra money paid for borrowing.
The amount is everything paid back: principal plus interest.
The rate is the per cent of interest charged each year.

practice.question: 200 rupees is lent for 1 year at 5% per year. How much is the interest?
practice.why: 5% means 5 rupees for every 100 rupees. 200 is two hundreds, so the interest is 2 × 5 = 10 rupees.
wrong: 5 rupees is the interest on 100 rupees; here there are two hundreds.
210 rupees is the amount, principal plus interest; the interest is only the extra.
You multiplied 200 by 5; 5% means 5 for every 100.

practice.question: The principal is 500 rupees and the interest is 40 rupees. What is the amount?
practice.why: Amount = principal + interest = 500 + 40 = 540 rupees.
wrong: You subtracted the interest; the borrower pays it on top of the principal.
40 rupees is only the interest; the amount also includes the principal.
500 rupees is only the principal; add the interest.

practice.question: Rani keeps 100 rupees in a bank for 3 years. The bank pays simple interest at 6% per year. How much interest does she get?
practice.why: Each year the interest is 6% of 100 = 6 rupees. For 3 years: 3 × 6 = 18 rupees.
wrong: 6 rupees is the interest for one year only; she keeps the money for 3 years.
118 rupees is the amount; the interest is only the extra 18.
You added 6 and 3; multiply the yearly interest by the number of years.

rounds.question: The extra money paid for borrowing is called the ...
rounds.why: The extra money paid back on top of what was borrowed is called interest.
wrong: The principal is the money borrowed at the start.
The amount is everything paid back: principal plus interest.
The rate tells how much interest is charged each year, as a per cent.

rounds.question: 300 rupees is lent for 1 year at 10% per year. How much is the interest?
rounds.why: 10% of 300 = 10 rupees for every 100 rupees = 3 × 10 = 30 rupees.
wrong: 10 rupees is the interest on 100 rupees only; there are 3 hundreds.
330 rupees is the amount; the interest is only the extra part.
You multiplied 300 by 10; 10% means 10 for every 100.

rounds.question: What does a rate of 4% per year mean?
options: 4 rupees of interest each year for every 100 rupees of principal
4 rupees of interest each year, whatever the principal
4 rupees of interest for every 1 rupee of principal
The money is borrowed for 4 years
rounds.why: Per cent means for every 100. So 4% per year is 4 rupees each year for every 100 rupees of principal.
wrong: The interest depends on the principal: 4 rupees for every 100 rupees.
Per cent means for every 100 rupees, not for every 1 rupee.
The number of years is the time; the rate tells the interest each year.

rounds.question: A farmer borrows 2000 rupees for 2 years at simple interest of 5% per year. How much interest does he pay in all?
rounds.why: Interest for one year: 5% of 2000 = 100 rupees. For 2 years: 2 × 100 = 200 rupees.
wrong: That is the interest for one year only; there are 2 years.
You multiplied 5 by 2; first find 5% of 2000.
2200 rupees is the amount; the interest is only the extra 200.

rounds.question: Everything paid back at the end, principal plus interest, is called the ...
rounds.why: The amount is everything paid back at the end: principal plus interest.
wrong: The rate is the per cent charged each year.
The time is the number of years.
The interest is only the extra money, not the whole payment.

rounds.question: 400 rupees is lent for 1 year at 5% per year. How much is the interest?
rounds.why: 5% of 400 = 5 rupees for every 100 rupees = 4 × 5 = 20 rupees.
wrong: 5 rupees is the interest on 100 rupees only; there are 4 hundreds.
420 rupees is the amount; the interest is only the extra part.
You multiplied 400 by 5; 5% means 5 for every 100.

rounds.question: Arun borrows 600 rupees. At the end he pays back 648 rupees in all. How much is the interest?
rounds.why: Amount = principal + interest, so interest = 648 − 600 = 48 rupees.
wrong: 648 rupees is the amount, everything paid back.
You added the principal and the amount; subtract to find the extra.
600 rupees is the principal, the money borrowed.

rounds.question: Latha keeps 500 rupees in a bank for 1 year. The bank pays interest at 4% per year. How much does she have at the end of the year?
rounds.why: Interest: 4% of 500 = 5 × 4 = 20 rupees. Amount = 500 + 20 = 520 rupees.
wrong: 20 rupees is only the interest; she also has her 500 rupees.
You added 4; the interest is 4 rupees for every 100, so 20 rupees.
That is the amount after 2 years; the money stays for 1 year.

entries.concept: what a proportion is, the :: sign, extremes and means
entries.evidence: 'Are four numbers in proportion?' and 'The missing term of a proportion' use a : b :: c : d and 'the product of the extremes equals the product of the means' without saying what a proportion, the double colon, the extremes or the means are.

screens.title: Two equal ratios
text: 1 pen costs ₹5, so 2 pens cost ₹10. Pens: 1 : 2. Rupees: 5 : 10, which is also 1 : 2. The two ratios are equal.

check.question: In 3 : 4 :: 6 : 8, which two numbers are the extremes?

screens.ask: Is {@a} : {@b} :: {@c} : {@d} a proportion?

why: The outer pair, {a} and {d}, are called the extremes.
The inner pair, {b} and {c}, are called the means.

lines: {if ad = bc}{ad} = {bc}: yes{else}{ad} and {bc} are not equal: no{end}
why: {if ad = bc}The products are equal, so the two ratios are equal.{else}The products are not equal, so the two ratios are not equal.{end}

after: When two ratios are equal, the four numbers are in proportion. We write 1 : 2 :: 5 : 10, read '1 is to 2 as 5 is to 10'.
In every proportion the extremes multiplied and the means multiplied give the same number: 1 × 10 and 2 × 5 are both 10.

practice.question: When two ratios are equal, the four numbers are said to be in ...
practice.why: Two equal ratios make a proportion, written with = or ::.
wrong: Extremes are only the first and last numbers of a proportion.
Means are only the two middle numbers of a proportion.
The word for four numbers forming two equal ratios is proportion.

practice.question: In 2 : 5 :: 4 : 10, which two numbers are the means?
practice.why: The means are the two middle numbers: 5 and 4.
wrong: 2 and 10 sit at the two ends; they are the extremes.
2 and 5 are the first ratio; the means are the two middle numbers.
4 and 10 are the second ratio; the means are the two middle numbers.

practice.question: Which of these is a proportion?
practice.why: Extremes: 3 × 10 = 30. Means: 5 × 6 = 30. The products are equal.
wrong: Adding 2 to both terms does not keep the ratio: 3 × 7 = 21 but 5 × 5 = 25.
Adding 3 to both terms does not keep the ratio: 3 × 8 = 24 but 5 × 6 = 30.
The second ratio is the wrong way round: 3 × 6 = 18 but 5 × 10 = 50.

practice.question: 2 pencils cost 6 rupees. So 2 : 5 :: 6 : ? gives the cost of 5 pencils. What is the missing number?
practice.why: Product of means: 5 × 6 = 30. Product of extremes: 2 × ? = 30, so ? = 15.
wrong: You added 3 because 5 is 3 more than 2; test with products: 2 × 9 = 18, not 30.
30 is the product of the means; divide it by 2 to get the missing extreme.
You added 5 and 6; the products of extremes and means must be equal.

rounds.question: In a proportion, what are the first and last numbers called?
rounds.why: The first and last numbers sit at the two ends. They are called the extremes.
wrong: The means are the two middle numbers.
A ratio is a pair like 1 : 2; the two end numbers are the extremes.
A product is the answer to a multiplication.

rounds.question: In 3 : 4 :: 9 : 12, which two numbers are the extremes?
rounds.why: The extremes are the first and last numbers: 3 and 12.
wrong: 4 and 9 are the middle numbers, the means.
3 and 4 are the terms of the first ratio.
9 and 12 are the terms of the second ratio.

rounds.question: Are 4, 6, 8, 10 in proportion, that is, is 4 : 6 :: 8 : 10 true?
options: Yes, because the numbers go up by 2 each time
Yes, because all four numbers are even
No, because 4 × 10 is not equal to 6 × 8
rounds.why: Extremes: 4 × 10 = 40. Means: 6 × 8 = 48. The products are not equal, so it is not a proportion.
wrong: Equal steps do not make equal ratios; test the products.
The test uses products, not sums: 40 is not 48.
Being even does not make ratios equal; test the products.

rounds.question: 4 bananas cost 20 rupees. So 4 : 6 :: 20 : ? gives the cost of 6 bananas. What is the missing number?
rounds.why: Product of the means: 6 × 20 = 120. So 4 × ? = 120, and ? = 30.
wrong: You added 2 because there are 2 more bananas; ratios multiply.
You added 6 to 20; use extremes × = means ×.
120 is the product of the means; divide it by 4.

rounds.question: How is 2 : 3 :: 4 : 6 read?
rounds.why: The sign : is read 'is to' and :: is read 'as'. So: 2 is to 3 as 4 is to 6.
wrong: The sign : does not mean times.
The sign : does not mean minus.
Read the numbers in the order they are written.

rounds.question: In the proportion 5 : 2 :: 10 : 4, what is the product of the extremes?
rounds.why: The extremes are the first and last numbers, 5 and 4. 5 × 4 = 20.
wrong: You multiplied 5 and 10; the extremes are 5 and 4.
You multiplied 2 and 4; the extremes are 5 and 4.
You added 5 and 4; a product means multiply.

rounds.question: A car uses 2 litres of petrol for 30 km. So 2 : 30 :: 5 : ? gives the distance for 5 litres. What is the missing number?
rounds.why: Product of the means: 30 × 5 = 150. So 2 × ? = 150, and ? = 75.
wrong: You added 3 because there are 3 more litres; ratios multiply.
150 is the product of the means; divide it by 2.
You doubled 30; 5 litres is two and a half times 2 litres.

entries.concept: what a ratio is and what a : b means
entries.evidence: 'A ratio in its simplest form' goes straight to simplifying 117 : 65 (and the proportion skill listed before it uses a : b = c : d); the meaning of the colon, 'for every', appears only in a side note of one alternative method.

screens.title: For every
text: Meena mixes 1 glass of lemon juice with 3 glasses of water. For a big jug she uses 2 of juice and 6 of water. It tastes the same: for every 1 glass of juice, still 3 of water.

check.question: A box has 4 red beads and 7 blue beads. What is the ratio of red beads to blue beads?

screens.ask: A class has {@g} girls and {@b} boys. Write the ratio of girls to boys simply.

why: Girls first, because the question says girls to boys.
Dividing both numbers by the same number keeps the ratio the same.
The class splits into 5 groups. Each has {x} {x|girl|girls} and {y} {y|boy|boys}.

screens.note: Use two numbers in the 5 times table that share no other factor, like 10 and 15.
after: A comparison like this is called a ratio. 1 : 3 is read '1 to 3'. The sign : means for every.
The order matters: water to juice is 3 : 1. Both amounts must be in the same unit.
2 : 6 and 1 : 3 are equal ratios, just as 2/6 and 1/3 are equal fractions.

practice.question: How is the ratio 2 : 5 read?
practice.why: The ratio 2 : 5 is read as 2 to 5, or 2 is to 5.
wrong: The sign : means 'for every', not multiply.
The sign : is not a minus sign; it means 'for every'.
The sign : is not a decimal point; it compares two quantities.

practice.question: A house has 3 cats and 8 dogs. What is the ratio of cats to dogs?
practice.why: Cats come first, then dogs: 3 : 8.
wrong: That is dogs to cats; the order of the terms matters.
11 is all the animals; the question compares cats with dogs.
That compares dogs with all the animals; compare cats with dogs.

practice.question: For tea, Amma mixes 2 cups of milk with 5 cups of water. What is the ratio of water to milk?
practice.why: Water is asked first, so water to milk is 5 : 2.
wrong: That is milk to water; the question asks for water first.
7 is the total number of cups; compare water with milk only.
That compares milk with the total; compare water with milk.

practice.question: Which ratio is equal to 6 : 9?
practice.why: Divide both terms by 3: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3, so 6 : 9 = 2 : 3.
wrong: The terms are in the wrong order; 6 : 9 becomes 2 : 3.
You subtracted 3 from both terms; divide both terms by the same number.
You subtracted 1 from both terms; divide both terms by the same number.

rounds.question: In a ratio, what does the sign : mean?
rounds.why: The sign : means for every. 1 : 3 says: for every 1 of the first there are 3 of the second.
wrong: A ratio compares two quantities; it does not add them.
A ratio compares two quantities; it does not multiply them.
It is not a decimal point: 1 : 3 is not 1.3.

rounds.question: A box has 4 red pens and 9 blue pens. What is the ratio of red pens to blue pens?
rounds.why: Red comes first: 4 red to 9 blue is 4 : 9.
wrong: That is blue to red; the order matters.
13 is all the pens; the ratio asked for is red to blue.
13 is all the pens, and red should come first against blue.

rounds.question: A ribbon is 50 cm long and a rope is 2 m long. What is the ratio of the ribbon's length to the rope's length?
rounds.why: Use the same unit: 2 m = 200 cm. 50 : 200, divide both terms by 50: 1 : 4.
wrong: One length is in cm and the other in m; change 2 m to 200 cm first.
You simplified 50 : 2, but the units differ; 2 m is 200 cm.
That is rope to ribbon; the ribbon comes first.

rounds.question: A painter mixes 3 tins of blue with 4 tins of white. Which mix makes a bigger batch of the same colour?
options: 6 tins of blue with 8 tins of white
4 tins of blue with 5 tins of white
6 tins of blue with 4 tins of white
4 tins of blue with 3 tins of white
rounds.why: 6 : 8, divide both terms by 2: 3 : 4. It is an equal ratio, so the colour is the same.
wrong: Adding 1 tin to each changes the ratio; multiply both terms instead.
Only the blue was doubled; both terms must be doubled.
The order was swapped; that is 4 blue for every 3 white.

rounds.question: What are the two numbers in a ratio called?
rounds.why: The two numbers of a ratio are called its terms.
wrong: Factors are numbers that are multiplied together.
Units are things like cm or glasses; the numbers are the terms.
The sign is the : between the numbers.

rounds.question: A team won 7 matches and lost 2. What is the ratio of wins to losses?
rounds.why: Wins come first: 7 wins to 2 losses is 7 : 2.
wrong: That is losses to wins; the order matters.
9 is all the matches; the ratio asked for is wins to losses.
That compares losses with all the matches.

rounds.question: The ratio of juice to water in a drink is 1 : 4. Which is true?
options: For every 4 glasses of juice there is 1 glass of water
There are 4 more glasses of water than juice
The drink has 1.4 glasses in all
For every 1 glass of juice there are 4 glasses of water
rounds.why: Juice comes first. 1 : 4 means for every 1 glass of juice there are 4 glasses of water.
wrong: The order is swapped; juice is the first term.
A ratio is 'for every', not 'more than': 2 glasses of juice go with 8 of water.
The sign : is not a decimal point.

rounds.question: A mason mixes 10 spades of sand with 4 spades of cement. What is the ratio of sand to cement in its simplest form?
rounds.why: Sand to cement = 10 : 4. Divide both terms by 2: 5 : 2.
wrong: That is cement to sand; sand comes first.
You took 2 away from each term; divide both terms by 2 instead.
14 is the whole mix; the second term should be the cement, 4.

entries.concept: what a rational number is
entries.evidence: The skill begins 'rational numbers follow the same rules as fractions' and works out −2/7 × (−2/3), but a rational number is not defined anywhere before class 9 and negative fractions have never been met.

screens.title: Fractions that can be negative
text: Half a degree below zero is −1/2 °C. It is a fraction, and it is negative.

check.question: Is −2/3 to the left or to the right of 0 on the number line?
check.answer: To the left, because it is negative

screens.ask: Is −7 rational? Where is −3/2 on the number line?

why: A rational number is an integer over a non-zero integer.
Every integer is rational.
3 halves is 1 and a half.
Negative numbers go left from 0.

after: A number that can be written as one integer over another, with the bottom not zero, is called a rational number. The word comes from ratio.
3/4, −1/2 and 7/5 are rational. So is every integer: 5 = 5/1. So are decimals such as 0.3 = 3/10.
On the number line, −1/2 is halfway between 0 and −1. −1/2 and (−1)/2 are the same number.

practice.question: What do we call a number that can be written as one integer over another integer that is not zero?
practice.why: Any number that can be written as an integer over a non-zero integer is a rational number.
wrong: Integers are rational, but so are fractions such as 3/4; the name for all of them is rational number.
Rational numbers can be positive too, such as 7/5.
Decimals such as 0.3 are rational, but the name for all such numbers is rational number.

practice.question: How can −4 be written as one integer over another?
practice.why: −4 = −4/1: an integer over a non-zero integer.
wrong: −1/4 is a quarter below zero, not −4.
4/1 is 4; the minus sign must stay.
The bottom integer must not be zero.

practice.question: Which of these is NOT a rational number?
practice.why: The bottom integer must not be zero, so 3/0 is not a rational number.
wrong: −2/7 is an integer over a non-zero integer; rational numbers can be negative.
0.7 = 7/10, an integer over a non-zero integer.
6 = 6/1, an integer over a non-zero integer.

practice.question: Where is −5/2 on the number line?
practice.why: −5/2 = −2 1/2, which is halfway between −2 and −3.
wrong: That is 5/2; a negative number lies to the left of 0.
That point is −3/2; −5/2 is −2 1/2.
You read the 5 as the whole part; −5/2 means 5 halves below zero, which is −2 1/2.

rounds.question: Which is true of every rational number?
options: It can be written as one integer over a non-zero integer
It must be a whole number
It cannot be written as a decimal
rounds.why: A rational number is any number that can be written as one integer over another integer that is not zero.
wrong: Rational numbers can be negative, like −1/2.
Fractions such as 3/4 are rational too.
Decimals such as 0.3 = 3/10 are rational.

rounds.question: How can 0.7 be written as one integer over another?
rounds.why: 0.7 is 7 tenths, so 0.7 = 7/10.
wrong: 7/100 is 0.07; the 7 is in the tenths place.
0/7 is zero.
7/1 is the integer 7.

rounds.question: Which is the same number as −3/5?
rounds.why: The minus sign can be written in front or on the top: −3/5 and (−3)/5 are the same number.
wrong: 3/5 is positive; −3/5 lies to the left of 0.
Top and bottom were swapped; that is a different number.
−3/5 is a fraction, not the decimal −3.5.

rounds.question: A coin lies a quarter of a metre below the ground. Which rational number shows its position?
rounds.why: A quarter is 1/4, and below the ground is negative: −1/4 m.
wrong: 1/4 m would be above the ground; below needs the minus sign.
−4 m is four whole metres down; a quarter is 1/4.
1/4 is not the decimal 1.4.

rounds.question: Why is the integer 9 a rational number?
options: It is not rational: it is an integer
rounds.why: 9 = 9/1, an integer over a non-zero integer, so it is rational.
wrong: Being positive is not the reason; −9 = −9/1 is rational too.
Integers are rational too, because each can be written over 1.
Odd or even does not matter; what matters is that 9 = 9/1.

rounds.question: Which of these is a rational number lying to the left of 0 on the number line?
rounds.why: Negative fractions lie to the left of 0. −2/3 is between 0 and −1.
wrong: 2/3 is positive, to the right of 0.
0 is at zero itself, not to its left.
3/2 is positive, to the right of 0.

rounds.question: Is 0/5 a rational number?
options: No, because the top is zero
No, zero cannot appear in a fraction
No, because it is equal to 5
Yes: it is an integer over a non-zero integer, and it equals 0
rounds.why: Only the bottom must not be zero. 0/5 = 0, an integer over the non-zero integer 5.
wrong: The top may be zero; only the bottom may not be.
Zero is allowed on the top, just not on the bottom.
0/5 is 0, not 5.

rounds.question: A diver is 7/2 m below the surface, at −7/2 m. Between which two whole-metre marks is the diver?
rounds.why: −7/2 = −3 1/2, halfway between −3 and −4.
wrong: The number is negative, so it lies to the left of 0.
7 is the top number; 7/2 is 3 1/2.

entries.concept: what Roman numerals are and the value of each letter
entries.evidence: 'Reading a Roman numeral' says 'each letter always stands for the same number' and works out XXI and DCCCLXXXVII, but no lesson lists what I, V, X, L, C, D and M stand for.

screens.title: Seven letters for numbers
text: Look at an old clock face. You may see I, II, III, IV, V in place of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. These are Roman numerals.
Each letter has a value: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000.

check.question: Which number does the letter V stand for?

screens.ask: What is XII?

why: Each letter stands for its own value.
A smaller letter after a bigger one is added.
Letters side by side, biggest first, add up to the number.

after: A smaller letter just before a bigger one is taken away: IV = 5 − 1 = 4 and IX = 10 − 1 = 9.
There is no letter for zero.

practice.question: Which number does the letter X stand for?
practice.why: In Roman numerals X = 10.
wrong: 5 is the value of V.
50 is the value of L.
100 is the value of C.

practice.question: What number is VII?
wrong: You took the two I's away; letters written after a bigger one are added.
You counted only one I; there are two: 5 + 1 + 1.
You took V as 10; V = 5 and X = 10.

practice.question: What number is XL?
practice.why: X (10) is smaller and comes just before L (50), so it is taken away: 50 − 10 = 40.
wrong: You added; a smaller letter just before a bigger one is taken away. 60 is LX.
You took L as 5; L = 50 and V = 5.
You took L as 100; L = 50 and C = 100.

practice.question: A chapter in a book is numbered XXVI. Which chapter is it?
wrong: You took the I away; it comes after V, so it is added.
You counted only one X; there are two.
You counted three X's; there are only two.

rounds.question: Which letter stands for 50 in Roman numerals?
What number is XVI?
wrong: You took the I away; the letters are biggest first, so add them all.
There is only one X: 10 + 5 + 1.
You left out the I at the end.

rounds.question: What number is XC?
rounds.why: X is smaller than C and is written just before it, so it is taken away: 100 − 10 = 90.
wrong: A smaller letter just before a bigger one is taken away, not added.
C is 100, not 50, and the X before it is taken away.

rounds.question: The short hand of an old clock points to VIII. What hour is it?
wrong: The I's come after V, so they are added, not taken away.
V is 5, not 10.
There are three I's after the V, not two.

rounds.question: How many different letters are used to write Roman numerals?
rounds.why: Only seven letters are used: I, V, X, L, C, D and M.
wrong: Ten is the number of digits 0 to 9 in our own numbers.
26 is the whole alphabet; only seven letters are used.
There are seven: do not forget D and M.

rounds.question: What number is LX?
rounds.why: L = 50 and X = 10. The bigger letter is first, so add: 50 + 10 = 60.
wrong: 40 is XL; here the X comes after L, so it is added.
L is 50, not 5.
L is 50, not 100.

rounds.question: How is the number 4 written in Roman numerals?
rounds.why: A smaller letter just before a bigger one is taken away: IV = 5 − 1 = 4.
wrong: The special rule writes 4 as one I before V.
VI is 5 + 1 = 6; the I must come before the V.
Only one I is written before the V.

rounds.question: A film is called 'Part XIX'. Which part is it?
wrong: The I is just before the last X, so it is taken away, not added.
IX is 9, not 1.
There are only two X's: X is 10 and IX is 9.

entries.concept: what an irrational number is
entries.evidence: The skill is called 'Construct irrational lengths such as √n' and the next skill proves numbers irrational, but 'irrational' is only explained in the real-numbers skill that comes after both in the list.

screens.title: Lengths that are not fractions
text: Draw a square with sides 1 unit long. By Pythagoras, its diagonal d satisfies d² = 1² + 1² = 2, so d = √2. You can draw this length, so it certainly exists. But what number is it?
1.4² = 1.96 and 1.5² = 2.25, so √2 lies between 1.4 and 1.5. Working out more digits gives 1.41421356... and the digits never stop and never settle into a repeating block.

A rational number is one that can be written as a fraction p/q with integers p and q, q ≠ 0. Its decimal either stops or repeats. A number that cannot be written as any such fraction is called irrational. √2 is irrational, and so are √3, √5 and π.
So an irrational length cannot be measured off exactly on a ruler marked in fractions of a unit. It can still be built exactly, as the hypotenuse of a right triangle. That is what this lesson does.

check.question: Is √16 rational or irrational?

screens.ask: Are √9 and √5 rational or irrational?

why: A rational number can be written as a whole number over a whole number. 3 is 3/1, so it is rational.
A root is only irrational when it does not come out exactly.
5 lies between 4 and 9, so its square root lies between 2 and 3. It is not a whole number.
The square root of a whole number is either a whole number or irrational. There is nothing in between.
The digits go on for ever without settling into a repeating pattern. That is the mark of an irrational number.

practice.question: What do we call a number that cannot be written as a fraction p/q with integers p and q?
practice.why: A number that cannot be written as any fraction p/q (q ≠ 0) is called irrational.
wrong: Rational numbers are exactly the ones that can be written as p/q.
Every integer n can be written as n/1, so it is rational.
A perfect square such as 9 is an integer, so it can be written as a fraction.

practice.question: Which of these numbers is irrational?
practice.why: 7 is not a perfect square (2² = 4, 3² = 9), so √7 is irrational.
wrong: √4 = 2 = 2/1, which is rational.
√25 = 5 = 5/1, which is rational.
7/2 is already a fraction of two integers, so it is rational.

practice.question: The decimal 0.3333... goes on for ever with the digit 3 repeating. What kind of number is it?
options: Irrational, because its digits never stop
Irrational, because it is not an integer
practice.why: A decimal that stops or repeats belongs to a rational number. This one repeats.
wrong: Never stopping is not enough; an irrational decimal also never settles into a repeating block.
Rational numbers need not be integers; fractions are rational too.
This decimal does not stop; it is rational because it repeats.

practice.question: A right triangle has shorter sides 1 unit and 3 units. Its hypotenuse h satisfies h² = 1² + 3². What is h?
practice.why: h² = 1 + 9 = 10, so h = √10. 10 is not a perfect square (3² = 9, 4² = 16), so √10 is irrational.
wrong: 10 is not a perfect square, so √10 cannot be written as a fraction.
You halved 10; the square root is the number whose square is 10.
You added 1 and 3; add the squares, 1 + 9 = 10, then take the square root.

rounds.question: What is true of the decimal of an irrational number?
options: It stops after a few digits
It never stops and never repeats
It repeats one block for ever
It always stops at the second decimal place
rounds.why: A rational number's decimal stops or repeats. An irrational number's decimal does neither.
wrong: A decimal that stops is a fraction, so it is rational.
A decimal that repeats a block is rational.
A decimal that stops is rational, wherever it stops.

rounds.question: Which of these numbers is rational?
rounds.why: √16 = 4 = 4/1, a fraction of integers, so it is rational.
wrong: 3 is not a perfect square, so √3 is irrational.
π is irrational: its digits never end or repeat.
2 is not a perfect square, so √2 is irrational.

rounds.question: Is √49 irrational?
options: Yes, because it has a root sign
No, because √49 = 24.5, a decimal that stops
rounds.why: 49 is a perfect square: √49 = 7 = 7/1, which is rational.
wrong: A root sign alone does not make a number irrational; work the root out.
Odd or even does not matter; check whether 49 is a perfect square.
The square root is not half: 7 × 7 = 49, so √49 = 7.

rounds.question: A right triangle has shorter sides 2 units and 3 units. Its hypotenuse h satisfies h² = 2² + 3². What is h?
rounds.why: h² = 4 + 9 = 13, so h = √13. 13 is not a perfect square, so √13 is irrational.
wrong: 13 is not a perfect square, so √13 cannot be written as a fraction.
You added the sides; add their squares, then take the root.
13 is h², not h; take the square root.

rounds.question: Which describes a rational number?
options: Its decimal never stops and never repeats
It can be written as p/q with integers p and q, q ≠ 0
rounds.why: A rational number can be written as a fraction p/q with integers p and q, q ≠ 0.
wrong: That describes an irrational number.
Some roots are rational (√9 = 3) and some are not (√2).
Sign does not decide it: −1/2 is rational and −√2 is not.

rounds.question: Between which two whole numbers does √7 lie?
rounds.why: 2² = 4 and 3² = 9. 7 lies between 4 and 9, so √7 lies between 2 and 3.
wrong: You halved 7; compare 7 with the squares 4 and 9.
Those are the neighbours of 7 itself, not of its square root.
2² = 4 is already less than 7, so √7 is more than 2.

rounds.question: π is often taken as 22/7 in sums. Is π a rational number?
options: Yes, because 3.14 is a decimal that stops
No, because π is more than 3
No: 22/7 is only close to π, and π is irrational
rounds.why: 22/7 and 3.14 are only close values. The digits of π never end or repeat, so π is irrational.
wrong: 22/7 is only an approximate value of π.
3.14 is only an approximate value of π.
Size does not decide it; what matters is that π cannot be written as p/q.

rounds.question: A square has an area of 5 cm², so its side is √5 cm. Can a ruler marked in fractions of a centimetre measure this side exactly?
options: No, because 5 is an odd number
rounds.why: 5 is not a perfect square, so √5 is irrational: it is not any fraction of a unit.
wrong: 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25, not 5; the root is not half.
2.2 × 2.2 = 4.84, not 5; the digits of √5 never end.
Odd is not the reason: 9 is odd and √9 = 3. The reason is that 5 is not a perfect square.

entries.concept: what a share, a shareholder and a dividend are
entries.evidence: The only lesson opens 'a share has a face value and a market value; a dividend is a percentage of the face value' without saying what a share is, why companies sell them or why a dividend is paid.

screens.title: Owning a small part of a company
text: A company needs money for a factory. It splits the sum into small equal parts and sells them. Each part is a share.

check.question: A share has a face value of 10 rupees and a 10% dividend is declared. How much dividend does one share earn?

screens.ask: A share has face value ₹100 and market value ₹{@mv}. It pays a {@p}% dividend. You buy {@k} {k|share|shares}. Find the cost and the yearly income.

steps.do: Cost: you pay the market value.
why: The market value is today's price. That is what you pay for each share.

steps.do: Dividend on one share: use the face value.
why: The dividend is worked out on the face value printed on the share, never on the price you paid.
{p}% means {p} out of every 100.
Each share pays {p} {p|rupee|rupees}, and you hold {k} {k|share|shares}.

after: Where people slip: taking {p}% of {mv}. The dividend ignores the market price.
A shareholder owns a small part of the company. The printed value is the face value. The day's price is the market value.
Above face value a share is at a premium. Below it, at a discount.

practice.question: What is the value printed on a share called?
practice.why: The value printed on the share is its face value, also called nominal value.
wrong: Market value is the changing price in the stock market.
The dividend is the payment made out of the company's profit.
A share is at a premium when its market price is above the face value.

practice.question: A share has a face value of 100 rupees. An 8% dividend is declared. How much does one share earn?
practice.why: Dividend = 8% of the face value = 8% of 100 = 8 rupees.
wrong: That adds the dividend to the face value; the dividend alone is 8 rupees.
That is 80% of 100; 8% of 100 is 8.
You divided 100 by 8; 8% means 8 for every 100.

practice.question: A share has a face value of 50 rupees and a market value of 80 rupees. A 10% dividend is declared. How much does one share earn?
practice.why: The dividend is a per cent of the face value: 10% of 50 = 5 rupees.
wrong: You took 10% of the market value; the dividend is always worked on the face value.
You took 10% of both values and added; use the face value only.
30 rupees is the premium (80 − 50), not the dividend.

practice.question: A share with a face value of 100 rupees is selling at 90 rupees in the stock market. How is it described?
practice.why: The market value 90 is below the face value 100, so the share is at a discount of 100 − 90 = 10 rupees.
wrong: Premium means the market value is above the face value; here it is below.
90 rupees is the market value itself; the discount is the gap, 10 rupees.
A dividend is a payment out of profit; the 10 rupees here is the gap between the two values.

rounds.question: The price of a share in the stock market, which changes from day to day, is called its ...
rounds.why: The price at which a share is bought and sold in the stock market is its market value.
wrong: The face value is the fixed value printed on the share.
The dividend is the payment out of the company's profit.
Nominal value is another name for the face value.

rounds.question: A share has a face value of 100 rupees and a market value of 150 rupees. How much do 20 shares cost today?
rounds.why: Shares are bought at the market value: 20 × 150 = 3000 rupees.
wrong: You used the face value; shares are bought at the market value.
You added face value and market value; only the market value is paid.
You paid only the premium of 50 rupees per share; the full 150 is paid.

rounds.question: A share has a face value of 10 rupees and a market value of 25 rupees. A 20% dividend is declared. How much does one share earn?
rounds.why: The dividend is a per cent of the face value: 20% of 10 = 2 rupees.
wrong: You took 20% of the market value; the dividend is on the face value.
20 is the per cent, not the rupees earned.
You took 20% of both values and added; use the face value only.

rounds.question: A share with a face value of 10 rupees is selling at 14 rupees in the stock market. How is it described?
rounds.why: The market value is above the face value by 14 − 10 = 4 rupees, so it is at a premium of 4 rupees.
wrong: A discount is when the market value is below the face value.
The premium is only the extra over the face value: 4 rupees.
A dividend is paid by the company out of profit; this is about the price.

rounds.question: Who is a shareholder?
options: A part owner of the company who has bought shares
rounds.why: A person who buys shares is a shareholder: a part owner of the company.
wrong: A shareholder owns part of the company; the money is not a loan.
A shareholder need not work for the company.
A shareholder buys shares, not the company's goods.

rounds.question: A share has a face value of 100 rupees. A 6% dividend is declared. What is the income from 50 shares?
rounds.why: One share earns 6% of 100 = 6 rupees. 50 shares earn 50 × 6 = 300 rupees.
wrong: That is the dividend on one share; there are 50 shares.
You took 6% of the number of shares; take 6% of the face value, then multiply by 50.
You added the value of the shares; the income is only the dividend.

rounds.question: Shares have a face value of 100 rupees and a market value of 120 rupees. A 10% dividend is declared. What is the income from 5 shares?
rounds.why: Dividend per share: 10% of the face value 100 = 10 rupees. 5 shares: 5 × 10 = 50 rupees.
wrong: You took 10% of the market value; the dividend is on the face value.
600 rupees is the cost of the 5 shares, not the income.
That is the dividend on one share; there are 5 shares.

rounds.question: A share with a face value of 50 rupees is at a discount of 5 rupees. What is its market value?
rounds.why: At a discount the market value is below the face value: 50 − 5 = 45 rupees.
wrong: Adding gives a premium; a discount is below the face value.
5 rupees is the discount, not the price.
The discount is 5 rupees, not 5 per cent.

entries.concept: the − sign
entries.evidence: The first taking-away lesson opens with '19 − 6 = ?' without naming the − sign or saying which number is which.

screens.title: Minus means take away
text: Hold up 5 fingers. Fold down 2. Count the ones still up: 1, 2, 3.

check.question: What is 3 − 1?

screens.ask: You have {@a} biscuits. You eat {@b}. How many are left?

why: The first number is what you start with.
The − sign means take away.
The number after = is how many are left.

screens.note: You can only eat some of the biscuits. Use a smaller number.
after: The sign − is called minus. It means take away.
Read {a} − {b} = {d} as {a} minus {b} equals {d}.

practice.question: What is the sign − called?
practice.why: The sign − is called minus. It means take away.
wrong: Plus is the sign +. It means put together.
Equals is the sign =. It means makes.
Add goes with the sign +. The sign − is minus.

practice.question: What is 5 − 1?
practice.why: You have 5. Take away 1. Count what is left: 1, 2, 3, 4.
wrong: You put 1 more in. Minus means take away.
You did not take 1 away. Count what is left.
1 is how many go away. Count how many are left.

practice.question: Look at 6 − 2 = 4. How many go away?
practice.why: The number after − is how many go away. That is 2.
wrong: 6 is how many you had at first.
4 is how many are left.
You added 6 and 2. The number after − goes away.

practice.question: You have 4 balloons. 2 fly away. Which one shows this?
practice.why: You had 4. 2 go away. Count what is left: 1, 2. So 4 − 2 = 2.
wrong: Fly away means take away, so use −, not +.
The first number is how many you had. You had 4, not 2.
2 balloons went away, so fewer than 4 are left.

rounds.question: What does the sign − mean?
rounds.why: The sign − is called minus. It means take away.
wrong: Put together is what + means.
Makes is what = means.
Count on is for adding. Minus means take away.

rounds.question: What is 3 − 2?
rounds.why: You had 3. 2 go away. 1 is left. So 3 − 2 = 1.
wrong: You put 3 and 2 together. Minus means take away.
You did not take the 2 away.
2 is how many go away. Count what is left.

rounds.question: Look at 7 − 3 = 4. How many are left?
rounds.why: The number after = is how many are left. Here it is 4.
wrong: 7 is how many you had.
3 is how many go away.
You added 7 and 3. The number after = is how many are left.

rounds.question: 6 fish are in a pond. 1 fish swims away. Which one shows this?
rounds.why: There were 6. 1 goes away. 5 are left. So 6 − 1 = 5.
wrong: The fish swims away. That is minus, not plus.
The first number is how many there were: 6, not 1.
1 fish went away, so fewer than 6 are left.

rounds.question: How do we read 5 − 2 = 3?
rounds.why: − is read minus and = is read equals. So it is 5 minus 2 equals 3.
wrong: The sign − is called minus, not plus.
Read the signs too: − is minus and = is equals.
The signs are in the wrong places. − comes first, then =.

rounds.question: What is 6 − 3?
rounds.why: You had 6. 3 go away. Count what is left: 3. So 6 − 3 = 3.
wrong: You put 6 and 3 together. Minus means take away.
You did not take the 3 away.
You took away only 2. Take away 3.

rounds.question: Look at 8 − 5 = 3. How many did you have at first?
rounds.why: The first number is how many you had. Here it is 8.
wrong: 5 is how many go away.
3 is how many are left.
You added 8 and 5. The first number is how many you had.

rounds.question: Anu has 7 laddus. She gives 2 laddus to Ravi. Which one shows this?
rounds.why: She had 7. 2 go away. 5 are left. So 7 − 2 = 5.
wrong: She gives laddus away. That is minus, not plus.
The first number is how many she had: 7, not 2.
2 laddus went away, so fewer than 7 are left.

entries.concept: random variable X, P(X = k), a probability distribution, and success/failure trials
entries.evidence: The first class 12 probability lesson begins 'X has a binomial distribution with n = 3 and p = 4/7. Find P(X ≤ 1)' and later uses E(X); what X, a distribution or E(X) is comes only in the later random-variables skill.

screens.title: A random variable: a number that depends on chance
text: Toss two coins and count the heads. Before you toss, you do not know the count. It could be 0, 1 or 2. A number like this, decided by chance, is called a random variable. We name it with a capital letter, usually X.
P(X = 1) means 'the probability that the count is 1'. P(X ≤ 1) means 'the probability that the count is 1 or less', so you add P(X = 0) and P(X = 1).
The list of every value of X with its probability is called the probability distribution of X. The probabilities in it always add up to 1.
The mean of X, written E(X), is the average value you would get over very many tries. Multiply each value by its probability and add.

check.question: For the two coins, what is P(X ≥ 1), the probability of at least one head?

screens.ask: Toss two coins. X is the number of heads. Find its probabilities, P(X ≤ 1) and E(X).

why: Each coin can land two ways, so 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes.
Count the outcomes with that many heads, out of 4.
"At most 1 head" means 0 heads or 1 head: add them.
Each value times its probability, added: the average number of heads over many tosses.

screens.title: Success, failure and the binomial pattern
text: Many experiments repeat the same simple try again and again: toss a coin, plant a seed, take a shot at goal. Each try is called a trial.

Suppose each trial has only two results. We call one 'success' and the other 'failure'. The probability of success is p. The probability of failure is q = 1 − p. The trials are independent: one does not change the chance in the next.
Let X be the number of successes in n trials. Then X is said to have a binomial distribution with n and p.
To get exactly k successes: one fixed order has probability p multiplied k times and q multiplied (n − k) times. There are nCk such orders. Multiply the two.

check.question: A seed sprouts with probability p = 3/4. What is q, the probability that it does not sprout?

screens.ask: Two tosses, success = head. Find P(exactly 1 head) by the binomial rule.

why: n trials, p the chance of success each time, q = 1 − p the chance of failure.
One success and one failure: multiply their chances.
The head can be on toss 1 or toss 2.
The same as counting outcomes directly: the rule works.

practice.question: Three coins are tossed and X is the number of heads. What is X called?
practice.why: X is a number decided by chance, so it is a random variable.
wrong: A trial is one try of the experiment, such as one toss.
The distribution is the list of all values of X with their probabilities, not X itself.
The mean E(X) is the long-run average of X, not X itself.

practice.question: X takes only the values 0, 1 and 2. P(X = 0) = 0.2 and P(X = 1) = 0.5. What is P(X = 2)?
practice.why: The probabilities add up to 1, so P(X = 2) = 1 − 0.2 − 0.5 = 0.3.
wrong: 0.7 is P(X = 0) + P(X = 1); subtract it from 1.
It need not match P(X = 1); the three probabilities must add up to 1.
1 is the total of all the probabilities, not the share of one value.

practice.question: P(X = 0) = 0.1, P(X = 1) = 0.3 and P(X = 2) = 0.6. What is P(X ≤ 1)?
wrong: That is only P(X = 1); 'or less' also includes X = 0.
That is P(X ≥ 1) = 0.3 + 0.6; ≤ means 1 or less.
That is P(X = 2), which is more than 1, not 1 or less.

practice.question: A shot at goal scores with probability p = 1/3. Two independent shots are taken. What is the probability of exactly one goal?
wrong: That is one order only; goal-miss and miss-goal are 2 orders.
That is p × p, the probability of two goals.
You doubled p; multiply p and q for one order, then by the 2 orders.

rounds.question: What does P(X = 2) mean?
options: The probability that X is 2 or less
rounds.why: P(X = 2) is read 'the probability that the value of X is 2'.
wrong: P stands for probability; nothing is multiplied.
X is decided by chance; P(X = 2) tells how likely the value 2 is.
'2 or less' is written P(X ≤ 2).

rounds.question: X takes only the values 1, 2 and 3. P(X = 1) = 0.4 and P(X = 3) = 0.25. What is P(X = 2)?
rounds.why: The probabilities add up to 1: 1 − 0.4 − 0.25 = 0.35.
wrong: 0.65 is the sum of the other two; subtract it from 1.
You subtracted 0.25 from 0.4; subtract both from 1.
1 is the total of all three probabilities, not P(X = 2).

rounds.question: P(X = 0) = 0.5, P(X = 1) = 0.3 and P(X = 2) = 0.2. What is the mean E(X)?
wrong: You averaged the values 0, 1, 2; each must be multiplied by its probability.
You added the values; multiply each by its probability first.
You added 0.3 and 0.2 without multiplying 0.2 by its value 2.

rounds.question: A seed sprouts with probability p = 3/4. Two seeds are planted, independently. What is the probability that both sprout?
rounds.why: Two successes in two trials: p × p = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16. There is only one order, 2C2 = 1.
wrong: 3/8 is the probability of exactly one sprouting: 2 × 3/4 × 1/4.
3/4 is for one seed; both must sprout, so multiply.
You added; a probability cannot be more than 1. Multiply for 'both'.

rounds.question: In a trial the probability of success is p. What is q?
rounds.why: q = 1 − p is the probability of failure.
wrong: The number of trials is n.
p × p is the chance of two successes in a row, not q.
The number of successes is the random variable X.

rounds.question: A fair dice is rolled 5 times. Success means rolling a six. X is the number of sixes. What are n and p?
rounds.why: There are 5 trials, so n = 5. A six has probability 1/6 on each roll, so p = 1/6.
wrong: You swapped them: 5 is the number of rolls and 6 the number of faces.
5/6 is q, the probability of not rolling a six.
Each roll is a trial, and there are 5 of them.

rounds.question: P(X = 0) = 0.2, P(X = 1) = 0.3, P(X = 2) = 0.4 and P(X = 3) = 0.1. What is P(X ≤ 2)?
wrong: 0.4 is only P(X = 2); '2 or less' includes 0 and 1 as well.
You left out P(X = 2); ≤ includes the value 2 itself.
0.1 is P(X = 3), the part that is not included.

rounds.question: A bulb is faulty with probability 1/5. Three bulbs are tested, independently. What is the probability that exactly one is faulty?
wrong: That is one fixed order only; there are 3C1 = 3 orders.
You multiplied 3 by 1/5 and left out the two good bulbs, each 4/5.
That is the probability that all three are faulty.

entries.concept: the notation nCr (number of ways to choose r things from n)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Probability by counting selections' says each selection is 'counted with ⁿCᵣ' and its example writes 'All selections: 8C2 = 28' with no explanation of the symbol or how to work it out.

screens.title: Choosing a group: nCr
text: Four friends A, B, C and D. Two must fetch the carrom board. The pairs are AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD: 6 pairs. AB and BA are the same pair.

check.question: What is 3C2? (Hint: how many pairs can you make from A, B, C?)

screens.ask: In how many ways can 2 bulbs be chosen from {@n}? Find {n}C2.

steps.do: Top: count down from {n}, two numbers.
why: There are {n} ways to pick the first bulb and {n1} ways to pick the second.
Bulb A then B is the same pair as B then A. Each pair was counted twice.
So there are {c} different pairs. In a choice, order does not matter: that is what C means.

after: nCr is the number of ways to choose r things from n when order does not matter. Say it n choose r. The friends gave 4C2 = 6.
The rule: multiply r numbers counting down from n, then divide by r × (r − 1) × … × 1.

practice.question: How is 5C2 read?
practice.why: 5C2 is the number of ways to choose 2 things out of 5, read '5 choose 2'.
wrong: The C does not mean multiply; it means choose.
It is not the fraction 5/2; it counts ways of choosing.
The first number is the total and the second is how many are chosen.

practice.question: What is 5C2?
practice.why: Two numbers counting down from 5: 5 × 4 = 20. Divide by 2 × 1 = 2. 20 ÷ 2 = 10.
wrong: You forgot to divide by 2 × 1; 20 counts each pair twice.
You added 5 and 2; use (5 × 4) ÷ (2 × 1).
You subtracted 2 from 5; use (5 × 4) ÷ (2 × 1).

practice.question: Seven players are in a club. In how many ways can 2 of them be chosen as a doubles pair?
wrong: 42 counts AB and BA as different; order does not matter, so divide by 2.
You multiplied 7 by 2; use (7 × 6) ÷ (2 × 1).
You added 7 and 2; use (7 × 6) ÷ (2 × 1).

practice.question: A shop has 4 flavours of ice cream. In how many ways can you choose 3 different flavours?
wrong: You forgot to divide by 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
You multiplied 4 by 3; use three numbers counting down, then divide by 3 × 2 × 1.
You divided 24 by 3 only; divide by 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

rounds.question: What does 6C2 count?
options: The ways to choose 2 things out of 6, when order does not matter
The ways to choose 6 things out of 2
The ways to put 6 things in a row
rounds.why: nCr is the number of ways to choose r things out of n when order does not matter. Here n = 6 and r = 2.
wrong: C stands for choose; it is not a times sign.
The first number is the size of the whole group: choose 2 out of 6.
A row has an order; nCr counts groups, where order does not matter.

rounds.question: What is 6C2?
wrong: You forgot to divide 6 × 5 by 2 × 1.
You did 6 × 2; multiply 6 × 5 and divide by 2.
You added 6 and 2; multiply 6 × 5 and divide by 2.

rounds.question: Two letters are chosen from A, B and C. AB and BA are the same pair. What is 3C2?
rounds.why: The pairs are AB, AC and BC: 3 pairs. Also (3 × 2) ÷ (2 × 1) = 3.
wrong: You counted AB and BA as different; order does not matter.
You added 3 and 2; list the pairs or use (3 × 2) ÷ (2 × 1).
You did 3 × 3; the two letters must be different and order does not matter.

rounds.question: A box has 10 different sweets. In how many ways can you choose 2 of them?
wrong: You forgot to divide 10 × 9 by 2 × 1.
You did 10 × 2; multiply 10 × 9 and divide by 2.
You added 10 and 2; multiply 10 × 9 and divide by 2.

rounds.question: Which symbol stands for the number of ways to choose 3 things out of 7?
rounds.why: nCr chooses r things out of n. With n = 7 and r = 3 it is 7C3.
wrong: The size of the whole group, 7, is written first.
7 × 3 is a product, not a count of groups.
7³ means 7 × 7 × 7.

rounds.question: What is 12C1?
rounds.why: nC1 = n: one thing can be chosen from 12 in 12 ways.
wrong: There are 12 different things, so 12 ways to pick one.
66 is 12C2; here only one thing is chosen.
You subtracted 1; any of the 12 things can be chosen.

rounds.question: What is 6C3?
wrong: You forgot to divide 6 × 5 × 4 by 3 × 2 × 1.
You divided by 3 only; divide by 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
You did 6 × 3; multiply 6 × 5 × 4 and divide by 6.

rounds.question: A test paper has 9 questions. You must answer any 2 of them. In how many ways can you choose the 2 questions?
wrong: You forgot to divide 9 × 8 by 2 × 1.
You did 9 × 2; multiply 9 × 8 and divide by 2.
You added 9 and 2; multiply 9 × 8 and divide by 2.

entries.concept: a continuous random variable and why probability becomes an area under a density curve
entries.evidence: The lesson opens with 'probability is AREA under the density curve: P(b ≤ X ≤ c) is the integral of f(x)' without showing what a continuous random variable is or what the height f(x) of a density means.

screens.title: When X can be any number in a range
text: A bus comes some time in the next 10 minutes, every moment equally likely. X is your wait in minutes. X can be 3.5 or 7.25: any number from 0 to 10. It is a continuous random variable.
There are endlessly many values, so we ask for the chance that X falls in an interval.
We draw a curve y = f(x), the probability density function. The probability that X is between two numbers is the area under the curve between them.
The curve is never below the axis, and the whole area under it is 1, because X must land somewhere. The integral of f is the tool that measures such areas.

check.question: For the same bus, what is P(0 ≤ X ≤ 5), the probability of waiting at most 5 minutes?

screens.ask: f(x) = 1/10 from 0 to 10. Find P({@b} ≤ X ≤ {@c}).

why: Every moment is equally likely, so the graph is flat.
For any probability density, the total area must be 1: the bus surely comes.
For a continuous X, probability is the area under f between the two values.

screens.note: Make the first number smaller than the second.

practice.question: Your waiting time X can be any number from 0 to 10 minutes, such as 3.5 or 7.25. What kind of variable is X?
options: A random variable with only the values 0, 1, ..., 10
practice.why: X can take any number in a range, not just separate values, so it is a continuous random variable.
wrong: X is not limited to whole numbers; it can be 3.5 or 7.25.
The density function is the curve f(x) drawn over the values of X, not X itself.
A constant never changes; X depends on chance.

practice.question: What is the whole area under a probability density curve?
practice.why: X must land somewhere, so the total probability, the whole area, is exactly 1.
wrong: An area of 0 would mean X can never happen; the total probability is 1.
10 was the width of the bus interval; its height 1/10 makes the area 10 × 1/10 = 1.
The shape can differ, but every density curve has total area exactly 1.

practice.question: f(x) = 1/4 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, a flat line. What is P(1 ≤ X ≤ 3)?
practice.why: The area is a rectangle 2 wide (from 1 to 3) and 1/4 high: 2 × 1/4 = 1/2.
wrong: 2 is only the width; multiply by the height 1/4. A probability cannot be more than 1.
1/4 is only the height of the curve; probability is the area, width × height.
That is the area from 0 to 3; start from 1.

practice.question: A train comes at some moment in the next 20 minutes, every moment equally likely, so f(x) = 1/20 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 20. What is the probability of waiting 15 minutes or more?
practice.why: From 15 to 20 is a rectangle 5 wide and 1/20 high: 5 × 1/20 = 1/4.
wrong: That is the area from 0 to 15, waiting at most 15 minutes.
5 is only the width; multiply by the height 1/20.
1/20 is only the height of the curve; probability is the area.

rounds.question: The curve y = f(x) whose area gives probabilities for a continuous random variable is called ...
rounds.why: The curve drawn over the possible values of X is the probability density function.
wrong: The continuous random variable is X itself, not the curve.
The mean is one number, an average value.
An interval is a stretch of values, such as 2 to 5.

rounds.question: For a continuous random variable X, how is the probability that X lies between b and c found?
options: The height of the curve at b
The height at c minus the height at b
The area under the density curve from b to c
rounds.why: The probability that X lies between b and c is the area under the curve from b to c.
wrong: A height is not a probability; the area over the interval is.
Subtracting heights does not give the probability; measure the area.
The width alone is not enough; multiply by the height to get the area.

rounds.question: f(x) = 1/5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, a flat line. What is P(1 ≤ X ≤ 4)?
rounds.why: A rectangle 4 − 1 = 3 wide and 1/5 high: 3 × 1/5 = 3/5.
wrong: 1/5 is only the height; multiply by the width 3.
3 is only the width; multiply by the height 1/5.
You used the width from 0 to 4; the interval starts at 1.

rounds.question: A phone call will come at some moment in the next 30 minutes, every moment equally likely, so f(x) = 1/30 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 30. What is the probability that it comes in the first 10 minutes?
rounds.why: A rectangle 10 wide and 1/30 high: 10 × 1/30 = 1/3.
wrong: 1/30 is only the height; multiply by the width 10.
2/3 is the probability of the last 20 minutes.
10 is only the width; a probability cannot be more than 1.

rounds.question: Why can we not list a probability for each single value of a continuous random variable?
options: Its probabilities add up to more than 1
There are endlessly many possible values
Its values are only whole numbers
rounds.why: X can be any number in a range, so there are endlessly many values. We use intervals instead.
wrong: The values need not be negative: a waiting time is 0 or more.
The whole area, the total probability, is still exactly 1.
Whole-number values could be listed; a continuous X takes every number in a range.

rounds.question: A density curve is a flat line over 0 ≤ x ≤ 8 and zero elsewhere. What must its height be?
rounds.why: The whole area must be 1. A rectangle 8 wide needs height 1/8: 8 × 1/8 = 1.
wrong: Height 8 would give area 8 × 8 = 64, not 1.
Height 1 would give area 8, not 1; it is the area that must be 1.
Height 1/2 would give area 4, not 1.

rounds.question: A curve dips below the axis for some values of x. Can it be a probability density function?
options: Yes, if the whole area is 1
No, because a density curve must be flat
No, a density curve is never below the axis
rounds.why: A probability density curve is never below the axis, since a probability cannot be negative.
wrong: Area 1 is one rule; the curve must also never go below the axis.
Two rules must hold: never below the axis, and whole area 1.
A density curve need not be flat; its height shows where X is more crowded.

rounds.question: A lift will arrive at some moment in the next 40 seconds, every moment equally likely, so f(x) = 1/40 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 40. What is the probability that it arrives between 5 and 35 seconds from now?
rounds.why: A rectangle 35 − 5 = 30 wide and 1/40 high: 30 × 1/40 = 3/4.
wrong: 30 is only the width; multiply by the height 1/40.
1/40 is only the height; multiply by the width 30.
You used the width from 0 to 35; the interval starts at 5.

entries.concept: what probability is, the notation P(event), and 'equally likely'
entries.evidence: The class 6 lesson 'Probability from the sample space of two dice or spinners' uses 'P(event) = pairs that fit ÷ all pairs' and 'equally likely', but probability itself is first explained in class 7 (chance-language).

screens.title: Measuring chance with a fraction
text: A bag has red and green sweets. You take one without looking. Which colour will it be? You cannot be sure, but one may be more likely.

check.question: A fair coin has two sides, head and tail. What is P(head)?

screens.ask: The bag has {@r} red {r|sweet|sweets} and {@g} green. Find P(red) and P(green).

why: Each sweet has the same chance of being picked.
These are the sweets that fit red.
Probability = sweets that fit ÷ all the sweets.
{r}/{t} + {g}/{t} = 1, because some sweet is always picked.

after: Probability is a number that says how likely something is.
Each sweet that could come out is called an outcome. Here each outcome is equally likely: each sweet has the same chance.
'The sweet is red' is called an event. P(red) is read 'the probability of red'. It is 0 if the event cannot happen and 1 if it must.

practice.question: What does P(blue) mean?
options: The number of all the outcomes
practice.why: P(event) is short for 'the probability of the event', so P(blue) is the probability of blue.
wrong: That is only the top of the fraction; P(blue) divides it by all the outcomes.
That is only the bottom of the fraction; P(blue) is fitting outcomes ÷ all outcomes.
P does not mean certain; an event that must happen has probability 1.

practice.question: A bag has 2 red balls and 3 yellow balls. You take one without looking. What is P(red)?
practice.why: All outcomes: 2 + 3 = 5. Outcomes that fit 'red': 2. P(red) = 2/5.
wrong: You divided by the yellow balls; divide by all the outcomes, 5.
That is P(yellow); 2 outcomes fit 'red'.
Two colours do not mean two equally likely outcomes; count the balls: 2 out of 5.

practice.question: A bag has only 4 green marbles. You take one without looking. What is P(red)?
practice.why: No outcome fits 'red', so P(red) = 0 ÷ 4 = 0. The event cannot happen.
wrong: 1 means the event must happen; that is P(green) here.
1/4 is the chance of one particular marble; no marble is red.
4 is the number of marbles; a probability is never more than 1.

practice.question: A fair dice has six faces numbered 1 to 6. You roll it once. What is P(4)?
practice.why: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and 1 of them is the face 4. P(4) = 1/6.
wrong: Only one face shows 4; the number on the face is not the count of outcomes.
You divided by the face number; divide by all the outcomes, 6.
4 is the face, not a probability; a probability is never more than 1.

rounds.question: Each thing that can happen, such as each sweet that could be picked, is called ...
rounds.why: Each thing that can happen is called an outcome.
wrong: An event is the thing we are hoping for, such as 'the sweet is red'.
Probability is the number that says how likely something is.
A fraction is how we write a probability, not the thing that happens.

rounds.question: A box has 5 blue pens and 2 black pens. You take one without looking. What is P(black)?
rounds.why: All the outcomes: 5 + 2 = 7 pens. Outcomes that fit 'black': 2. P(black) = 2/7.
wrong: You divided by the blue pens; divide by all 7 pens.
5/7 is P(blue).
There are two colours, but 7 pens: the outcomes are the pens.

rounds.question: A bag has only 6 red beads. You take one without looking. What is P(red)?
rounds.why: All 6 outcomes fit 'red': 6 ÷ 6 = 1. The event must happen, so its probability is 1.
wrong: A probability is never more than 1; divide 6 by all 6 outcomes.
1/6 is the chance of one particular bead; every bead is red.
0 is for an event that cannot happen; here red must happen.

rounds.question: A spinner has 8 equal parts numbered 1 to 8. You spin it once. What is P(5)?
rounds.why: There are 8 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 5. P(5) = 1/8.
wrong: Only one part shows 5, so one outcome fits, not five.
Divide by all 8 outcomes, not by the number 5.
A probability is a number from 0 to 1, not the number on the spinner.

rounds.question: What does 'equally likely' mean?
options: Each outcome has the same chance
The outcomes all look the same
rounds.why: Equally likely means each outcome has the same chance of happening.
wrong: Only one outcome happens each time; they just have the same chance.
One of the outcomes will happen; each has the same chance.
It is about chance, not looks: a red and a green sweet can be equally likely.

rounds.question: A tray has 4 laddus and 6 jalebis. You take one sweet without looking. What is P(laddu)?
rounds.why: All the outcomes: 4 + 6 = 10 sweets. Outcomes that fit 'laddu': 4. P(laddu) = 4/10.
wrong: You divided by the jalebis; divide by all 10 sweets.
6/10 is P(jalebi).
All 4 laddus fit the event, out of 10 sweets.

rounds.question: A bag has 7 white buttons and 1 black button. Arun says: 'There are two colours, so P(black) = 1/2.' What is P(black) really?
rounds.why: The outcomes are the 8 buttons, each equally likely. Only 1 is black, so P(black) = 1/8.
wrong: The two colours are not equally likely; count the buttons.
Divide by all 8 buttons, not only the white ones.
7/8 is P(white).

rounds.question: The names of 5 children, Asha among them, are written on 5 slips and put in a bowl. One slip is drawn without looking. What is P(Asha)?
rounds.why: There are 5 equally likely slips and 1 of them says Asha. P(Asha) = 1/5.
wrong: 5 is the number of outcomes; a probability is never more than 1.
Count Asha's slip among the outcomes too: there are 5 slips.
4/5 is the probability that it is not Asha.

entries.concept: the factorial sign (!)
entries.evidence: The worked example of 'Counting arrangements that meet a condition' says 'the other 2 can be arranged in 2! ways' and the sign ! is never explained.

screens.title: What 3! means
text: Three friends, A, B and C, stand in a row for a photo. How many different rows can they make?

check.question: What is 2! ?
check.answer: 2 (2 × 1). Two people can stand in a row in 2 ways.

screens.ask: In how many orders can A, B and C stand in a row?

why: Start with each letter in front and list the two ways to finish.
3 choices for first, then 2 for second, then 1 left.
3! (three factorial) counts the orders of 3 things.

after: 3 × 2 × 1 comes up so often that it has a sign. 3! means 3 × 2 × 1, said 'three factorial'. Here ! is a maths sign, not surprise.
n! counts the ways to put n different things in a row.

practice.question: How is 5! read?
practice.why: The sign ! after a number is read 'factorial'.
wrong: Squared is the small raised 2; the sign ! means factorial.
Here ! is a maths sign, not surprise.

practice.question: What is 5! ?
wrong: You added 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1; factorial multiplies.
You stopped at 5 × 4; keep multiplying down to 1.
That is 5 × 5; factorial multiplies 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.

practice.question: Which of these is the same as 4! ?
practice.why: 4! means multiply 4 by every counting number below it, down to 1.
wrong: 4 × 4 is 4 squared, not 4 factorial.
Factorial multiplies the numbers; it does not add them.
Do not stop at 3; go all the way down to 1.

practice.question: In how many ways can 4 different books be put in a row on a shelf?
practice.why: n! is the number of ways to put n different things in a row: 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
wrong: 4 is only the number of choices for the first place; multiply by the choices for the other places.
You added 4 + 3 + 2 + 1; multiply instead.
That is 4 × 4; after a book is placed, one fewer is left for the next place.

rounds.question: What does n! count?
options: The number of ways to put n different things in a row
The number n, said with surprise
rounds.why: n! is the number of ways to put n different things in a row.
wrong: n multiplied by itself is n², the square.
n added to itself is 2 × n.
The ! here is a maths sign, not surprise.

rounds.question: How is 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 written with the factorial sign?
rounds.why: 4! means 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, which is the same product as 1 × 2 × 3 × 4.
wrong: 4² means 4 × 4.
10 is the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + 4; the sign goes after the biggest number, 4.
24 is the value of the product; it is written 4!.

rounds.question: What is 2! ?
wrong: You did 2 × 2; 2! means 2 × 1.
You added 2 and 1; 2! means 2 × 1.
You left out the 2; 2! means 2 × 1.

rounds.question: 5! = 120. In how many ways can 6 children stand in a line?
rounds.why: 6 children can stand in a row in 6! ways. 6! = 6 × 5! = 6 × 120 = 720.
wrong: You added 6 to 120; 6! is 6 times 5!.
You did 6 × 6; the number of rows is 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
You added 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1; factorial multiplies.

rounds.question: Which sign is short for 3 × 2 × 1?
wrong: 3² means 3 × 3.
3 × 1 leaves out the 2.
6 is the value of 3 × 2 × 1; it is written 3!.

rounds.question: Three friends stand in a row. The first place can be filled in 3 ways. In how many ways can the second place then be filled?
rounds.why: One friend has taken the first place, so 2 friends are left for the second place.
wrong: One friend is already in the first place, so only 2 are left.
1 friend is left only for the last place.
6 is the number of whole rows, 3 × 2 × 1.

rounds.question: What is 3! + 2! ?
wrong: 120 is 5!; work out each factorial first, then add.
You added 3 and 2 and forgot the factorial signs.
You multiplied 6 by 2; the sign between them is +.

rounds.question: Amma has 3 different bowls: rice, dal and curd. In how many orders can she serve them one after another?
rounds.why: 3 different things can be put in order in 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways.
wrong: 3 is only the number of choices for the first bowl.
You did 3 × 3; after the first bowl only 2 are left.
There is more than one order: rice first, or dal first, or curd first.

entries.concept: the distance between two points from their coordinates
entries.evidence: The 'shape of three points' lesson says 'find PQ² with (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²', but the distance formula is only taught in class 9 (MATH.coordinate.distance).

screens.title: How far apart are two points?
text: On a grid, to go from P(1, 2) to Q(4, 6) you can walk 3 steps across (from 1 to 4) and then 4 steps up (from 2 to 6). The straight path PQ is the slanting side of a right triangle whose other sides are 3 and 4.
Pythagoras' theorem gives the slanting side: PQ² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, so PQ = 5.

In general, write the points as (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂). The small 1 and 2 are only labels: 'first point' and 'second point'. The step across is x₂ − x₁ and the step up is y₂ − y₁. So PQ² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². A negative step does not matter, because squaring makes it positive.

check.question: How far is the point (6, 8) from (0, 0)?

screens.ask: Find the distance from P(1, 2) to Q(4, 6).

why: Subtract the matching numbers.
Across and up meet at a right angle. PQ is the longest side.
Check it: 5 × 5 = 25, so PQ is 5.

practice.question: In the point (x₁, y₁), what does the small 1 tell us?
options: It is a label for the first point
practice.why: The small 1 and 2 are only labels: 'first point' and 'second point'.
wrong: The small 1 is not a multiplier; it only names the first point.
Nothing is subtracted; the small 1 only names the first point.
A power is written raised, above the letter; this small 1 below is only a label.

practice.question: How far apart are A(2, 3) and B(7, 15)?
wrong: You added the steps 5 and 12; square them, add, then take the square root.
That is AB²; take the square root to get AB.
You subtracted the steps; use 5² + 12² and take the square root.

practice.question: How far apart are P(5, 2) and Q(1, 5)?
wrong: You added the steps 4 and 3; square them, add, then take the square root.
That is PQ²; take the square root.
You took (−4)² as −16; squaring makes a negative step positive, so 16 + 9 = 25.

practice.question: On a map grid a school is at (1, 2) and a park is at (9, 8). How far is the straight path between them, in grid units?
practice.why: Across: 9 − 1 = 8. Up: 8 − 2 = 6. Distance² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100, so the distance is 10.
wrong: That is the walk 8 across and 6 up; the straight path is the slanting side.
That is the distance squared; take the square root.
You subtracted the steps 8 and 6; use 8² + 6² and take the square root.

rounds.question: To go from (x₁, y₁) to (x₂, y₂), what is the step across?
rounds.why: The step across is the change in x: x₂ − x₁.
wrong: y₂ − y₁ is the step up.
The step is a difference, not a product.
The step is a difference, not a sum.

rounds.question: How far apart are A(0, 2) and B(8, 17)?
wrong: You added the two steps; square them, add, then take the root.
289 is AB²; take the square root.
You subtracted the steps; square them and add.

rounds.question: How far apart are P(2, 5) and Q(2, 11)?
wrong: 36 is PQ²; take the square root.
0 is only the step across; the step up is 6.
You added 2 and 11; use the steps 0 across and 6 up.

rounds.question: On a field grid a tree is at (3, 2) and a well is at (12, 14). How far is the straight path between them, in grid units?
rounds.why: Across: 12 − 3 = 9. Up: 14 − 2 = 12. Path² = 81 + 144 = 225, so the path is 15.
wrong: You added the two steps; the straight path is the slanting side.
225 is the square of the path; take the square root.
You subtracted the steps; square them and add.

rounds.question: P and Q are joined by a step across and a step up. Which side of the right triangle is the straight path PQ?
rounds.why: The straight path PQ is the slanting side of the right triangle whose other sides are the two steps.
wrong: The step across is one of the two sides at the right angle.
The step up is one of the two sides at the right angle.
The slanting side is the longest side, not the shortest.

rounds.question: How far apart are A(3, 3) and B(4, 4)?
rounds.why: Across: 1. Up: 1. AB² = 1² + 1² = 2, so AB = √2.
wrong: 2 is AB², or the two steps added; take the square root of 2.
1 is only one of the steps; use both steps.
You added the steps and squared; square each step, add, then take the root.

rounds.question: How far apart are A(−1, 2) and B(2, 6)?
wrong: You took the step across as 2 − 1 = 1; it is 2 − (−1) = 3.
You added the steps 3 and 4; square them, add, then take the root.
25 is AB²; take the square root.

rounds.question: On a city grid a bus stop is at (3, 1) and a library is at (15, 17). How far is the straight path between them, in grid units?
rounds.why: Across: 15 − 3 = 12. Up: 17 − 1 = 16. Path² = 144 + 256 = 400, so the path is 20.
wrong: You added the two steps; the straight path is the slanting side.
400 is the square of the path; take the square root.
You subtracted the steps; square them and add.

entries.concept: a letter for an unknown number, and an equation
entries.evidence: The lesson begins 'each fact is one linear equation' and solves 3x + 2y = 163 by 'making coefficients match', but no earlier-class skill teaches equations (solving equations starts in class 6).

screens.title: A letter for a hidden number
text: A shopkeeper says: {@n} pens cost {@t} rupees. The price of one pen is hidden. Call it x.

check.question: x + 5 = 9. What number is x?

screens.ask: {n} pens cost {t} rupees: {n}x = {t}. Find x.

why: {n} pens cost {n} times x. We write that as {n}x.
{n}x means {n} times the hidden number x.
Dividing undoes multiplying.
So one pen costs {p} rupees.

screens.note: Pick a total the pens share equally, like 3 pens for 30 rupees.
after: x is a letter that stands for a number we do not know yet.
A number written next to a letter means multiply. The number in front, here {n}, is called the coefficient.
{n}x = {t} is called an equation: a sentence with = and a hidden number. Solving it means finding the number that makes it true.

screens.title: Two hidden numbers need two facts
text: A pencil costs x rupees. An eraser costs y rupees. Both prices are hidden.
Fact 1: 1 pencil and 1 eraser cost {@s} rupees. So x + y = {s}.
Fact 2: 2 pencils and 1 eraser cost {@t} rupees. So 2x + y = {t}.

check.question: x + y = 10 and x = 6. What is y?

screens.ask: Solve x + y = {s} and 2x + y = {t}.

steps.do: Take the first fact from the second.
why: The y parts are the same, so they cancel. Only x is left.
Put x = {x} into the first fact.
Both facts are true. (x, y) = ({x}, {y}).
